#3200. Apple earnings suggest the iPhone 18 launch strategy is really working

Yesterday’s AAPL earnings report revealed record revenue for a September quarter, and within it was an arguably even more significant record: iPhone revenue.

That’s because this year’s quarter only includes just two new iPhone models compared to the four released last year …

Apple reported fiscal quarter four revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% year on year. Within that was iPhone revenue of $57.58 billion, which was also a quarterly record. What makes this significant is the year-on-year comparison, when you consider the new iPhone launch revenue included within each quarter.

(Although the iPhone Duo was announced at the same time, pre-orders didn’t open until October, so none of this revenue is included in Apple’s fiscal Q4.)

The main thing that changed this year is that Apple didn’t launch a base model iPhone 18 alongside the Pro models: that launch won’t happen until early next year. The biggest factor in this decision was likely component shortages, Apple wanting to ensure that it could fulfill demand for premium models, but the revenue figures suggest that the timings also influenced purchase decisions.

Many people upgrade their iPhones on a fixed cycle, be that every one, two, or three years – and that cycle begins each September. When upgrade time rolled around and there was no base model iPhone 18 available, it seems likely that a significant number of those who would have bought it decided to instead opt for the iPhone 18 Pro rather than wait.

That may suggest rather modest sales of the base model iPhone 18 when it rolls around, but if Apple managed to persuade a significant number of would-be buyers to opt for a more expensive model, the company won’t be shedding any tears about that.

Of course, there are a couple of other factors in the mix here. First, the iPhone 17 proved extremely popular and remains on sale today, so it will have contributed something to this year’s Q4 revenue. Second, Apple cited revenue rather than profit, and the $100 price increase for this year’s Pro models will played a role. But overall I do think it paints a very encouraging picture for this split launch strategy.

What’s your take? Do you think it reflects well on iPhone 18 Pro sales, or do you think it can be explained away by the price increase and continuing popularity of the iPhone 17? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3199. Prediction: Rigetti Computing Stock Is Going to Sink After Nov. 10

Meaningful revenue from quantum computers could be many years away.

Quantum computers have the potential to outperform traditional computers in data-intensive areas like science and cryptography, because they can use a concept called superposition to simulate several solutions to a given problem at the same time. However, even the most sophisticated quantum computers available today still make too many errors to solve real-world problems.

As one of the industry leaders, Rigetti Computing (RGTI -5.16%) is making strides, but the company is burning through a ton of cash because it's investing aggressively in research and development while bringing in minimal revenue. That isn't a very attractive proposition for investors, which explains why Rigetti stock has plummeted by 80% from its all-time high.

However, the stock continues to trade at a sky-high valuation, which leaves the door open to more potential downside. Rigetti is scheduled to release its operating results for the third quarter of 2026 (ended Sept. 30) after the market closes on Nov. 10, and here's why I predict they could be a negative catalyst for the stock.

Rigetti has a massive advantage over many other companies in the quantum computing space because it built its own supply chain, which means it can bring new systems to market much faster. It has its own fabrication facility to produce chips, its own quantum programming language, and even its own cloud computing platform where it rents quantum capacity to enterprises for a fee.

Rigetti developed one of the industry's largest multichip quantum computers called Cepheus-1-108Q. It has a single-qubit gate fidelity of 99.9%, meaning it typically makes one error for every 1,000 quantum operations. However, its 2-qubit gate fidelity is just 99.1%, implying nine errors for every 1,000 operations. Qubits are highly sensitive to interference, so getting two of them to work together in harmony is one of the industry's biggest challenges.

Solving important real-world problems might require an error rate of one in a billion, so although Cepheus-1-108Q is a great system by current standards, it still isn't very useful. Rigetti thinks it will take another three years to achieve a 2-qubit gate fidelity of 99.9%, because it will require better chip designs, materials, and production processes. Even then, it probably won't be solving humanity's most pressing issues.

Ark Investment Management, which was founded by seasoned tech investor Cathie Wood, predicts the industry could be up to 40 years away from delivering truly disruptive quantum computers. Bigger financial investments and unexpected breakthroughs could accelerate that timeline, but companies like Rigetti are facing a long journey.

Rigetti generated $5.1 million in revenue during the second quarter of 2026 (ended June 30). Although it was an eye-popping 185% increase from the year-ago period, it was a tiny amount of money for a company that currently has a market capitalization of $3.7 billion.

According to Wall Street's consensus estimate (provided by Yahoo! Finance), Rigetti might have generated just $3.7 million in revenue during the third quarter. It would be an 88% increase year over year, but it would represent a sequential decline (compared to the second quarter).

The bottom line might be an even bigger concern for shareholders. Rigetti's second-quarter operating expenses of $30.2 million eclipsed its revenue, contributing to a $52.6 million net loss. The company might have been even deeper in the red during the third quarter if its revenue declined sequentially, especially if overall expenses increased. We will officially find out on Nov. 10.

Rigetti had $541 million in cash and cash equivalents on hand as of June 30, so it can sustain its losses for the foreseeable future. However, given how long it might take to develop truly useful quantum computers, the company might have to tap investors for more money in the future.

Based on Rigetti's modest revenue and its sizable market cap, its stock is trading at a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 278, making it a whopping 44 times as expensive as the Nasdaq-100 index. In other words, it's heavily overvalued compared to a group of America's highest quality technology companies.

Even if we value Rigetti stock based on Wall Street's 2027 revenue estimate of $43.9 million, it still has a hefty forward P/S ratio of 85.

Even if Rigetti stock plummets by 90% from last Friday's closing price of $11.25, it will still be more expensive than the Nasdaq-100 by this metric. I'm not predicting a decline of that magnitude, because many investors are likely to hold quantum stocks because of the technology's significant long-term potential.

Nevertheless, there could be significant downside ahead, and recent history suggests there won't be anything in Rigetti's upcoming third-quarter report on Nov. 10 capable of preventing it. In fact, a disappointing set of operating results could actually accelerate the losses for shareholders.

Investors didn’t seem overly happy about yesterday’s Apple earnings call despite the record results. That likely reflects the company’s cautious take on margins in the current quarter, but some have also criticized what they describe as a very “scripted” approach by new CEO John Ternus.

Bloomberg was the biggest critic, describing it as a “timid” performance that left analysts “sorely disappointed” …

Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions.

Lee acknowledged that the slump in pre-market trading will have been largely driven by Apple’s caution about rising expenses in the current quarter. The company said that memory costs were continuing to rise and that building out Siri AI data centers we’re going to add to the RAM bill. But he argued that Ternus missed an opportunity to talk up the company.

In front of Ternus on Monday night was a chance to counteract the gloom and doom by instilling in Wall Street the fundamentals of the Ternus Doctrine — what he sees Apple becoming under his tenure, the “product guy” taking the company to a new era of innovation. Instead, he spoke like a man glancing at the clock and wishing the minutes away.

Fortune’s Sebastian Herrera was less vocal but echoed some of the criticism.

Ternus fielded some questions but also delegated answers to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh and Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan, who Apple said would participate in earnings calls moving forward, something the company hasn’t done for years. Ternus projected confidence on the call, but he appeared to stick mostly to scripted marketing points.

It will of course take Ternus some time to develop his own style when it comes to all of the varied aspects of the role, including addressing analysts in earnings calls, but I thought he took a measured but optimistic approach. Given the famously reticent style of his predecessor, the criticism strikes me as rather odd.

Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks have generated tremendous growth for investors over the past few years. This period represented the early part of the AI boom, as large language models were trained, fueled by powerful chips, and we began to see the potential of AI. Investors rushed to get in on shares of these companies, aiming to bet on technology that would reshape industries and our daily lives.

Over the past year, however, investors have become more cautious about AI stocks. As tech giants from Amazon to Alphabet spend hundreds of billions of dollars on an infrastructure build-out, investors question whether this spending is sustainable and worthwhile considering the future revenue opportunity. This sentiment has weighed on AI stocks this year, causing ups and downs for some and even declines for others.

But this moment of uncertainty also means that certain high-quality AI stocks, ones with bright long-term outlooks, are now trading at reasonable or even cheap valuations. With this in mind, let's check out one of these once-in-a-decade buying opportunities. Here's one AI stock to buy before it soars 60%, according to Wall Street.

This particular stock climbed more than 300% over the past three years, but this year, it's only advanced about 9%. Meanwhile, this player's earnings continue to roar higher. I'm talking about Nvidia (NVDA -1.26%). This tech giant was the star of the earliest stage of the AI boom because its AI chips, known as graphics processing units (GPUs), were the first to market and demonstrated their speed and efficiency. As rivals joined the space, Nvidia's commitment to innovation kept it a step ahead.

Since, the company has added a wide range of products and services to its portfolio, making itself the "go-to" place for anything AI. Nvidia has also developed platforms to serve the needs of specific industries, such as drug development for biotech and pharma companies. And Nvidia has expanded its presence in the AI field, most recently offering to buy the open-source AI platform Hugging Face.

Nvidia's work in AI has resulted in explosive growth in revenue and profit, particularly compared to levels many years ago -- when its GPUs primarily served the video gaming market.

And this has continued through the latest quarter, when Nvidia reported a 100% increase in revenue to $96 billion and a triple-digit gain in net income to $59 billion.

But as I mentioned above, general concerns about tech spending on AI have held Nvidia stock back from the increases investors had grown accustomed to in the earlier stages of the AI boom. The idea is that if cloud giants see that investments aren't translating into strong enough growth, they may slow spending. That could hurt Nvidia's revenue, particularly considering data center makes up more than 90% of it.

Against this backdrop, however, analysts remain optimistic. The average Wall Street estimate calls for a 60% increase in Nvidia stock over the coming 12 months.

Now, here's why I think such a gain is possible. First, Nvidia today is trading at 21x forward earnings estimates, which is a bargain for a company with such market leadership, a solid track record of earnings growth, and long-term prospects that remain positive. Investors may jump to get in on this opportunity.

And this brings me to my second point, and that's the long-term AI story. It's very possible that growth may ebb and flow, and any slowdown could weigh on the stock. But, over time, revenue growth should be significant considering the capabilities of AI and the fact that its rollout to address real-world problems is just beginning. Companies will clearly continue to apply this technology to their situations in order to gain in efficiency, reduce costs, and become more innovative.

All of this means Nvidia stock, well positioned for gains, may be a once-in-a-decade buy right now.

#3194. Opera will run AI locally in your browser now – why that’s a gamechanger and how to try it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Thanks to the newly proposed WebAI web standard, the company will start shipping local AI models with its flagship browser.

Opera just made a bold choice: Thanks to the newly proposed WebAI web standard, the company will soon be shipping local AI models with its browser. By doing so, Opera’s AI ensures that your queries and/or data remain on your machine.

Also: How Opera’s new Air browser helped me to keep calm and surf on

According to Opera, because this new feature uses open-weight AI models, anyone can build on top of those models without running expensive AI infrastructure or paying for every request. That equates to more innovation for the Opera browser.

This is a bigger deal than you might think.

Most browsers include AI that depends on the cloud for responses; a user’s data is not limited to the local machine and could be used by third-party organizations to train LLMs or even build profiles.

Opera aims to resist that trend by leaning into local AI, made possible by open-weight models that have become smaller and more capable, while hardware continues to become more powerful.

“A lot of what people want from AI doesn’t need a data center. Your laptop can already do it, without sending your data anywhere,” said Krystian Kolondra, EVP Browsers and AI at Opera. “We first shipped local models to developers in 2024. Now we’re bringing them to everyone. More models and tools are coming, and you’ll always decide what runs on your machine.”

Opera also plans on bringing more open models optimized for specific devices, as well as more tools to make it easier to build browser experiences on local AI.

WebAI is a newly proposed web standard (backed by companies like Google and Microsoft) that allows websites and extensions to use browser-hosted AI. Opera’s implementation of WebAI is model-agnostic and built around open-weight models, so users can select models from the likes of Google and Apple.

Also: Opera now detects and blocks malicious clipboard content

WebAI is also opt-in; nothing is downloaded until the user does so. Developers can check out example extensions that use WebUI from WebAI: Local AI for the web, now in Opera.

I’ve been a fan of the Opera browser for a long time — it has served as my default for the past five years on Linux, MacOS, and Android.

I’ve seen Opera features come and go, but the good ones always stick around. Opera was one of the first browsers to integrate AI into the UI, making it very easy (and free) to use. The longer I use AI, the more one particular issue has become my calling card — local AI.

I’m a champion of local AI, and that’s the hill I will die on.

The problem thus far is that using local AI with browsers isn’t always easy. Firefox made it possible with Smart Window, but it’s not set up to use local AI by default. (You have to choose a custom provider and have Ollama installed and running on your machine.)

Also: Firefox is the browser to beat right now if you use AI

Opera is ready to make this reality even easier.

To try the local-first version of Opera, do the following:

According to Opera, WebAI is an early preview, available on Windows PC (64-bit, Intel/AMD) and Macs with Apple silicon. It isn’t available on Intel-based Macs, Linux or Windows on Arm.

The surprising truth behind your home's property value and data centers

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As AI drives demand for more computing power, the next wave of development is heading to America's neighborhoods.

According to an April 2026 Pew Research Center analysis, 67% of planned U.S. data centers are located in rural areas, compared with just 13% of facilities already operating. Perhaps more surprisingly, 39% of planned facilities are in counties that don't currently have a single data center. For some states, AI data centers are even on the ballot this Election Day as communities that have never had to consider the effects of a massive computing facility, now could soon face questions about electricity costs, water supplies, noise and property values.

A new analysis from Jones & Swanson brings several of these concerns together, examining how America's expanding data center footprint could affect the people living nearby.

And while the findings raise legitimate questions about the costs of AI infrastructure, they also challenge one common assumption: Living near a data center doesn't necessarily mean your home will lose value.

For homeowners, one of the biggest questions is whether a nearby data center will make their property less desirable.

The answer may be surprising. An August 2026 Realtor.com study examined 43 ZIP codes where large data centers opened between 2019 and 2025. Researchers compared those locations with similar neighborhoods that didn't receive a data center.

The analysis found no statistically significant difference in home price appreciation during the first two years after a facility opened. Oddly enough, homes near newly opened data centers generally gained value at roughly the same rate as comparable homes elsewhere.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Something to note, is that the study examined ZIP-code averages, rather than the experiences of individual properties. It also excluded Texas and 11 other states where transaction prices aren't publicly disclosed, and only tracked home prices for two years following a facility's opening.

There's another reason this matters. Realtor.com found that the median large data center opening in 2026 was located in an area with just 32 residential housing units per square mile, down from 116 in 2017.

As data centers move into less densely populated areas, their impact on individual communities could look different from what researchers have observed so far.

The biggest financial concern may be your electricity bill. Even if a nearby data center doesn't reduce your home's value, there's another potential cost homeowners should consider: electricity.

These facilities need enormous amounts of power to run servers and keep their equipment cool. And as more data centers connect to the grid, utilities may need to build additional power plants, transmission lines and substations.

The question is who ultimately pays for those upgrades. A June 2026 report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates that data centers could account for 9.5% to 15.3% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030, with a central estimate of 11.8%. That's a substantial share of national electricity demand for one category of infrastructure..

Virginia remains America's data center capital, with 674 facilities listed as operating, under construction, planned or land-banked, according to the Jones & Swanson analysis. Texas follows with 537, while California has 296 and Georgia has 276.

The Pew Research Center found that 87% of existing data centers are in urban areas. The pipeline of proposed facilities looks almost completely different, with two-thirds planned for rural locations.

The South and Midwest account for approximately three-quarters of planned facilities, with the South alone representing 48%.

But despite all the water, energy and land use, it's worth remember that not every data center is dedicated to AI. These facilities support everything from cloud storage and websites to streaming services and, yes AI.

If a data center is proposed near your home, there are several things worth investigating before local officials approve the project. Start with electricity costs. Ask your utility or local regulators whether new transmission lines, substations or generation capacity will be required and how those expenses will be allocated.

Water use is another important consideration. Developers should be able to explain where cooling water will come from, how much the facility expects to use and what happens if the community experiences a drought.

Residents can also ask about noise limits, backup generator testing, construction hours and whether landscaped buffers or other protections will separate the facility from nearby homes. Much of this information may be available through local zoning applications, planning board meetings, utility filings or environmental permit reviews.

It's also worth distinguishing between a project that has been proposed and one that has received all the necessary approvals. As the Pew research shows, a substantial portion of the country's future data center footprint remains in the planning stages.

America's AI boom is becoming a physical infrastructure boom, and its effects are reaching well beyond Silicon Valley and Northern Virginia. For homeowners, the latest research offers both reassurance and reasons to keep paying attention.

The evidence so far doesn't show that large data centers consistently reduce nearby home values, but questions about electricity costs, water demand, noise and infrastructure spending remain important, particularly as development moves into rural communities.

The game is back on for AMD vs Intel handheld gaming

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AMD finally dropped FSR 4 for integrated silicon — officially bringing next-generation upscaling to the Z Extreme handhelds and Strix Halo laptops. It’s built to be AMD’s silver bullet against Nvidia’s DLSS. A massive, free software upgrade that magically boosts picture quality and hands you more frames per second.

So over the past week, I’ve updated my ROG Xbox Ally X20 and TUF Gaming A14 with the new drivers and fired up the benchmarking tools to see what AMD has cooked.

And what I found completely breaks the current narrative. We’re all trained to think a new version of AI game scaling tech will send your frame rates skyrocketing. If you come in with that assumption, you’ll be left disappointed.

However, if you understand the optical illusion AMD has actually pulled off here (and how Performance mode is now the new Balanced), it completely changes how you will game on Team Red’s silicon.

If you have a compatible AMD handheld or APU, they have thankfully baked this early-access driver directly into their software. Here is how to activate it on the ROG Xbox Ally X20:

Open Armory Crate and navigate to the Update Center. Go to the Preview Updates tab and install the new AMD Radeon graphics driver (dated October 23 or newer).

Once restarted, press the Armory Crate button to open the side Command Center, hit the Edit icon, and add the new AMD FSR Upscaling tile. Activate it.

You cannot toggle this on the fly mid-game. You must turn the FSR upscaling tile on in the Command Center before you launch your game, and then select the FSR setting inside the game's display menus.

As for with Strix Halo laptops, you just need the latest AMD Adrenalin drivers to get it, so get those updated!

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

So let’s get into the actual numbers. My standard FSR advice has always been to leave it on the Balanced preset. But when I ran one-to-one tests comparing FSR 3 against the new FSR 4 on the exact same settings, the new tech didn’t give me more frames.

2560 x 1600 high FSR Balanced (Frame gen)

So why is it slower? FSR 4 isn’t just a simple spatial algorithm anymore. It's a heavier, vastly more complex machine-learning model — requiring more overhead and compute power to analyze and reconstruct the image.

A direct preset-to-preset comparison doesn’t math. You have to change the way you use it.

Through my testing, one thing became abundantly clear: FSR 4 running in Performance actually delivers a notable picture quality increase over FSR 3 running in Balanced mode.

This is the true breakthrough. With FSR 3, dropping your game down to Performance meant accepting a blurry, pixelated picture — especially in motion. FSR 4 is so much sharper at rebuilding images that it’s not a compromise anymore.

In Dying Light: The Beast, you can see that foliage and stonework come through with much more clarity with FSR 4 vs FSR 3. At that lower internal resolution, AMD’s able to pick up and upscale more detail.

In Spider-Man: Miles Morales, it becomes so clear when you look at the fur detailing on the jacket collar. With FSR 3, it’s softer and clumpier, whereas individual hairs are more sharply defined with the 4th generation.

Moving over to Cyberpunk 2077, that NPC is rendered much more sharply — especially in the hair. Forza Horizon 6 shows a sharpening of the reflections on that wet asphalt, and there’s cleaner edges to details like computer screens and the robotic suit in Pragmata.

All of this on performance, and the numbers take a jump too.

2560 x 1600 high FSR Balanced (Frame gen)

FSR 4 is the biggest free upgrade AMD handhelds and laptops have received in a long time, but only if you rewire how you tweak your settings.

Make no mistake about it. FSR 4 is the biggest free upgrade AMD handhelds and laptops have received in a long time, but only if you rewire how you tweak your settings. It’s not a one-to-one swap for a Balanced preset — a confident drop to Performance mode will get you a better picture quality and frame rate to boost.

But after the past few months of watching Intel really take the gaming fight to AMD with Panther Lake chips and XeSS 3, is this enough to take on Team Blue? Sort of.

This is a catch up effort, but there are places where Intel continues to lead, such as with a stronger GPU silicon on handhelds and multi-frame generation. But that Arc G3 Extreme is definitely pricier.

It’ll be interesting to see how this all plays out! And if you've noticed differences in your own experiences, let me know in the comments box below.

#3190. Google Recently Warned That Quantum Computers Could Crack Bitcoin. Now It's Selling Protection.

Alphabet's planned crypto custody platform is catering to institutions that are increasingly concerned about their cybersecurity.

One day, it's technically possible that a hacker equipped with a quantum computer could crack the encryption that underpins Bitcoin (BTC -0.55%). That day may be drawing nearer; in March 2026, security researchers at Alphabet (GOOGL -0.30%) estimated that a future quantum machine could break Bitcoin's wallet cryptography in less than 10 minutes, and that a quantum computer of sufficient power could be far easier to create than what had previously been believed. And now, on Oct. 28, Google Cloud previewed its new crypto custody system targeting banks that offer crypto products to their clients, positioning the quantum threat to Bitcoin as one of the risks that justify buying its services.

So what does this mean for Alphabet's stock, and what does this mean for Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies?

Google's new custody system is designed to protect crypto assets from one particular threat: theft of users' private keys.

In case you aren't familiar, a private key is the secret password that enables the control of a crypto wallet. According to Chainalysis data, hacked or otherwise illegally obtained private keys accounted for 43.8% of the crypto stolen in 2024.

Google's new service is called Multi-Party Compute (MPC), and it's useful for preventing that because it splits each private key into fragments which are then stored on separate systems, making it much more difficult to gain access to the keys by hacking individual networks or computers. Commercial launch of MPC is planned for early 2027.

But as of now, there's little reason to expect MPC to be very beneficial for Alphabet shareholders.

Per Alphabet's third-quarter earnings, Google Cloud revenue climbed 103% year over year to $30.7 billion, accounting for 24% of the company's total revenue. As there's no information available on the service's pricing yet, and plenty of other crypto custody options and cybersecurity services that appeal to institutional investors, it's unclear how the new initiative will capture much market share or generate much revenue at all.

And the entire endeavor's connection to quantum cybersecurity is, to some degree, a long shot; most timelines don't expect quantum computers that are powerful enough to be relevant to cryptocurrency encryption to even exist until five years from now at the earliest, and some estimates only see that happening after a decade or two.

Aside from the above, it's also important for investors to temper their concerns (and expectations) for Google's involvement in the quickly evolving field of quantum cybersecurity.

In theory, sufficiently sophisticated quantum computers could crack Bitcoin's encryption and steal funds by working backward from a public key, which is a wallet's cryptographic identifier that is visible to everyone on the blockchain, to get to the private key behind it. An attack like that wouldn't need to steal any key fragments, so it isn't helpful to split the keys across systems like Google's approach does.

More than 6 million bitcoins, a substantial portion of the 21 million coins that can ever exist (almost 29%), are held in wallets with exposed public keys, and those are the coins that are most at risk as quantum computing companies improve the technology over the coming years. A successful attack would likely mean that Bitcoin would lose a dramatic amount of value overnight as holders fled to safer assets.

Furthermore, Google has given no timetable for when post-quantum cryptography, encryption built to resist quantum attacks, will be implemented in its service, though it's clearly on the agenda to develop at some point. So for now, the quantum security pitch is ahead of what the product can actually do as it's presently known and envisioned.

Alphabet investors can thus treat MPC as a small bonus for now, although it probably isn't worth loading up on the stock due to this new offering.

On the other hand, if quantum computers continue developing faster than anticipated, there could be a growing demand (and perhaps even a market panic causing a clamor) for a quantum-safe custody option, which Google would in turn be well positioned to deliver on, especially if its service gains some early traction in advance of that.

#3189. The Wild World of Third-Party AI Apps for Ring Security, and Whether You Need Them

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Ring cameras offer broad capabilities, but third-party AI tools give HOAs, landlords and others even more ways to use them.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Basically, this software leverages Ring’s object recognition ability to use it for a wider range of monitoring possibilities. I’m trying out some of these apps to see just how they work, but if you or people in your neighborhood use Ring devices, you should know what they’re capable of. These mini apps range from casual fun to Flock-like levels of surveillance. Most require a Ring subscription and an additional monthly fee, typically a few dollars. Here are popular examples of those apps, how they work, if they’re legal and what they could be doing in your neighborhood.

For those annoyed by illegal trash dumping or other waste violations, the DumpWatch app promises to watch for trash miscreants using Ring’s AI for about $8 per month. The app records footage whenever it detects large amounts of waste being left in the camera’s field of view and creates a timestamped PDF that can be used to submit a complaint or file a police report.

Note that some examples DumpWatch uses show trash bins left on the sidewalk, a common occurrence on collection days, or extra trash placed beside bins, which may be allowed by local waste companies. It’s not guaranteed to capture only illegal activity.

Yes, these little apps can also serve as tools for homeowners associations if your neighborhood has strict rules about what’s permitted. One example is the $3 per month LawnWatch app, which is trained to monitor properties for HOA violations such as leaving toys cluttering a lawn, dog owners not cleaning up poop and so on. A somewhat more benevolent app, Greenlapse, tracks grass and plant growth over time, and is primarily designed to monitor your own landscaping projects.

Ring’s app store includes a slew of monitoring apps made specifically to track tenants and short-term rental guests, collecting info for landlords to use. One example is the $5-per-month ZoneGauge app, which continuously tracks how many people are in a space, letting owners know when someone is throwing a party, for instance.

Another option is the GuardCat app. It’s $8 per month and it summarizes guest check-outs, cleaner visits, “house rule violations” and more based on what Ring security cameras pick up using AI detection.

A quick reminder here: Companies such as Airbnb have banned indoor security cameras entirely. Apps like these shouldn’t be used indoors at all.

Using AI to monitor pets for unusual behavior that could signal health problems is nothing new. We’ve reviewed quite a few pet cameras and smart tracking collars that do something similar. But apps such as Pet Vet AI can use Ring cams as an alternative for $10 per month. Here, the app analyzes pet snapshots for issues such as limping, throwing up food, sleeping in unusual spots and more, then summarizes any problems for pet owners. The app says it works with birds, reptiles and fish, too, but I’ve never seen pet AI advanced enough to get any worthwhile analysis from the non-mammals in our homes.

Ring’s mini apps extend beyond the home and into many aspects of the workplace, too. Apps such as ProofClock and TimeStack are designed for construction, freight and similar industries to monitor when teams arrive at a location and how long they work, even when the Ring camera owner isn’t present. Some of these apps can also generate uptime and service-level agreement reports, although I’m dubious about tying Ring AI, which isn’t always reliable, so closely to payroll.

We’ve tested plenty of bird feeder cameras that can identify bird species with varying degrees of success. But if you’d like to point a Ring camera at a feeder or birdbath, an app such as What’s That Bird.AI can do something similar for $5 per month. It captures screenshots of nearby birds and attempts to identify them so you can see which species are stopping by.

There’s a small problem here: Feeders from Birdbuddy and similar brands give you bird recognition for free, so if you don’t mind buying a dedicated bird watching camera, there’s no need to pay a subscription at all.

No. Each app has its own requirements, displayed on their download pages. Some will work with nearly any Ring device that uses a camera. Others require a wired-in Ring device or a more recent Ring camera from the past year or so, or both.

Keep in mind that tools like these aren’t perfect and shouldn’t be the sole basis for filing a complaint or taking other action. They’re also expensive for what they do — such as charging $5 per month just to tell you when your mail arrives — so I don’t think they’re worth the cost for the average user. One exception may be pet AI, which could replace more expensive pet camera services. Either way, it’s important to know your options — and which apps your neighbors may be using.

#3188. These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s new

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Is your pricey Claude Enterprise account worth it? Anthropic is trying to surface insights with three tools.

By some measures, businesses are finally starting to see ROI on expensive AI adoption, but many still want better insights about whether the spend is worth the productivity gains.

Also: How I fixed a small business’s email overwhelm for $120

Attempting to give its enterprise clients more visibility, Anthropic is making three tracking features, all released in beta in September, generally available for Claude Enterprise plans: smart reports, pooled budgets, and in-app surveys.

Smart reports track what tasks employees are using Claude for and how often they’re running them, in addition to what they cost. The reports, which are off by default, also document “where sessions run into friction,” the company said, and note where you can create routine workflows from the tasks people run consistently.

Anthropic noted in the documentation that smart reports “aren’t designed and should not be used for evaluating individual performance or making employment decisions,” a relevant disclaimer given how AI is impacting HR.

Also: Managers are using AI to write performance reviews – and it shows

The pooled budgets feature sets a monthly spend cap for a group within an organization, in addition to each seat’s individual monthly limit. Admins can set individual and group spend limits based on previous monthly spend data. The feature aims to optimize budgets so that one highly active user isn’t hamstrung by a budget limit while others leave spend on the table. Users can belong to multiple pooled budgets, which you can order by priority.

With in-app surveys, admins can create surveys that appear in Chat to ask employees about their Claude usage and see aggregate responses in their Admin console.

Claude Enterprise is much pricier than a Claude Teams account — the former is billed at $20 per seat per month, in addition to API token rates. The latter also charges $20 per seat, but caps out at 150 users and includes tokens (meaning usage isn’t billed separately), making it more accessible to smaller teams.

If a company has already opted to invest enterprise-level spend in AI, odds are they can afford it, but that also makes the stakes on that spend much higher. Making these tools generally available may surface useful insights that incentivize larger customers who are getting antsy to stick it out.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude

Anthropic has been the market leader for enterprise AI, though OpenAI has caught up in recent months as both companies set their sights on IPOs. New data from Ramp also shows Anthropic spend peaked in July, but has been slightly lower in October thus far.

In a volatile market and facing a potential bubble, the company needs to keep customer growth high, given it filed its much-awaited IPO on Monday. As Anthropic put it in its prospectus: “If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops more slowly than we expect or declines, our growth may slow or stall, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.”

There’s always something new to watch on Netflix, but with a new month comes plenty of fresh additions, meaning the top 10 list can change up pretty quickly. With so many titles competing for your attention, deciding what deserves a spot on your watchlist can be tricky. That’s where I come in. Netflix’s top 10 is a good starting point, but not every trending series is necessarily worth your time. So, I’ve picked out three shows from this week’s most popular picks that I think deserve a look.

This week’s selection covers everything from an intimate documentary about the life, career and struggles of a much-loved sitcom star to the third season of a seriously charming romantic comedy. There’s also a gripping supernatural mystery about a seemingly ordinary town that traps anyone who enters, with its residents desperately searching for a way home. Whether you’re after real-life stories, a bit of romance or some seriously unsettling mysteries, there’s something here to keep you entertained.

Note: This list is based on the Netflix U.S. top 10 shows as of Tuesday, November 3, 2026.

“The One About Matthew Perry” is a three-part documentary that explores the life, career and tragic death of the beloved “Friends” star. Released just ahead of the three-year anniversary of his passing, the documentary was developed with input from people who knew Perry before and after his period of peak sitcom fame. It also takes inspiration from the classic “Friends” episode titles, choosing to steer clear of sensationalized Hollywood gossip and instead offers something raw and honest.

Through never-before-heard testimonies from his sister, lifelong friends and former colleagues, alongside previously unreleased family photographs and videos, the series looks back at Perry’s journey from aspiring actor to Hollywood favorite as Chandler Bing. It also takes a look at his long-running battle with addiction, repeated attempts at recovery and the advocacy work he became passionate about. From his rise to fame to his final days, it’s an intimate portrait of the man behind one of television’s most recognizable characters.

Stream "The One About Matthew Perry" on Netflix

Fancy a cozy romantic comedy to binge this week? Netflix’s “Nobody Wants This” is a great place to start, with all three seasons available to catch up on. Created by Erin Foster and loosely inspired by her own experience meeting her husband, the series brings a fresh, grown-up take on the rom-com. I especially love its mix of genuinely funny (and awkward) moments and more honest relationship drama, making it an easy watch if you’re after something funny, charming and a little bit heartfelt. Plus, the two leads have some sizzling chemistry.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

“Nobody Wants This” centers around Joanne (Kristen Bell), an outspoken podcast host who meets Noah (Adam Brody), a recently single rabbi, at a dinner party. Despite their very different backgrounds, the pair quickly hit it off and decide to see where things go. However, their new relationship soon brings them into each other’s complicated family lives, with Joanne’s sister Morgan (Justine Lupe) and Noah’s brother Sasha (Timothy Simons) never too far from the action. This Netflix comedy follows the couple as they figure out what building a future together might actually look like.

I couldn't be happier to see “From” land on Netflix, as it’s genuinely one of my favorite shows and deserves to reach a much bigger audience. It’s already great to see it making its way onto the platform’s trending list, and I'm hoping it climbs even higher over the next few days. For anyone who hasn’t watched it yet, this is one of the best mystery-box horror shows around, packed with bizarre twists and many questions. With season 5 set to bring the story to a close, I’m glad the creators have a clear endpoint in sight. Hopefully, that means we finally get the answers we’ve been waiting for.

“From” is set in a mysterious small town that traps everyone who enters, leaving its residents desperately searching for a way home. When the Matthews family takes a wrong turn during a road trip, they find themselves stuck alongside a group of strangers who have been trying to escape for years. Led by Sheriff Boyd Stevens (Harold Perrineau), the residents must find ways to survive, particularly after dark, when terrifying human-like creatures emerge from the surrounding forest. As new arrivals bring fresh questions, finding a way out proves harder than anyone imagined.

#3186. Will the iPhone Duo Fit in Your Pocket? Here’s How It Compares to Other iPhone Sizes

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The iPhone Duo has a palm-size build, but how does that measure up against Apple's other current phones?

The iPhone Duo is designed to be compact, but that hasn’t stopped some from wondering how its size compares with other iPhone models.

Fortunately, we have all the current iPhone devices on hand to show how the Duo, when folded shut, stacks up against the dimensions of everything from the iPhone Air to the iPhone 18 Pro Max. This should give you a better sense of how easily the Duo might fit into a pocket or bag.

The iPhone Duo is a $1,999 phone that, in case it wasn’t obvious from the price, isn’t for everyone. With a 5.4-inch cover screen and 7.6-inch inner display, it serves as a phone-tablet hybrid that’s ideal for multitasking, watching movies and working on the go. The Duo isn’t especially light or thin, but it’s also not too bulky. It measures 5.2 millimeters when unfolded and 11.3mm when folded, and it weighs 254 grams.

As a first-generation device, it has its shortcomings. The Duo doesn’t support FaceID, opting for TouchID instead. Its multitasking capabilities are limited compared to other foldable phones, and the cameras are more scaled back than the iPhone 18 Pro’s. But other details make the Duo feel refined and intuitive, from the matte texture of the inner display that reduces glare to dynamic software integration across both screens. The Duo can be a tempting option for anyone looking for a phone that feels refreshingly different.

Here’s how the iPhone Duo’s size compares to all current iPhone models.

Starting with Apple’s biggest nonfolding phone, the $1,299 iPhone 18 Pro Max has a 6.9-inch display. It measures 8.75mm thick and weighs 249 grams, making it just slightly lighter than the iPhone Duo, though that difference is negligible. What you will notice is how much shorter the Duo is, making it easier to slip into a pocket — even smaller women’s pockets.

Meanwhile, the $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro has a 6.3-inch display and, like its Pro Max counterpart, is 8.75mm thick. The 18 Pro weighs a noticeably lighter 211 grams, so the Duo does start to feel a little more hefty in comparison.

Apple has yet to unveil a baseline iPhone 18 model, which is expected early next year. In the meantime, here’s how the Duo compares to the $899 iPhone 17, which has a 6.3-inch display and measures 7.95mm thick. The iPhone 17 weighs 177 grams, making it significantly lighter than the iPhone Duo.

The $1,099 iPhone Air has a slightly larger 6.5-inch display compared to the iPhone 17. It measures a sleek 5.6mm thick, and it weighs a featherlight 165 grams. If you’re jumping from the Air to the Duo, you’ll definitely feel the biggest difference compared to other current iPhone models.

And finally, the slightly more budget-friendly $699 iPhone 17E has a 6.1-inch display, measuring 7.8mm thick and weighing 169 grams.

If you’re thinking about making the leap to the iPhone Duo, be sure to check out CNET’s in-depth review for more on using Apple’s first foldable phone.

#3183. Daylight Saving Time Ends Sunday. Get Ready to Change Your Clocks

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Most of the US gains an hour of sleep this weekend, but Hawaii and most of Arizona won’t change their clocks.

It’s time to change your clocks: Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, when clocks across most of the US move back to 1 a.m.

The timing lines up neatly with Halloween — trick-or-treaters on Saturday still get the later sunset, and the extra hour of sleep arrives overnight. Phones and computers update on their own, but oven, microwave and car clocks usually don’t.

The time shift is notorious for disrupting sleep patterns and schedules. Some politicians are advocating for the abolition of time changes and the permanent adoption of daylight saving time, or DST. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act in July, but it still needs Senate approval and the president’s signature to become law — meaning that, for now, we still have dark winter hours coming.

If you, too, dislike how early it gets dark each day through winter, just remember that brighter evenings will return in mid-March. Here’s what else to know about the switch, including which states skip it — and when the clocks spring forward again.

Daylight saving time in the US ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday. It will return at 2 a.m. local time on March 14, 2027. The end of DST is when we “fall back,” whereas in March, we “spring forward.”

The US isn’t alone in observing daylight saving time. Check out this list of other countries that use DST, along with their start and end dates. The UK, for example, fell back last weekend.

The official US time website shows where time zone boundaries are located.

The exact start dates for daylight saving time and standard time float a little. DST kicks off on the second Sunday of March and ends on the first Sunday of November with the return of standard time.

We spend about eight months of the year in DST. We can thank the Uniform Time Act of 1966 for bringing some order to what had been a complicated history of time changes in the US.

“Motivated by transportation improvements, this act mandated standard time within the existing time zones and established a permanent system of uniform DST, including the dates and times for twice-yearly transitions,” the Bureau of Transportation Statistics states in a history of time zones.

The country’s time zones date to the railroad boom of the late 1800s. DST formally entered the chat in 1918, but its application was inconsistent until 1966. The country tried year-round daylight saving time in January 1974 under President Richard Nixon to address the energy crisis. It didn’t go over well. Congress and President Gerald Ford restored standard time in October 1974.

If you truly hate time changes, then consider moving to Arizona (except for the Navajo Nation) or Hawaii. Those states are on standard time all year long, and their residents don’t have to deal with the physical and mental health impacts of the change. Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands also skip DST.

Read more: Why Is NASA Working on a Time Zone for the Moon?

Organizations such as the National Sleep Foundation, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms are united in calling for permanent standard time, saying it’s better for human biology.

“There’s a mismatch between the outside world and our internal clocks during daylight saving time that can result in some negative health consequences,” says Joseph Dzierzewski, senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation.

Dzierzewski cites mental health concerns and upticks in cardiovascular events and drowsy driving. He also calls out safety issues with young children walking to school or sitting at bus stops in the dark. Those safety issues were a big reason why permanent DST didn’t last in 1974.

Time changes aren’t popular. An October 2024 YouGov poll (PDF) of more than 1,100 US adults found that 63% would like to see the changing of the clocks eliminated. Only 17% wanted to keep time changes, and 20% weren’t sure.

Efforts to end the time changes have so far failed to pass into law. The bipartisan Sunshine Protection Act, which would have made daylight saving time permanent, passed the Senate in 2022 — the new version of the bill passed the House earlier this year and was sent on to the Senate to review in July.

While many people agree on eliminating time changes, the schism between daylight saving time and standard time remains. Standard time may have a bit of an image issue compared to DST.

“Part of the issue is that people associate daylight saving time with summer. People love summer, right?” Dzierzewski said. “But the simple fact of the matter is, it would still be summer if we were on permanent standard time.”

President Donald Trump criticized time changes in a 2024 Truth Social post: “The Republican Party will use its best efforts to eliminate Daylight Saving Time, which has a small but strong constituency, but shouldn’t! Daylight Saving Time is inconvenient and very costly to our Nation.”

Bills and resolutions at the state level haven’t had real-world impacts yet. Politicians are still split on whether they want permanent daylight saving or standard time. Dzierzewski is hopeful that permanent standard time will win out.

“This is the first time in several years where I’ve seen more legislation introduced at a state level in support of permanent standard time as the solution,” he said.

If you’d like to see time changes end and want to advocate for either daylight saving or standard time, contact your state and national representatives and express your opinion.

Daylight saving time is happening, so now it’s a matter of figuring out how to deal with it. It’s not just about the day of the time change.

“You’re in a better situation to cope with the effects of the clock change if you have good sleep health generally,” Dzierzewski said. He recommends exposure to bright light in the morning, physical activity during the day, eating meals at regular times and practicing a relaxing wind-down routine at night.

The majority of Americans struggle to get the National Sleep Foundation’s recommended 7 to 9 hours of sleep for most adults. A CNET survey found that more than half of US adults use some method to cope with sleep-related challenges. Check out some expert-backed tips for improving your sleep quality.

“If you’re doing these healthy sleep behaviors, you’re probably more resilient to some of these changes,” Dzierzewski said. “If you have poor sleep to begin with, you’re probably going to feel it a little bit more.”

Establishing a better sleep routine can take time. There are two things you can do in direct response to the time change. Dzierzewski suggests adjusting your bedtime and wake-up time gradually ahead of the change. For example, you could shift your schedule by 15 minutes per day and ease yourself into DST. He also recommends getting a good dose of bright morning light on the day of the time change to help set your internal body clock.

Think of DST as another kind of wake-up call, one that can motivate you to evaluate your sleep routine and quality and make positive changes. Start with these six simple habits. And don’t forget to change your clocks. Do it the night before, and you won’t have to worry about it later.

#3182. Your public Discord messages may soon appear in Google search results – how to opt out

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Discord announced a new feature that can make your server messages discoverable on Google. Here's how to opt out.

Also: My 5 favorite Discord alternatives – no ID verification required

Normally, in order to join a Discord server, you need an invitation link that has been generated by a current admin or member. These links usually have a very short lifespan, expiring after just a few minutes to help protect private groups from bad actors looking to cause trouble. However, for very large Discoverable Servers, Discord has an internal search function called Server Discovery that allows users to join communities without an invite link. The new policy will create a Server Web Page for each of these very large servers, discoverable in search engines like Google or DuckDuckGo, that will show a short description of the server and a summary of conversations in its public channels. New members can join servers directly from their Server Web Pages.

As for what exactly is shared on Server Web Pages, Discord’s related support page says, “From mid-December 2026, answers to questions your members sent in public channels can be found in a web search, in their own words.”

Server Web Pages will begin to go live on Nov. 16, 2026, but server admins have already been given access to tools for opting out entire channels from the program:

Once you’ve accessed the controls, you can either pick which channels will be shown in your community’s Server Web Page (something like a general chat for a content creator’s community server, or a hobby community’s rules page) or opt out of all channels so that only a server description will be visible. And even the server description can be disabled if you’re trying to keep your community as private as possible.

Discord plans to start adding chat summaries and individual example messages in mid-December, and regular users will be able to opt out of having their part of conversations shown.

Along with toggles to opt out of personalized ads and data collection (which I strongly suggest you turn off as well), you’ll see a button to block your message text and data from being used in Server Web Pages. And one toggle will cover permissions in every Discoverable Server that you belong to, so you won’t have to waste time updating your preferences for every community.

Also: Strangers can find your info with a 5-minute search – delete it ASAP

Don’t worry, the private server you have set up for playing games and chatting with friends, and even larger communities not designated as Discoverable Servers, aren’t affected by this announcement. Only official Discoverable Servers with at least 1,000 members, that are at least eight weeks old, and meet Discord’s activity and safety standards will have the new web pages and message summary features.

The move seems to position Discord as an alternative to Reddit in the market of obscure tech questions with answers that were previously only available on now-defunct Q&A forums market. Discoverable Servers will be analogous to sub-Reddit communities, offering vital information to hobbyists and pros alike that might otherwise be locked behind paywalls or “walled garden” private servers.

#3180. The S&P 500's Record Profits Are Hiding a Problem Investors Haven't Seen Before

Companies are recognizing revenue now. But the costs are only likely to start showing up in the years ahead.

Record corporate earnings have been the primary driver of higher stock prices for the past several quarters. Current estimates suggest year-over-year earnings growth for the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.51%) could hit 29% in Q3. Above-average earnings growth is expected to continue, especially within the mega-cap names, for the next couple of years.

But there's a risk hiding underneath those numbers. And it raises questions about just how sustainable some of those earnings really are. The way companies account for those investments and the revenue associated with them could be creating a problem that won't show up until far into the future.

Imagine a situation where a tech company decides to make a major investment into AI development. It needs chips. It needs servers. It needs other equipment and infrastructure. Let's say it spends $1 billion in total.

The companies selling those things recognize the revenue as they deliver those products. That spending then can also immediately support sales and earnings further down the AI supply chain.

But the company developing that project doesn't recognize the full $1 billion as an expense on its income statement right away. Instead, it usually chooses to depreciate the construction and equipment costs over their useful lives, which could be several years or more. Plus, depreciation usually doesn't begin until those projects are ready for use.

That creates a potential problem for the big AI companies. The revenue and earnings are showing up now, but the expense won't come until later. What happens when that earnings growth finally slows right at the time that expenses are increasing?

Not long ago, huge planned spending for AI development was viewed as a positive by Wall Street. Tens, if not hundreds, of billions of dollars of capex commitment by all of the big hyperscalers resulted in big rallies in their stock prices.

Now we're on the other side of the mountain. The markets are focused on the return on investment (ROI) from all that spending. Revenue and earnings growth rates have been strong thus far and are expected to continue into 2027 and beyond. But free cash flow is the number that people are watching and they're getting more anxious about what they're seeing.

Alphabet (GOOG -0.07%)(GOOGL -0.30%) just suffered an historic single-day drop and now sits 30% below its 2026 high after reporting ballooning infrastructure spending. It had a negative free cash flow of over $9 billion in the quarter, reiterated its 2026 capex forecast of around $200 billion and said spending could ramp up further next year.

Intel (INTC -8.80%) shares tanked by more than 25% following a weaker-than-expected Q4 outlook and a warning that they probably won't be free cash flow positive in 2027.

Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) fell sharply after it said it had negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, a massive capital expenditure forecast of roughly $220 billion for the year, and the expectation that spending will be higher in 2027.

Meta Platforms (META -1.34%) dropped sharply as well on similar concerns around heavy AI development spending and negative free cash flow expectations.

Suddenly, investors have moved past the "AI optimism" phase and are looking for results.

As Warren Buffett would point out, there's a difference between a company whose stock price is falling because the business model is failing and one whose stock price is falling because economic conditions are changing.

The big tech stocks fall into the latter category. They're not going anywhere, and they still generate massive revenue and profits. But there is a legitimate risk that they've pushed too far, too fast. They might be in the second half of the boom/bust cycle that often occurs with these revolutionary new technologies. Their stock prices may have suffered the brunt of it already.

But I think long-term asset allocations should remain intact. Investments in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -0.50%) and the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI -0.42%) are still sound even if there will be some heightened volatility. More risk-averse investors might seek out the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP +0.77%) to spread out exposure risk.

Free cash flow looks like the signal here, though. The longer that stays negative and the longer tech companies keep spending hundreds of billions of dollar on capex, the longer that risk remains elevated.

#3179. Apple’s new touchscreen MacBook Pros may be late, but they have one big advantage

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Apple finally revealed its new MacBook M5 Pro and Max with a touchscreen OLED display, bringing the best features from the iPhone to its laptops.

Steve Jobs might be rolling over in his grave, but at long last, Apple announced a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen display. The new MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max features a tandem OLED display Apple is calling “ProLED XDR”, scaling up to 2,000 nits of brightness and a 120Hz refresh rate. For the first time, the MacBook Pro will feature touchscreen capabilities and the Dynamic Island — a feature first introduced on the iPhone.

Also: Forget the touchscreen MacBook – Apple’s new M6 is the laptop I recommend for most people

The display and controversial form factor aren’t its only draws: it features a thinner, lighter design and brings back the illuminated Apple logo on the back — some of the most significant changes to the MacBook chassis in years. The new MacBook Pro with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips will come in both 14- and 16-inch sizes, with up to 128GB of unified memory, and weigh less than ever: the smaller model at three pounds and the 16-inch at four pounds.

The company, under new CEO John Ternus, is on a spree with new products, with its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, earlier this month (another product that’s been in development for years), and an all-new lineup of smart home products aimed at challenging Amazon’s dominance in that market.

The MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max feature new ProLED XDR displays that control color and pixel luminance at the sub-millisecond level, while monitoring and adapting usage over time, Apple says. The panels feature a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and cover both the P3 and Adobe RGB color gamuts, high-end specs indeed for a laptop display.

To reduce glare, Apple says it etched the nano-texture directly into the glass, since the touch sensor is built directly into the panel rather than layered on top of it.

The displays work with Apple’s ProMotion technology, which adjusts refresh rates based on what the device is actively doing: scaling down to 10Hz while idle for better power efficiency and ramping up to 120Hz during gaming or graphics-heavy tasks.

In terms of software and usability, Apple says apps should be ready to go on the new MacBook Pros, since they’re set to register touches as clicks.

Touchscreen laptops are nothing new, having been standard fare on laptops of all kinds for years now. Apple’s entrance into the market is notable because the company took such a hard-line stance against them for years (Jobs famously called them “ergonomically terrible“), but honestly, the everyday consumer in 2026 may struggle to see the big deal.

Either you like using your finger or a stylus on a screen, or you don’t. Can Apple really deliver a touchscreen experience that is worlds better than what’s available on Windows PCs or Chromebooks (or Googlebooks)? It’s debatable.

However, there are a few things Apple has up its sleeve that set it apart from the competition, and they have to do with its most successful product of all time (which also happens to have a touchscreen): the iPhone.

Also: iPhone Duo hands-on: The $2,000 foldable has some magical touches

Apple smartly made the iPhone’s usability wins core to its approach to the new MacBook. For example, it features a Dynamic Island cutout, doing away with the notch in favor of a dynamic multitasking hub. This allows it to adapt through unique touch-based interactions that were previously impossible on a MacBook.

The Dynamic Island serves as the new home for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri, changing how you interact with these features by putting them front and center. The design intent here appears to be to keep dynamic, time-sensitive events and apps in close view for quick reference, an interesting merge of how we use both our iPhones and laptops.

Also: Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook is days away – with another OLED surprise

Plus, with Apple’s vast App Store library, there is already a host of touch-optimized programs for Apple’s ecosystem. It doesn’t look like Apple is interested in bringing these directly to MacOS — this is still very much a MacBook Pro — instead, folding in the touch functionality as part of the feature set of these laptops’ premium displays.

In that sense, this is already well-trodden ground for Apple. Bringing the best features of the iPhone to the MacBook Pro isn’t even that revolutionary when you think about it; it’s a smart way to improve its product line.

You already know these new MacBooks aren’t going to be cheap. The base model with the lowest configuration starts at $2,899: the 14-inch M5 Pro with 24GB of unified memory and 1TB of local storage. The prices only scale up from there to seriously astronomical figures, particularly for the ultra-high-end storage options. 16TB of storage will start at $14 grand.

We haven’t seen these laptops in person yet, but I have no doubt the new ProLED XDR screens look fantastic. However, it’s a lot of money for a touchscreen laptop. These devices come hot on the heels of Microsoft and Nvidia’s recent RTX Spark devices, which also target the high end of the market, with AI enthusiasts looking for local AI performance to be front and center.

These laptops are niche, to be sure, but they also don’t speak to such a specific subset of users; instead, they focus on their impressive hardware and implications for creators, artists, and power users.

Also: Apple’s touchscreen Mac event: 3 things I’m excited for – and my one concern

Apple isn’t showcasing a reinvention of the MacBook Pro, but rather a bonus feature for its most powerful ultra-premium laptops. With the recent announcement of the M6 MacBook Pro, consumers looking for an accessible workhorse MacBook already have that option. This is for someone else entirely.

The new MacBook Pros with M5 Pro and M5 Max are now available for preorder, with general availability beginning Friday, Nov. 6.
