#3178. November 2026 Skywatching Guide: Meteors, Planets, Stars and a Full Moon

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

This month, you'll find three meteor showers and a planetary alignment starring four planets.

Autumn is marching right along, and so are the objects in the night sky. November is the final full month of fall, and with daylight saving time ending Nov. 1, the sun will set even earlier. That’ll give skygazers more time to see some cool sights without staying up horribly late or waking up unbearably early.

This month of fall is arguably the most active for amateur astronomers, with things to see as early as Nov. 2 and as late as Nov. 30. While there aren’t any major celestial events, a series of smaller ones makes up for it.

Every planet is visible during the month of November, though depending on the time and day, you’ll get a better or worse view of them. Mercury and Venus are the most difficult to see due to their proximity to the sun.

Mercury: Mercury was at its eastern elongation during October, so it starts November a bit too close to the sun to see safely. It reaches western elongation on Nov. 20, where it’ll be easily visible just before sunrise for the rest of the month.

Venus: Venus starts the month just ahead of the sun at sunrise, technically making it possible to see every morning in November. It gets further from the sun as the month goes on, making it easier and safer to see toward the end of the month.

Mars: Mars is high in the sky all month. It rises out of the eastern horizon shortly after midnight at the start of November and rises earlier as the month progresses. Early morning is the best time to see it, or right around midnight toward the end of the month.

Jupiter: Jupiter and Mars are close pals for all of November, rising at roughly the same time and right next to each other in the sky. The star Regulus joins in to form a trio, which is visible to the naked eye the entire month.

Saturn: Saturn is also visible every night in November. It’s in the eastern sky when the sun sets, and sets on the western horizon shortly before sunrise. Right after dark is the best time to see it, but you’ll need binoculars or a telescope to capture its glorious rings.

Neptune: Neptune and Saturn are teamed up for November, with both of them being very close in the sky and following a similar trajectory. Bring binoculars or a telescope.

Uranus: Uranus is in the night sky every day in November, rising in the east shortly before sunset and setting in the west right around sunrise. It reaches opposition on Nov. 25, which means it’s as far away from the sun as it can get, and will be the most visible. You’ll still want to bring some binoculars or a telescope for best results.

The month begins with a meetup among Mars, Jupiter and the moon. The three will appear close together in the night sky, making them easy to spot: The moon is easy to find, and both planets are visible to the naked eye. On Nov. 2, the moon will be closer to Mars, and the trio will follow one another across the sky throughout the night. Regulus will also be in tow and readily visible to the naked eye.

Nov. 3 continues the good vibes. The moon slides over to the other side of Regulus on that night, but all four celestial bodies are still quite close together and easy to spot. Mars, Jupiter and Regulus will get even closer to each other as November progresses, but the moon moves even further away after Nov. 3.

The Southern Taurids have technically been active since Sept. 20, and continue until Nov. 20. This long-running meteor shower peaks during the evening of Nov. 4 and morning of Nov. 5. It’s not a terribly strong meteor shower and should average about five meteors per hour. However, it often tosses bright fireballs, so what it lacks in quantity, it makes up for in quality.

The moon is 22% illuminated that night, which the American Meteor Society calls “favorable conditions” for viewing a meteor shower. You want to get as far away from light pollution as possible to give yourself even better odds, and make sure to dress for the weather. The Southern Taurids will appear to originate from the Taurus constellation, which rises in the east shortly after sunset and moves across the sky before setting in the west right before sunrise.

It’s no secret that the full moon is usually the most popular celestial event to happen every month, but skygazers also value the new moon. This is because the moon is a significant source of light pollution, making many stars and planets, such as Uranus and Neptune, harder to see. With the new moon on Nov. 9, it’ll be the darkest night of November — and perfect for stargazing and night-sky photography.

Nov. 9 also happens to be Carl Sagan Day, an unofficial holiday to honor the visionary astronomer. If you’re stuck inside that night, you can always use the occasion to watch Sagan’s legendary Cosmos series, which is available for free on the Internet Archive or through various user uploads on YouTube.

Most of the planets are visible in the night sky almost every night in November, but on Nov. 14 there’ll be a fun little planet parade. It’ll take place just before sunrise, so it’s mostly for early risers. Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter are set to line up nicely, making them easy to spot. This is especially true for Jupiter and Mars, which should be right next to each other that night.

The show will start around Nov. 14 and will last until around Nov. 25, depending on your location. The tricky part is catching Mercury in the sky before the sun comes up. It’s only about a 30-minute window since the sun closely follows Mercury up over the eastern horizon. The single best day to view it is Nov. 20, when Mercury is at its western elongation — as far from the sun as it can get.

Uranus is also visible at this time, bringing the number of visible planets to three. Saturn and Neptune are below the horizon. Uranus is on the other side of the sky, however, so it’s not technically part of the alignment.

If you miss the Southern Taurids, you only have to wait a week to catch a glimpse of the Northern Taurids meteor shower. This is another long-lasting meteor shower that started on Oct. 20 and runs until Dec. 10. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 11 and the morning of Nov. 12. The American Meteor Society notes that the moon is only 5% illuminated on Nov. 11, giving viewers even better conditions than during the Southern Taurids.

It is otherwise virtually identical to the Southern Taurids. The shower appears to originate from the same constellation, Taurus, which rises and sets at almost exactly the same times as it did a week earlier. The Northern Taurids promise about five meteors per hour under optimal conditions, with an increased chance of fireballs. Both showers are even fueled by the same comet, 2P/Encke. It’s the space equivalent of a sitcom rerun airing just one week later.

Leonids is usually the most active meteor shower in November. It starts on Nov. 6 and runs until Nov. 30, making it shorter than both Taurids meteor showers. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 16 and the morning of Nov. 17.

The good news is that the meteor shower is very easy to find. Meteors from it will appear to originate from the Leo constellation, which is right next to Mars and Jupiter, which are visible in the night sky.

The bad news is that this part of the sky doesn’t rise until around midnight, making this a meteor shower for night owls. It should produce about 15 meteors per hour under optimal conditions, though you can expect slightly fewer because the 41%-illuminated moon will create enough natural light pollution to obscure fainter meteors.

The Leonids have produced exceptional meteor storms in the past, with hundreds of meteors per hour. That isn’t expected to happen in 2026, but the odds aren’t zero. They may improve after the comet loops around the sun again in 2031.

A micro moon is noticeably smaller and less bright than a supermoon or even a regular full moon.

November’s Beaver Moon takes place just two days before Thanksgiving. It is also the first of a string of four consecutive supermoons that will close out 2026 and begin 2027. This happens when the moon is within 90% of perigee — its closest point to Earth. The phenomenon makes the moon appear about 7% larger than a regular moon and 14% larger than a minimoon — and noticeably brighter than both.

Per The Old Farmer’s Almanac, the Beaver Moon reaches its peak illumination on Nov. 24 at 9:53 a.m. ET, which is after sunrise for most people in the US. That means the best time to see it is either the night before (Nov. 23) or the evening after (Nov. 24). The moon remains over 90% full from Nov. 22-27. If you plan on going skygazing, avoid those days like the plague, since the moon creates a ton of light pollution.

It’s not often that the same event happens twice in a single month, but it turns out Jupiter, Mars and the moon just can’t seem to get enough of each other. The trio closes out the month the same way it started: hanging out very close together in the night sky. And yes, Regulus will once again tag along.

Unlike the prior meetup, this one only lasts for one night before the moon dashes away. Since all four of them are visible with the naked eye and the moon is still mostly full, people shouldn’t have any trouble finding them. Eagle-eyed stargazers may see Algieba nearby as well. It’s the second brightest star in the Leo constellation (behind Regulus), and it’s also visible without binoculars or a telescope.

The constellations continue their summer-to-winter shakeup. Prominent constellations in the sky include Taurus, Pegasus, Capricornus, Aquila, Pisces and Aries. Mainstays such as the Big Dipper and Little Dipper are still out there, but can be difficult to see if you live too far south. As a rule, we recommend using a sky map or a tool such as Stellarium to pinpoint each object so you can find it.

There are also some lesser-known asterisms to seek out, such as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters), the Great Square of Pegasus and the Circlet of Pisces. The Summer Triangle is still visible, while the Winter Triangle becomes much easier to spot as it rises above the horizon earlier in the evening.

#3177. DJI Mic Mini 2S review: Flagship audio power without the flagship price tag

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The DJI Mic Mini 2S offers impressive audio quality, clear voice isolation via environmental noise cancellation, and up to 40 hours of battery life with its charging case. It delivers flagship-level features at a fraction of the cost. However, some users may want to look elsewhere due to noticeable popping on plosives and a bulky receiver.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

I’m no YouTube sensation, but when I’m doing something exciting with friends and family, I like to make videos to remember the moment. And while I previously used my phone, I’ve discovered that adding a few gear upgrades makes all the difference. Using one of the best microphones for clear audio is one of the best upgrades I’ve made.

The DJI Mic Mini 2S is essential for content creators due to its great audio quality with environmental noise cancellation, making sure nothing gets in the way of your sound. The battery life is also impressive, and the mic is great value for money since you’re getting near flagship features at a fraction of the price.

It’s worth noting that the mic may not be suited to the most professional settings since it struggles with popping plosive sounds. The receiver is also a little bulky. To find out more, keep reading this full DJI Mic Mini 2S review.

The audio quality with the DJI Mic Mini 2S is great, and the environmental noise cancellation makes it easy to use. You don’t need to worry about any unwanted background noise. The battery life is more than enough for day-to-day use, and the price is very attractive compared to other mics in the DJI range, such as the DJI Mic 3, which costs £259.

With 32-bit float audio capture, the DJI Mic Mini 2S can record a huge dynamic range — more than the human ear can hear. So, if there are quieter parts of the recording that are important, it's very easy to boost these in post-production. It also means that screeching sounds, like screams, for example, won't be clipped, and instead can simply be made quieter in post.

This is a feature of the DJI Mic 3, but not the earlier Mic Mini models, so having a flagship feature on a cheaper product like the 2S is nothing to be sniffed at.

The mics have 14.5GB of internal storage, which means they can hold around 22 hours of 32-bit float audio, or 28 hours of 24-bit float audio recording.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The microphone records sound, and especially airy sounds known as fricatives and sibilance, very well. These include sounds such as ‘s’, ‘sh’ and ‘f’. Sounds like this tend to cause whistling in the microphone, which is harsh for listeners, but that wasn’t an issue with this microphone.

As you can hear in the audio recording above, the words are clear without any distortion. However, plosives are a different story, and I’ll discuss that later on.

Connectivity with the DJI Mic Mini 2S couldn't be easier. The most straightforward way to use the plug-in USB-C receiver, but if you have a DJI camera you open the door to the DJI OsmoAudio Ecosystem.

When using the mic as part of the ecosystem, you can connect to any DJI devices without needing the receiver. You can also connect to traditional cameras using a 3.5mm cable, USB-C or simply via Blueutooth.

The transmitters and receiver of the DJI Mic Mini 2S have backward compatibility with older models, too. These include the Mic Mini and Mic Mini 2 transmitters, and you can connect up to four. You can mix and match, allowing you to upgrade your older setup with the latest noise-cancelling capabilities and 32-bit float rate by simply buying a Mic Mini 2S transmitter.

When I made the recording you can listen to above, I had my work laptop in front of me. As any remote worker will know, it tends to pop and ping with notifications almost eternally, and it was no different when I was delicately performing my tongue twisters.

I had to stop to re-record the clip a few times because of the notifications, but I finally decided to just keep going, and to my surprise, there wasn’t a single notification sound on the finished recording. The DJI Mic Mini 2S microphones use two-level noise-cancelling technology, which identifies and reduces unwanted background noise. The standard Mic Mini 2 struggles a little here, making the audio sound underwater, so the 2S is certainly an upgrade.

Each DJI Mic Mini 2S transmitter has 11 hours of battery life, which is more than the eight hours of the DJI Mic 3. The receiver of the Mic Mini 2S holds 10 hours of battery and the charging case gives a total of 40 hours of runtime.

This is more than enough battery for my usage, which is talking to a camera three times a week, and recording voice-overs for my videos. And for amateur creators taking the microphone out on a weekend-long adventure, it has enough power to carry you through most recording stints without reaching for a power pack.

The DJI Mic Mini 2S is available for purchase in the U.K. for £169 from Amazon or the DJI online store. This is the version I tested, with two transmitters, but you can also get a cheaper version with one transmitter for £79.

Unfortunately, you cannot purchase the Mic Mini 2S in the U.S. just yet due to ongoing regulatory and import restrictions against DJI, but you can still buy the older DJI Mic Mini for $99 at Amazon U.S.

Depending on what you need the mic for, you could opt to get the DJI Mic Mini 2, but this only connects two mics to the receiver, whereas the 2S can connect four.

If you want the flagship DJI Mic 3, you’re going to be paying £259. Going for a cheaper option and getting similar battery life, the same core mic components, and a similar level of environmental noise performance is — to me — a no-brainer.

Although this is one of the best microphones for content creation, it comes with two minor flaws. The letter ‘p’ is picked up very strongly by the microphone, and the receiver is a bit too bulky.

Although the audio is generally very impressive, when it comes to plosives, the microphone seems to struggle. These are notoriously difficult sounds, including the likes of ‘p’, ‘b’, ‘d’ and ‘g’. The most noticeable issue was with the ‘p’ sounds at the start of words, which sounded very harsh. I could hear the air pushing into the microphone.

This makes listening quite tiresome, as the pinching and popping sounds will put people off listening to the audio. This issue isn’t present in the DJI Mic Mini 2. It’s worth noting that these sounds can also be due to microphone etiquette (how close you hold the microphone to your mouth), so your performance will be better or worse depending on how you use the microphone.

This isn’t the end of the world, but the plug-in receiver for the DJI Mic Mini 2S is quite bulky. Depending on what it’s plugged into, it can make your device top-heavy or sit awkwardly on the table. When plugged into my phone, I can’t stand the phone up or lay it flat, which makes it feel a little cumbersome.

For ease of use, the Insta360 Mic Air is a better choice because it’s less bulky. This makes it more comfortable for longer recording sessions.

So, how does the DJI Mic Mini 2S measure up against its competitors? It certainly holds its own, and although it costs more than the budget Insta360 Mic Air (£69), I think it’s worth the extra spend. The DJI Mic Mini 2 (£89) is a lot cheaper than the 2S, but it’s still worth the extra spend if you’re planning to record in noisy environments and want to keep ambient sound out of your audio. The additional AI noise cancellation technology is what steps up this microphone, as it makes editing audio in post-production far easier.

I think the DJI Mic Mini 2S is the perfect option for anyone who wants to up their content game but is new to wireless microphones. Another good option is the Rode Wireless Micro for £139, as these clip-on microphones are also good for filtering ‘pop’ sounds, but for professional video makers, the DJI is still the best choice for quality.

The DJI Mic Mini 2S microphone has great audio quality. The environmental noise cancellation technology silenced all outside noise in my recordings, and it isolated my voice so it was crystal clear. The microphones also have a long battery life, and with the charging case you can get up to 40 hours of use. I think this microphone is great value for money as you get all of the perks of the flagship DJI models at a fraction of the price.

Though I love the microphones, there are obvious popping sounds when pronouncing plosives. The receiver is also bulky, so you’ll need to keep this in mind depending on the device you’re transmitting to.

I recommend the DJI Mic Mini 2S for content creators who need to level up their audio, especially if a lot of their work is done outside with lots of ambient sound.

#3176. Ibotta: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Operating leverage is converting revenue growth into profit faster than the top line, a structural advantage that compounds as the network scales.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 2, 2026, Ibotta (IBTA +2.98%) reported revenue of $97.8 million, up 17% year over year. Redemption volumes are accelerating, and retail partnerships are expanding, both signs that the company's digital promotions network is gaining real traction. And because the business carries high operating leverage, revenue gains flow almost directly to profit. Three takeaways from management's comments highlight the road ahead.

Management expanded brand advertiser relationships and increased offer supply across digital channels. That drove higher engagement on partner platforms. Third-party publisher platforms, which are digital properties operated by retail and delivery partners, saw redemptions surge as consumer demand for savings picked up.

By signing regional grocers and delivery services to the Ibotta Performance Network, the digital infrastructure powering partner promotions, management is reaching more shoppers. Adding convenience stores and regional grocery chains gives consumer packaged goods, or CPG, clients broader distribution across a wider range of retail formats.

Digital promotions carry virtually no variable delivery cost. So as revenue grows, profit margins expand along with it. Adjusted EBITDA, or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization adjusted for non-recurring items, reached $23.8 million, growing faster than top-line revenue.

Redemption momentum across digital channels supports early projections for 2027 revenue growth of at least mid-single digits. Broad publisher distribution and automated measurement tools give the company structural advantages over legacy promotion channels. And management is watching how durable offer supply holds up as new retail partners ramp.

In the meantime, deepening brand relationships and tight cost controls back up the long-term margin story as the company scales.

#3175. The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from today

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

From a new smart alarm clock to an Alexa-powered 3D map of your home, here's what's new from Amazon, including prices and release dates.

Amazon announced several new smart home devices today, including two all-new device categories: the $200 Echo Time smart alarm clock and the $230 Alexa Photo Frame. Both are available now, along with an upgraded Echo Dot for $100 and a new Echo Studio with a built-in Home Camera for $250.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Dot can turn into a Wi-Fi extender – how it works

The company’s smart home lineup also now includes a redesigned $500 Echo Show 16, which is available for preorder, with devices shipping in mid-December. Finally, Amazon announced the Alexa Home Map, which lets you create a 3D interactive map of your home’s interior and exterior.

Here are all the biggest updates to know.

The Amazon Echo Time is a new bedside companion and a definite upgrade over the Echo Spot. It’s a rounded speaker with a display and no camera, designed to be the smartest combination of alarm clock and hub available.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Studio gives Alexa+ an AI camera to see inside your home

The Echo Time doubles as a smart home hub, since it supports Zigbee and Matter and acts as a Thread border router. It costs $200, so it’s a definite price hike compared to the Echo Spot, but it’s also a more capable speaker with hub capabilities.

The Amazon Alexa Photo Frame is another first for Amazon, arriving just in time for the holidays. The photo frame consists of a 10.1-inch matte display with Alexa+ built in, made to cycle through your own collection of photos. It also allows you to search for specific photos by voice, as well as record voice notes associated with individual photos.

The Alexa Photo Frame comes in three frame finishes, including Birch, Walnut, and Black, so it can fit in with your home decor. It costs $230 and is already available for purchase.

Amazon also announced some big upgrades coming to the Echo lineup. They include a redesigned Echo Show 16, a new Echo Dot, and an upgraded Echo Studio with Home Camera.

The new Alexa Home Map lets you create a 3D interactive map of your home’s interior and exterior, allowing you to navigate floors, zoom into rooms, and see the locations of all your devices while controlling them in real time.

The concept isn’t a novel idea for Amazon, but the Alexa Home Map elevates the experience offered by the Amazon Alexa app’s Map View feature, which we covered at launch three years ago. Map View lets you create a basic layout of the rooms inside your home to place and tap device icons.

Unlike Map View, which focuses on indoor smart devices within four walls, the new Alexa Home Map offers a 360-degree aerial view of your property. It uses your Ring cameras to generate animations of people and cars moving around your yard and uses the controversial Familiar Faces feature to let you know who was detected.

Also: Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Forget everything you knew about Amazon tablets

You create the 3D interactive map of your home by using a compatible smartphone with a lidar feature to scan each room and then putting them together. You can then place Alexa-compatible smart home devices in each room and interact with them in real time, like turning on a light or lowering the volume on a speaker.

For the exterior of your home, enter your address, and the app will generate an Alexa Home Map of your residence using existing map data.

Using integrations with compatible Alexa devices, including Echo devices, Ring and Blink cameras, Fire TV devices, and other “Works with Alexa” smart home devices, will improve your home security, Amazon says. But it also opens the door for a whole lot more surveillance of your home, both for potential bad actors and for Amazon itself.

Amazon claims that the Alexa Home Map will update dynamically in real time, gathering data from your smart devices in and around your home. As a result, it can show the color of your smart twinkle lights during the holidays, as well as animations of people and cars moving around your property.

A vulnerability in a single third-party smart device could theoretically be used to pivot deeper into your home network or manipulate the map interface, not to mention that the data in this 3D map will include sensitive and private behavioral patterns, like when the family leaves the home or when children return.

#3174. You Can End Spammy Election Phone Calls Now With This iPhone Trick

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

The election is almost over, and you can end spam calls now.

Election day is a few days away, and that means political campaigns are mounting one last push to advocate for their candidate and issue. So you might be getting more election-related phone calls than usual. While those calls are well-meaning, they can be annoying if you’ve already voted early or have made up your mind about who to vote for. Luckily, if you keep your iPhone updated to the most recent iOS version, you can enable call screening on your device.

Apple introduced call screening in iOS 26. It isn’t an Apple Intelligence feature, so any iOS 27-compatible iPhone, such as the iPhone 14 Pro, can use it. I enabled the feature over a year ago and my iPhone has diligently held back spam calls, like the Hoover Dam, ever since. But you have to enable it first.

Here’s how to enable call screening in a few easy steps and what to know about the new feature.

1. Tap Settings.2. Tap Apps near the bottom of the menu.3. Tap Phone.

Under the section Screen Unknown Callers, you’ll see three options: Never, Ask Reason for Calling and Silence. Here’s what you should know about each of these options and which one is right for most people.

Choosing Never is the default option and lets calls from unsaved numbers come through and ring on your phone. It also documents missed calls in your Recents list in your Phone app, just like before call screening was available.

If you tap Ask Reason for Calling, your iPhone will ask anyone who calls you from an unsaved number why they are calling you without ringing your iPhone. After the caller answers a few questions, your iPhone will notify you with a transcript of the caller’s answers. Then you can decide whether you want to answer the call.

You can also pick Silence, which is the nuclear option for phone calls. Any unsaved numbers that call you will be silenced and sent to voicemail, no questions asked.

Ask Reason for Calling is the best option for most people who want to screen calls. I chose it, and while it notified me when scam callers answered some questions, which they rarely did, it also notified me when my doctor’s office called to go over some test results. If I had chosen Silence, I would have missed my doctor’s office (and choosing Never would mean checking every call if I was expecting something important).

If you choose Ask Reason for Calling and dislike it, you can always follow the steps above again and choose one of the other options. And remember, you can always silence your iPhone and not be bothered by any phone calls at all. My wife has not taken her phone off silent in months, and she remains blissfully unbothered by spam calls.

For more iOS news, here’s what to know about iOS 27.2 and iOS 27.1 as well as our iOS 27 cheat sheet for other tips and tricks.

#3173. What a $100 Monthly Investment in BlackRock Could Grow Into Over 20 Years

A $100 contribution each month for 20 years could help you build a lot of wealth.

BlackRock (BLK +1.71%) has been opportunistic and exhibited foresight over the past 20 years in building the world's largest investment management company. When BlackRock went public in 1999, it was owned by PNC Financial Services (PNC +1.67%) and was a middling player in the asset management business. That would change with major acquisitions, including the 2006 purchase of Merrill Lynch Investment Management, which immediately raised its profile as a top-10 asset manager.

But the biggest move came in 2009 when BlackRock acquired the world's largest asset manager at the time, Barclays Global Investors, or BGI. This transformed a minor player just a few years earlier into the world's largest money manager. It also brought BlackRock BGI's iShares family of exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which transformed how people invested and propelled BlackRock to the market dominance it has enjoyed since.

BlackRock anticipated the ETF boom, and now it looks to the next big change in the industry: private markets.

A few years ago, BlackRock made a big bet on private markets and alternative investments, making several acquisitions to build out its leadership position in these areas.

CEO Larry Fink believes it is a pivotal change for the company. "We see an opportunity to do for the public-private market divide what we did for index vs. active," Fink wrote in his 2025 shareholder letter -- that is, breaking down the separate silos that exist. He eventually sees indexing private markets, just like it does with the S&P 500.

By 2030, Fink expects private markets and technology to account for 30% of its anticipated $35 billion in revenue.

Ultimately, this strategy is designed to sustain BlackRock's market leadership for the next 10 or 20 years as it forges new revenue streams.

Can BlackRock stock match the success it has achieved over the past 20 years?

Since 2006, BlackRock stock has posted an average annualized total return of 13.4%, beating the S&P 500.

If you invested $10,000 in BlackRock stock 20 years ago and subsequently contributed $100 per month to that investment, you would have about $231,500 right now.

Without the $100 contribution per month, you would have about $123,700 -- that's about 46% less. Or, put differently, you would have 87% more by investing $100 per month in BlackRock stock.

So it really shows the importance of investing in the right stock, being patient, and consistently reinvesting in it, no matter what the stock price does at any given time.

It is impossible to know whether BlackRock will match that 13.4% return over the next 20 years, but the company seems to be anticipating the next big trend and investing in it. That should make investors feel pretty confident about BlackRock's future growth prospects.

#3172. 200,000 Folds and Counting for the iPhone Duo. How Far Can Our Fold-a-Phone Take It?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

We're folding Apple's iPhone Duo over and over -- 900 times an hour -- to test the durability of its hinge.

Happy November! The air is getting chillier, retailers are shifting from Halloween to the holidays, and the machine in CNET’s lab continues to test Apple’s first folding phone, the $1,999 iPhone Duo. We purchased this poor phone more than a week ago, and since then its only job has been to bend and flatten, bend and flatten, until it breaks.

So how many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? On Monday, Nov. 2, we passed 200,000 folds.

I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. Over the last week, I’ve seen a lot of chatter about the sturdiness of the Duo’s folding hinge and its potential to fail or crack. I’ve periodically examined the Duo we’re testing in our machine, and so far, I haven’t seen any signs of damage. And the crease isn’t any more visible than it was when we took it out of the box. If that changes, I’ll let you know here and on our livestream.

In the meantime, let me explain what we’re doing. My team and I designed and built a proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

#3171. Mistral’s Le Chonk is now a top open model for coding, ranking alongside Codex GPT-6.1 Terra

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Mistral has released the weights for Large 4, along with some impressive Artificial Analysis scores.

French AI lab Mistral shipped its latest model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), nicknamed “Le Chonk” for its trillion-parameter size, in preview on Oct. 6. As promised, the lab has released the model’s weights, alongside some new benchmark scores that show Western open models gaining ground over their Chinese peers.

Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot

After three weeks of testing with a select group of partners, Mistral’s model sets a new standard for Western-made open models, ranking at the top of Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index among open models globally. The model also comes with three reasoning modes now (low, medium, and high), as is common for heftier models to give users more options based on their level of task complexity.

ML4’s score on the agentic coding benchmark Terminal-Bench 4.0 jumped to 41% from its preview version’s 28% to 41%, beating Opencode’s GLM-5.3 by one small but important point. On the overall Index, however, which shows a model’s composite score across three relevant benchmarks, ML4 is a point behind GLM-5.3, scoring a 48 to GLM-5.3’s 49. Codex GPT-6.1 Terra also scores a 48 overall.

As a reminder, benchmark scores themselves should be taken with a grain of salt, especially considering how many models cheat.

Still, that improvement in performance is meaningful for just a few weeks of extra training. As proprietary AI remains expensive to use, economical models that don’t sacrifice performance are eye-catching. ML4 “rivals top open models such as GLM-5.3 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index while using 47% less tokens per task on average,” Mistral said.

When Mistral released ML4 in preview earlier this month, it touted how the model prioritizes cyber defense capabilities, advertising customizable control and data sovereignty. The company has spent the last few weeks working with developers and leaders to assess the model’s cybersecurity capabilities, a practice that’s becoming commonplace for proprietary American labs like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic as concerns about model security mounts.

Similarly to Anthropic’s Project Glasswing and OpenAI’s rollout of Astra, Mistral’s initial testing partners got access to a less guardrailed version of ML4 with “expanded cybersecurity capabilities.”

At least by some measure, ML4’s promises seem to have come true: Le Chonk scored just above DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on the CyberGym benchmark for defensive cybersecurity, which measures how well models find “real memory-safety vulnerabilities in C/C++ open-source projects, reproducing them with proof-of-concept inputs, and patching them without breaking the projects’ tests.”

Recent AI security incidents have somewhat pitted open and proprietary models against each other. Initially framed as less safe because of their malleability, open models are viewed as a new option for cyber defense after proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI proved just as risky.

Mistral said ML4 is built for security that stays under user control — unlike proprietary models, which frontier labs can technically rescind access to at any time.

“The cyber defense capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyberattacks,” Mistral co-founder Guillaume Lample said during a briefing for the Oct. 6 preview release.

Following the Hugging Face breach, Mistral was one of many companies that signed Nvidia’s Open Secure AI Alliance, a cross-industry partnership that argues open models are crucial to democratizing defenses against increasingly common AI security incidents.

Also: This new ChatGPT scam tricks you into installing malware

By Nvidia’s logic, and its Alliance that aims to democratize AI security tools, the race is between Mistral and other open models to achieve state-of-the-art security prowess.

Training a competitive model in a compute shortage is no small task for a trimmer lab like Mistral, which doesn’t have the same resources as a pre-IPO giant like Anthropic.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“ML4 was trained from scratch on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs over two months, deployed in Mistral’s own data centers in Europe,” the company said. For context, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said on X that OpenAI trained GPT-6 Astra on roughly 100,000 GPUs.

#3167. The 10-Year Treasury Eased to 4.9%. Here's Why Oklo, Archer, and Rocket Lab All Got Crushed -- and Which One I'd Buy Anyway.

Rising Treasury yields were bad news for many companies.

The 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.9%, but is still pressuring speculative growth stocks. Oklo (OKLO -6.85%), Archer Aviation (ACHR -0.71%), and Rocket Lab (RKLB -4.86%) have all taken a beating, but their long-term growth cases remain compelling.

Here's why they fell so sharply, and which one still looks like the best buy.

Higher Treasury yields make future earnings less valuable in today's dollars, which tends to hurt speculative growth stocks like Oklo.

The company has yet to scale its nuclear business before generating any meaningful revenue. As a result, investors may be less willing to pay a premium for profits that could be years away. Higher rates can also make financing its capital-heavy projects more expensive.

Still, the long-term case for advanced nuclear energy is intact. Oklo is developing its Aurora powerhouse, an advanced nuclear power plant designed to supply electricity to customers such as artificial intelligence data centers and industrial facilities.

The company is also working to establish a broader business around nuclear fuel recycling and isotope production.

Of course, Oklo faces risks, including potential issues with regulation, construction, and financing. The stock also trades at a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of about 3,600 times, suggesting that investors have high expectations that it will grow dramatically. But if commercialization takes longer than expected, the stock could see some significant downside.

Nuclear power isn't the only industry facing higher capital costs. That same pressure is hitting companies transforming how people travel.

Archer still needs to scale production and launch electric commercial air taxi services, so investors may be less willing to pay for growth that could take years to materialize. Like with Oklo, higher borrowing costs can also make funding its expansion more expensive. Despite that, encouraging developments are emerging.

Archer is working to establish air taxi networks, develop the infrastructure needed to support them, and build relationships with aviation and transportation partners. Plus, Archer is developing autonomous and hybrid-electric aircraft with military contractor Anduril, giving it exposure to the defense industry.

Archer still has to navigate risks around aircraft certification, production scaling, and customer adoption. The stock also trades at a P/S ratio of about 460 times, as investors expect that electric air taxis will become viable and that Archer can capture a meaningful share. If that doesn't happen, the stock could continue to face steep losses.

Meanwhile, the next company already has a developed business supporting its long-term ambitions.

Rocket Lab has an established business, but it's still investing heavily in new rockets and space systems, with much of its growth potential still years ahead. Like the others, though, higher borrowing costs could make its ambitious expansion plans less affordable to fund.

Still, Rocket Lab has built a broad space business that spans rocket launches, satellite components, and other space systems. Its Electron rocket has a track record of delivering small satellites into orbit, serving both commercial and government missions.

Rocket Lab is also developing Neutron, a medium-lift rocket that could serve a broader range of commercial and government launches. If successful, Neutron could expand its addressable market and tap more lucrative launch opportunities.

Even so, the company faces execution risks, competition, and the possibility that Neutron's inaugural launch could be delayed again. Its P/S ratio of about 45 times also reflects high expectations for growth. That means the stock could give back a lot more if those expectations aren't met.

All three stocks are feeling the pressure of higher yields, but one still looks like a buy.

Oklo is focused on advanced nuclear power, Archer is trying to establish an electric air taxi business, and Rocket Lab is expanding its existing business in the space industry.

Of these three stocks, Rocket Lab could be the top pick. It combines an established business with opportunities to expand into larger launch vehicles and advanced space systems. But looking ahead, if Treasury yields remain elevated and the stock sees a sharper pullback, it could be an opportunity to buy at a discount.

#3166. Firefox and Chrome patch 200+ security flaws combined – update both ASAP

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The latest version of Firefox fixes 167 security vulnerabilities, most of which are of high severity, while the newest version of Chrome patches 52 flaws, four of which are critical.

With security vulnerabilities continually plaguing the software we use, it’s time once again to update both Firefox and Chrome browsers to protect yourself from the latest exploits.

Also: Half of all cyberattacks start in your browser: 10 tips for staying safe

This week, Mozilla updated Firefox to version 159, not just for Windows but also for Android, MacOS, and Linux. The latest version includes fixes for 167 security bugs. Among these, 108 are rated of high severity, while the rest are considered moderate or low.

Almost 100 of them are defined as use-after-free (UAF) vulnerabilities, which are memory management flaws that an attacker could exploit to crash the browser or trigger malicious code. Several of the bugs also refer to Firefox’s Sandbox, which means that hackers could break through the browser’s protected Sandbox area to execute malicious code.

Given the nastiness of the security bugs, you’ll want to update Firefox ASAP. For that, open the browser, click the three-line icon at the upper right, move to Help and Report, and select About Firefox. The latest update will then be installed. Restart Firefox to finish the process.

Also: I dumped Firefox, but these 5 features finally won me back

Beyond the security patches, Firefox 159 adds a few handy new features.

With Firefox for the Mac, sharing a page in the browser now displays the built-in MacOS share picker. Here, you can see a preview of the page you want to share along with recent contacts and specific apps such as AirDrop and Messages.

Next up, you’re now able to access Firefox’s passwords tool in the sidebar. This lets you more easily view any website passwords that you’ve saved to the browser. To see this in action, first make sure the sidebar is visible. For that, click the Sidebar button on the Address bar and then click the key icon to display your saved passwords.

And as perhaps the most helpful new feature, Firefox’s AI-powered Smart Window can now watch specific web pages for changes and send you a notification when the page is updated. For this, turn on the option for Smart Window if it’s not already enabled. Click the Firefox icon in the upper right and select Smart Window. Navigate to the website for which you’d like to be notified of any changes. At the chat window, type /watch, fill out the form, and then click the Create Task button.

That takes us to Chrome with version 56.0.8078.73/.74 for Windows and Mac and version 156.0.8078.73 for Linux. Here, the latest update patches 52 security bugs. Out of these, four are rated critical, while 46 are rated high.

The four severe ones point to a memory corruption problem. But like some of the Firefox bugs, they also reference the browser’s Sandbox. In this case, an attacker who exploits any of these vulnerabilities could bypass Chrome’s protected Sandbox area to run malicious code. Also as in Firefox, several of the bugs point to use-after-free (UAF) issues that would allow an attacker to exploit memory management flaws to crash the browser or install malicious code.

Also: Chrome warns you about suspicious websites now

To update Chrome, click the three-dot icon at the top, move to Help, and select About Google Chrome. If prompted, allow the latest update to download and then restart the browser to finish.

Beyond many of the bugs themselves, Firefox and Chrome also share an increasing reliance on AI to find and resolve security flaws. In its advisory, Mozilla cited Amy Burnett, a security research and analyst at OpenAI, for uncovering many of the bugs. In its blog post, Google attributed the discovery of several flaws to Anthropic’s Claude and a few to OpenAI.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

With the midterms tomorrow, surveys from ABC News, NBC News and CNBC all show that majorities oppose new AI data centers near their communities.

A single large AI data center can use as much electricity as tens of thousands of homes, and residents in a growing number of communities worry about what that could mean for their utility bills. That concern has carried over from public hearings into tomorrow’s midterm elections.

Recent polls show majorities of Democrats and independents, along with a sizable share of Republicans, oppose new data centers in their areas. That leaves candidates in both parties answering questions about projects once courted by state and local leaders. Supporters say the facilities bring jobs, tax revenue and an advantage in AI development.

Further, a new poll from ABC News, the Washington Post and Ipsos found that a majority of Americans (57%) believe AI is bad for society, with many more pointing to its dangers than the potential benefits the tech could bring. An even larger number of those polled (66%) are opposed to the construction of new data centers in the US, and more (72%) would be opposed if it were in their community.

Opposition to AI crosses party lines. The technology has faced a surge in public disapproval this year, putting political candidates on blast and potentially affecting outcomes in key races, political and polling experts told CNET.

Ambivalence about AI also feeds into negativity toward data centers, which have, in a short time, become a rare bipartisan issue everyone’s talking about, according to Christopher Lee, partner and senior political strategist for Foresight Strategic Advisors.

Lee, who has closely followed election trends in southwestern states such as Nevada and Arizona, said the issue of data centers — massive AI server and compute farms that consume vast electricity and water resources — is going to “hammer” some candidates, especially those who weren’t transparent with constituents in the past about the cost to communities. If a politician voted for the construction of a data center earlier this year, their “political career is going to run into a stone wall,” he said.

The ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos survey asked a wide range of questions about how Americans will vote in the midterms and what they think of the political parties. Alongside the economy, immigration and the war against Iran, the AI rollout is a critical issue.

As noted by CNET reporter Katelyn Chedraoui, AI regulation and data center construction have been the subject of controversy, protests and increased legal action in communities.

The poll confirmed as much: 67% of respondents felt the government isn’t doing enough to regulate AI, with risks including widespread job losses, psychological dependency, economic inequality and even human extinction. Fears and negativity toward AI also extend to the election process itself, with AI election interference among Americans’ top 10 fears for 2026.

A national PR campaign funded by tech leaders and supported by the Trump administration, meant to tout the alleged benefits of data centers, such as job creation and technological advancements, doesn’t seem to be having the intended effect. Some politicians, especially those running for congressional seats, seem to be better at reading the room.

According to Lindsey Cormack, an associate professor of political science at Stevens Institute of Technology and co-host of the podcast Government That Doesn’t Suck, many candidates are paying close attention to how they communicate about AI developments, with a particular focus on the problems they present rather than the benefits they provide.

“It’s difficult to persuade people with promises of economic development when they’re worried about their electricity bills or water supply,” she said.

Cormack, creator of the congressional newsletter archive DCinbox, has tracked a sharp rise in lawmakers linking data centers to consumer energy costs. In an email to CNET, she noted that between January and September 2025, just 5% of Republican newsletters discussing data centers mentioned electricity bills or ratepayers (4 of 76). Over the same period in 2026, that figure surged to 54% (97 of 180). Democrats showed a similar focus, with 40% of their data center newsletters (71 of 176) raising the issue in 2026.

The midterms won’t be the end of the battle. AI and data centers are “going to be an issue in 2028 and 2030 and way beyond that,” Lee said.

#3163. Your headphones have hidden LE Audio features you’ll want to know about

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Your JBL, Sony, or Bose Bluetooth headphones got a top-to-bottom wireless makeover -- not just Auracast.

The shift from Classic Bluetooth to LE Audio is in full swing, as JBL and Sony release flagship headphones and earbuds with built-in LE Audio. Bose is the latest to upgrade its flagship headphones via an OTA firmware update.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Auracast, the Bluetooth protocol that enables one-to-many audio streams and is the most popular LE Audio feature, but several other LE Audio upgrades don’t get as much attention. These features improve wireless voice call quality, reduce battery drain in true wireless earbuds, and remove ecosystem barriers to low-latency mobile gaming. Here’s why they matter just as much as Auracast.

LE Audio includes the Low Complexity Communication Codec (LC3), which includes the unified Telephony and Media Audio Profile (TMAP) to handle audio streams and voice calls simultaneously. Bluetooth Classic relies on the Advanced Audio Distribution Profile (A2DP) and Hands-Free Profile (HFP), which handle the same functions but require both profiles.

Also: Bluetooth’s latest could solve a common connectivity problem

The profiles in Bluetooth Classic, given that they must alternate, result in extremely poor voice quality during hands-free calls over cellular or video calls on Zoom or Teams. These profiles also account for degraded voice quality when chatting while playing a mobile game.

LE Audio consolidates these two profiles, creating higher-quality, bidirectional audio and preserving voice call quality when using wireless headphones.

Earlier this year, JBL gave its flagship Tour Pro 3 earbuds an OTA firmware update to support LE Audio, and Sony’s WF-1000XM6 earbuds, released in February, have LE Audio support out of the box. There’s one major true wireless earbud improvement wrapped in LE Audio: native multi-stream audio.

Also: Frustrated with multipoint? How it works – and why it sometimes won’t

In Bluetooth Classic, your source device, such as your phone, sends audio to one earbud, which then retransmits it to the other earbud. This complex audio transmission method is why one of your earbuds always has a lower battery than the other. Though premium earbuds usually have an independent stream workaround, many midrange and budget earbuds don’t, and that’s where LE Audio comes in handy.

LE Audio enables independent audio streams built into the Bluetooth stack, so manufacturers don’t need to implement their own methods to avoid asymmetrical battery drain.

Software ecosystems, like Apple’s iOS and Samsung’s Galaxy, dictate which audio features are reserved for devices inside of them and withhold features from devices outside of them. Hardware ecosystems are equally responsible for the fragmentation of audio features across manufacturers, typically through codecs.

Sony’s LDAC codec for high-quality audio is only available on Sony headphones, earbuds, and smartphones with the proper hardware, which is limited in the US market. Snapdragon’s AptX codecs aren’t as widely available on phones either, leaving most people to rely on Bluetooth Classic SBC and AAC codes, even though their headphones support more advanced ones.

Also: Your iPhone may support Bluetooth Channel Sounding – and it’s a big deal

LE Audio eliminates the tedious codec issue, especially in wireless gaming contexts, delivering lower latency, improved voice audio streams, and eliminating asymmetrical audio transmission.

For now, as long as you have a compatible Android phone, you have access to several models of headphones, earbuds, and Bluetooth speakers that support LE Audio. As more manufacturers update their devices to support the Bluetooth audio streaming protocol, this suggests the technology is becoming more reliable.

So, what about your AirPods? I wouldn’t bet on it anytime soon.

#3159. Stop Charging Your Phone to 100%. Here’s What to Do Instead

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

A few changes to when and how you charge, plus one built-in setting, can keep your phone’s battery healthier for longer.

A phone running a game while plugged into a fast charger gets hot, and that heat wears down the battery faster than almost any other charging habit. Leaving it at 100% for hours causes similar damage more gradually. Both habits are easy to avoid once you know what to watch for, and most phones now include settings that can help. Here’s what to change in your routine.

Voltage stress at the top of the charge range, heat from fast charging and the cumulative effects of full discharge cycles all accelerate capacity loss. The damage may not appear immediately, but it’s measurable after one year and obvious after two.

Age is part of it, sure, but the overnight charging habit accelerates the process considerably. Lithium-ion batteries lose capacity faster when they spend extended time at the top of their charge range, which is precisely where an overnight charge leaves them. The fix doesn’t require a new phone or even a new charger. It requires a small adjustment to a habit most people have never thought twice about.

Keeping a lithium-ion cell pinned at 100% creates voltage stress, and the heat generated from sitting on a charger could end up meaning the difference between keeping your current phone a little longer or having to buy a new one. So once and for all, does keeping your phone plugged in really hurt the battery? Here’s what the experts suggest.

It isn’t about immediate damage but rather how fast your battery ages over time. Understanding the difference between what will and won’t break your phone is key. Here is the truth about your charging habits.

Battery health is not just about how many times you charge your phone. It is also about how it manages voltage, temperature and maintenance. Lithium-ion batteries age fastest when they are exposed to extreme levels: 0% and 100%.

Keeping these batteries near full charge for long stretches of time puts additional voltage stress on the cathode and electrolyte. This is why many devices use “trickle charging” or temporarily pause at 100%, topping up only when needed.

Still, the biggest threat is not overcharging, but heat. When your phone is plugged in and running demanding apps, it produces heat that accelerates chemical wear inside the battery. If you are gaming, streaming or charging on a hot day, that extra warmth does far more harm than leaving the cable plugged in overnight.

The Apple battery guide describes lithium-ion batteries as “consumable components” that naturally lose capacity over time. To slow that decline, iPhones use Optimized Battery Charging, which learns your daily routine and pauses charging at about 80% until just before you typically unplug, reducing time spent at high voltage.

Apple also advises keeping devices between 0 and 35 degrees Celsius (32 and 95 degrees Fahrenheit) and removing certain cases while charging to improve heat dissipation. You can read more on the official Apple battery support page.

Samsung offers a similar feature called Battery Protect, found in the One UI battery and device care settings. When enabled, it caps charging at 85%, which helps reduce stress during long charging sessions.

Other Android makers like Google, OnePlus and Xiaomi include comparable options — often called Adaptive Charging, Optimized Charging or Battery Care — that dynamically slow power delivery or limit charge based on your habits. These systems make it safe to leave your phone plugged in for extended periods without fear of overcharging.

Even with these safeguards, some conditions can accelerate battery wear. As mentioned before, the most common culprit is high temperatures. Even for a short period of time, leaving your phone charging in direct sunlight, in a car or under a pillow can push temperatures into unsafe zones.

Heavy use, such as gaming or 4K video editing, while charging can also cause temperature spikes which can degrade the battery faster. And cheap, uncertified cables or adapters may deliver unstable current that stresses cells. If your battery is already several years old, it will naturally be more sensitive to this kind of strain.

There is no need to overhaul your habits, but a few tweaks can help your battery age gracefully. Start by turning on the optimization tools on your phone: Optimized Battery Charging on iPhones, Battery Protect on Samsung devices and Adaptive Charging on Google Pixels. These systems learn your routine and adjust charging speed so your phone is not sitting at 100% all night.

Keep your phone cool while charging. According to Apple, phone batteries perform best between 62 and 72 degrees Fahrenheit (16 to 22 degrees Celsius). If your phone feels hot, remove its case or move it to a better ventilated or shaded spot. Avoid tossing your phone under a pillow or too close to other electronics, like your laptop. Skip wireless chargers that trap heat overnight. Use quality chargers and cables from your phone manufacturer or trusted brands. Those cheap “fast-charge” kits you find online often deliver inconsistent current, which can cause long-term issues.

Finally, try not to obsess over topping off the charge. It is perfectly fine to plug in your phone during the day for short bursts. Lithium-ion batteries actually prefer frequent, shallow charges rather than deep full cycles. There is no need to keep it between 20% and 80% all the time, but just avoid extremes when possible.

Keeping your phone plugged in overnight or on your desk all day will not destroy its battery. That is a leftover myth from a different era of tech. Modern phones are smart enough to protect themselves, and features such as Optimized Battery Charging or Battery Protect do most of the heavy lifting for you.

Still, no battery lasts forever. The best way to slow the inevitable is to manage heat, use quality chargers and let the software on your phone do its job. Think of it less as “babying” your battery and more as charging with intention. A few mindful habits today can keep your phone running strong for years to come.

With this weekend’s fall-back time change, your Apple Watch should’ve automatically updated to the correct time without intervention. But what if that’s not the case?

According to Apple, a bug is causing some Apple Watches to display the wrong time — off by an hour — on the home screen. While this hiccup doesn’t appear terribly widespread, it could not doubt lead to confusion, especially if you use your Apple Watch as an alarm clock.

Fortunately, there are two very easy ways to correct the issue if your Apple Watch is showing the wrong time. The first involves simply restarting your watch by holding down the side button until the slider appears, and then again until the Apple logo reappears.

However, if that doesn’t work, try the old watch face swaperoo trick — listed out in five easy steps below — for a surefire fix.

Read on to see full illustrated instructions for each step.

If your Apple Watch is showing the incorrect time by default, the first thing you'll want to do is open the Apple Watch app on your iPhone and tap on the "Face Gallery" at the bottom center of the screen.

Next, choose any of the watch faces by tapping "Get." We're only switching to this watch face temporarily, so it really doesn't matter which one you choose.

Once it's downloaded to your phone (this should take just a few seconds), tap on the preview of the new watch face, and then tap "Add to Watch" to temporarily install the face.

With the new watch face installed, your Apple Watch should now be showing the correct time, which means it is time to revert back to your original watch face. To do this, tap on "My Watch" at the bottom left of the screen to return to the Apple Watch app's main screen. Next, tap on your preferred watch face from the "My Faces" carousel at the top.

Finally, scroll down to the bottom of the watch face customization page and tap "Set as current Watch Face." This will reinstall your original watch face.

And just like that, your preferred Apple Watch face should be showing the correct daylight-savings-adjusted time.

#3157. Barclays Turned Bearish on NuScale Power at a 52-Week Low. Here's the Single Missing Contract That Would Prove It Wrong.

NuScale Power needs to sign its first reactor contract before it can take its next big step as a business.

Shares of NuScale Power (SMR -4.80%) are down more than 85% from their 52-week high. Barclays reduced its price target on the stock in late October, dropping it from $11 to $5. The stock currently trades at around $5 per share, so the Wall Street firm is basically suggesting the stock is fully valued. A signed contract with ENTRA1 Energy or RoPower could prove Barclays wrong. Here's what you need to know.

Nuclear power isn't new, and NuScale Power isn't trying to reinvent the wheel. What it has basically done is downsize existing nuclear power technology while using the most modern safety protocols in its small modular nuclear reactor (SMR) design. That design has received key regulatory approvals, so the company has achieved significant success.

There's just one problem. NuScale Power has yet to find an official customer. It has irons in the fire, but nobody has signed on the dotted line yet. That's a big reason why Barclays turned bearish on the stock. Essentially, until the company actually has an agreement to sell an SMR, there's no way to really know how much of an opportunity there is for the business. And if it can't get that first contract, well, then there is no opportunity at all.

As a money-losing start-up, the clock is ticking. That's not to suggest that NuScale Power is at imminent risk of running out of money, but at the end of the second quarter of 2026 it had a little over $1 billion of cash on its balance sheet. At the start of the year, it had a bit over $1.2 billion. There's more room for the company to burn through cash as it awaits its first contract, but at some point the cash will run out.

NuScale Power has two potential sales lined up, and either one could materially improve the business outlook. In Romania, RoPower, a utility company, has given the green light to a nuclear power plant project that would use six NuScale SMRs. But RoPower still has to find funding for the project before it can begin. NuScale Power just has to wait and hope.

ENTRA1 Energy is in "advance discussions" with the Tennessee Valley Authority around a "power purchase agreement for potentially the largest nuclear power deployment program in U.S. history." NuScale Power's SMR technology is in the mix. But, like RoPower, there's no final agreement yet. Barclays notes that ENTRA1 Energy and the Tennessee Valley Authority are likely to be negotiating until at least early 2027. So there's no near-term catalyst for NuScale Power's business there, either.

A signed contract for a NuScale SMR would be a huge step forward, but even that has to be taken with a grain of salt. Once a deal is inked, NuScale Power will have to build and deliver its SMRs, and they would have to operate as expected, before the company's technology is fully proven out. So a signed contract is important, but it is just a step along the way.

NuScale Power is only appropriate for more aggressive growth investors. Right now, it is bleeding cash as it tries to find its first official customer. Once it does, it will likely continue to bleed cash as it works to build and deliver its first SMR. A signed contract will change the story in a big way, perhaps even proving Barclays' negativity wrong. But there's still a lot of work to be done even after the first contract is signed. Most investors should probably watch from the sidelines for now.

#3155. Google’s Legend of Zelda Easter Egg Will Take You Back in Time. Here’s How to Find It

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Crank up Céline Dion: You can catch a glimpse into what Google was like back in 1998.

Nintendo is gearing up to release its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Thursday, and Google is marking the occasion with an Easter egg that transports the search engine back to 1998 – the year the original game was released.

If you go to Google.com now and search for “Zelda,” the game’s legendary Master Sword appears in the bottom right corner of the screen. In The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, the sword is a means to travel back and forth in time. (Searching for “Master Sword” also manifests the legendary weapon.)

When you click the sword, it thrusts into a pedestal and an animation plays before revealing a pre-2000s search page. In this view, you see the classic blue links, the I’m Feeling Lucky button and instead of seeing “Google” in the top-left corner of the page, you see the retro-looking “Google!” with an exclamation point. (Google removed the exclamation point from its logo in 1999.) If you stay real quiet and listen closely, you might also be able to hear Céline Dion’s My Heart Will Go On in the background.

What you won’t see on this page are any ads, AI overviews or random social media posts. It’s such a retro experience, and a fun reminder of what using Google was like back in the day. The neater, less cluttered layout made me feel instantly calmer than Google’s normal view.

However, this change isn’t permanent. As soon as you search for something else in this view, you’re transported back to the current version of Google Search. I wish there were an option to permanently enable this view, but for now, I’ll enjoy this slice of internet nostalgia.
