#3118. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

My Amazon smart display has been filling with AI garbage. Here's how to clear it out if you're struggling.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

With Amazon announcing a new Echo Show 16 to square off with Apple’s upcoming HomeView, the smart displays are having a moment, but I’ve noticed something seems off. In the past week or two, my Echo Show has started showing me a lot of lazy, annoying AI-generated ads under a playback feature called Created For You. So I figured out how to improve my experience with a few settings changes.

Not only is this AI slop vague and accompanied by poorly generated images, but it also doesn’t seem to have anything to do with my recorded interests or personalization, either. The slides range from questions about squirrels finding nuts and how to make cornfield mazes to facts about daylight saving time. Basically, it’s very general content I don’t really care about and don’t want showing on a central display at home.

I suspect Amazon is pushing its AI podcasts and similar chatty content with this latest round of generated ads, but if you’re not interested in viewing any of these canned clips, they can come across as irksome. So I reviewed my settings options and found out how to push my Show display away from these creations and toward more interesting content.

The good news is you can control what your Echo Show, well, shows you — but you have to know what settings to change. This isn’t very easy through the Alexa app, but I found a better way using the Show’s own touchscreen controls. Here’s what to do when you have a minute.

First, when an AI slide like this appears, tap the three-dot menu button and tap the thumbs-down option to indicate your dislike. It’s not a perfect solution, but it should help start weeding out these types of ads.

Next, swipe down on your Echo Show device to access the main menu, and choose Settings. Then choose Display & Appearance, and head to Content Categories.

Here you have two options. You can manually turn off all the categories you don’t want to see, especially those connected to the AI slop that you’ve been seeing. Keep focus on topics that you’re interested in if you still want to see other related content. You can also toggle the Rotate Once setting on, which will show you Amazon’s slides only once, my preferred option for handling this kind of unwanted content.

As an alternative, you can switch your Echo Show to show only a photo album of your choosing. I like getting some Alexa recommendations like recipes and updates, so this option isn’t for me, but if you have a good photo album to share with Alexa, you can limit your slides to only your own content.

With these settings adjusted, you should see far fewer AI-generated images and more slides tailored to your own interests. I’ll keep an eye on my Echo Shows and let you know if anything changes, but this has worked well for me so far.

#3114. You can easily update your AirPods firmware in just a few simple steps

AirPods firmware updates can bring new features and improvements, but installing them is a bit obtuse.

Similar to how your iPhone gets regular software updates, AirPods sometimes receive firmware updates. At times, these updates simply improve reliability and fix bugs, but some also introduce new features. For example, some AirPods models gained a Custom EQ feature with the iOS 27 update. But you may have never heard of AirPods firmware updates since Apple hides this process from view.

It's not like updating iOS, where there's a dedicated page inside Settings to check for updates — everything happens silently in the background. The good news is that there are a few ways to trigger AirPods firmware updates, plus ways to check which version your earbuds are running.

Before updating your AirPods, you need to make sure you have an iPhone, iPad or Mac running the latest software. That's because new AirPods firmware updates often require the latest version of iOS or macOS. This is as simple as opening the Settings app, going to General and then choosing Software Update. If an update is available, you'll find it there. If not, your device will say you're running the latest version.

Now it's time to check which firmware version your AirPods are currently running. On an iPhone or iPad, connect your earbuds and open Settings — you'll see an AirPods menu at the top. Tap and scroll down until you find Version in the About section. On a Mac, open System Settings and go to the Bluetooth menu. Find your AirPods and click the i button on the right to find the same information.

Apple has an AirPods firmware page where you can check the latest version available for each model, so compare this to what you found to see if there's a newer release available. If the number doesn't match, your AirPods probably need a firmware update.

Now comes the tricky part. There's no way to directly force AirPods to install a new firmware update, and Apple says that firmware updates are "delivered automatically." However, the company does explain how to best prepare your earbuds for an update. First, make sure your AirPods are paired with your iPhone, iPad or Mac, and that the connected device has Bluetooth on. Your device also must be connected to Wi-Fi, because the update won't download over 4G or 5G.

Once everything looks good, put your AirPods in the charging case and plug it into a power source with the lid closed. Keep the earbuds within range of your device and wait about 30 minutes. After that, reconnect your AirPods and check the firmware version again.

The process is pretty much the same for AirPods Max — just put them in the case and plug them into a charger. If for some reason you use AirPods but don't have an Apple device, take your AirPods to an Apple Store or an Apple Authorized Service Provider, and they'll update the firmware for you.

Most new AirPods features are added through firmware updates, and sometimes these updates are major. Features such as Live Translation, studio-quality audio recording and remote camera control were all introduced with firmware updates for AirPods. Although new features are often exclusive to the latest models, even older models may still benefit from updates. Custom EQ, for example, works with all AirPods that have an H2 chip.

Of course, not every AirPods firmware update brings new features. Many of them are limited to the standard "bug fixes and other improvements" release notes. Still, these firmware updates can fix connection issues and other annoyances you might encounter while using AirPods, so it's always a good idea to keep them updated.

#3113. The reason why some USB ports are black

As with most USB colors, it indicates the port’s capabilities. At least it should.

In most cases (not all), a black USB port denotes a USB 2.0 connection, also known as Hi-Speed USB, which supports data transfer rates up to 480 Mbps. However, as our previous articles on orange and purple USB ports noted, this is not an industry standard. It's a common convention, sure, but a black USB 2.0 port on one PC doesn't mean another PC's black USB port is also USB 2.0.

The best way to know for certain is to check the markings beside the port and the manufacturer's documentation. Oftentimes, digging through the manual is the only way, because symbols, icons or letters may not be enough to positively identify a port. Some may not even have any labels at all.

Note that USB-A port colors and their meanings do not transfer over to USB-C. In fact, most USB-C ports don't have any colors at all. If one does, it's likely cosmetic. USB-C ports have a much wider range of capabilities, and color-coding them would likely get confusing.

If you've confirmed that a particular USB-A port is USB 2.0, you're good to use it for everyday accessories. Think basic flash drives, keyboards and mice, wired game controllers, mics, headsets and other similar devices. You generally don't want to waste a much faster port on these accessories.

Where USB 2.0 ports fall short is with more demanding peripherals. An external HDD or SSD is a prime example. Copying large video files or backing up a drive can be agonizingly slow over USB 2.0 due to limited transfer rates; don't let the "Hi-Speed" label fool you. USB 2.0 may also have power limitations that prevent certain drives from working properly. Seagate, for example, states that a drive like the Wireless Plus 2TB may not be detected on certain USB 2.0 connections if they supply insufficient voltage.

That said, many USB 3.0 devices will likely work fine when connected to a USB 2.0 port, though the device will be limited to USB 2.0's maximum throughput. The reverse works as well. A USB 2.0 accessory can connect to a USB 3.0 port, but the accessory won't perform any better than it normally would. Thus, you should match the port to the device: Use USB 2.0 ports for low-speed, low-power devices and reserve your faster or "Always On" ports for ones that will benefit.

According to convention, black USB ports are faster. White ones are typically USB 1.x, which maxes out at 1.5 Mbps in low-speed mode and 12 Mbps at full speed. The USB 2.0 "Hi-Speed" protocol that black USB ports support tops out at 480 Mbps, making them 40 times faster.

All this still boils down to the manufacturer's choice, of course. Most USB port colors you'll encounter will match the standard capabilities listed online, but not all. Some PCs and motherboards will use the same color for all their USB ports, even though they will support different protocols. Without any set-in-stone standards, manufacturers can use whatever colors they desire and label them accordingly, or not at all. Fortunately, most stick to the common ones.

If you're not sure, it's best to go to the source. Pull out that boring manual or check the manufacturer's website. Black and white USB ports (or those with other colors) shouldn't have the same capabilities, but "shouldn't" is not a guarantee.

When buying bonds, look beyond the yield and pay attention to the interest rate risks. Short-term bonds can be safer.

Bond yields on widely watched benchmarks like the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond have recently reached 24-year highs. Higher bond yields are making some investors wonder if now is a good time to buy bonds.

The answer depends on "what kind of bonds?" Based on your investment timeline, your risk tolerance, and your overall financial goals, not all bonds are the right choice for every investor.

If you want to earn a higher yield on your cash, ultra-short-term bond exchange-traded funds (ETFs) might be worth a look. These bond ETFs let you put your money to work without as much interest rate risk as longer-term bonds.

According to Bloomberg research, ultra-short-term bond ETFs have attracted $75 billion of new investor money in October 2026. Some short-term bond ETFs are offering yields of up to 5%.

Let's look at why now could be a good time to invest in bonds -- especially short-term bonds.

Longer-duration bonds, like 20-year or 30-year U.S. Treasuries, pay a fixed rate of income for decades – currently about 5.35% for the 20-year Treasury, or 5.32% for the 30-year Treasury. This might sound like a good deal. And long-term bonds can be a good investment if interest rates go lower after you buy them -- because the bonds' price will go up in that scenario.

But those longer-term bonds also have higher interest rate risk. If bond yields (and interest rates) go higher after you buy a bond, the bond's price goes down. This can cause bigger volatility for longer-term bonds.

Investors who want decent yield on their bonds without the risks of rising interest rates might want to consider ultra-short-term bond ETFs. Short-term bonds are still not risk-free. In case interest rates go higher after you buy into an ultra-short-term bond ETF, the price of the ETF could go down. But these short-term bonds are less sensitive to interest rate risk than longer-duration bonds (like 10-year or 20-year Treasuries, for example).

If you want to buy ultra-short-term bond ETFs, look for a fund that holds bonds with short durations, such as less than one year.

The iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond ETF (SGOV +0.03%) is an example of an ultra-short-term bond fund. As its full name suggests, SGOV only holds U.S. Treasuries, and all of them are set to mature within three months. This bond ETF is delivering a 30-day SEC Yield of 3.79% as of Oct. 29. In the past five years, it's delivered annualized returns of 3.78%. This fund charges a low expense ratio of 0.09%.

Ultra-short-term bond ETFs might not always outperform the best high-yield savings accounts or money market funds. Depending on how much cash you have available to put into bonds, or where you hold your short-term liquid assets, ultra-short-term bond ETFs aren't always the right choice.

Some bond ETFs called "short duration bond ETFs," could also be worth considering if you want higher yields and can accept the possible risks. The iShares Short Duration Bond Active ETF (NEAR +0.02%) is an actively managed bond fund that was paying a 30-day SEC Yield of 4.99% as of Oct. 29.

This fund holds a broader mix of bonds, including U.S. Treasuries and (mostly) investment-grade corporate bonds. Instead of focusing on 0-3 month maturities, about 91% of the NEAR portfolio is short-term bonds with maturities of less than 5 years.

This fund charges a 0.25% expense ratio, so be sure to consider if it's worth paying that fee. In the past five years, NEAR has delivered annualized returns of 3.78% -- the same as the lower-cost, possibly lower-risk iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond ETF.

There's no guarantee that either of these bond funds will be risk-free, beat inflation, or do better than cash in a high-yield savings account. But if you want to earn a decent yield on your short-term liquid assets without worrying about the risks of rising interest rates, choosing shorter-duration bond ETFs is a good move.

#3111. As Fed Holds Steady, Are 7.5% Mortgage Rates Still Possible?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

The Fed voted to hold rates steady, but mortgage rates still have room to grow.

On Wednesday, Oct. 28, the Federal Reserve announced that central bankers would leave the federal funds rate unchanged. Since this was in line with market expectations, mortgage rates shouldn’t have much of a reaction — yet.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage slid 10 basis points to 7.17% APR in the week ending Oct. 28, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

Central bankers have twin goals when setting monetary policy: Getting inflation as close to 2% as possible, and maintaining maximum employment. When inflation gets too high, the Fed can raise the federal funds rate, which causes consumer borrowing rates (like mortgage rates) to rise as well. When unemployment gets too high, they can lower the federal funds rate to make it cheaper for businesses to access credit and hire more employees.

Since the latest jobs report showed that employment was relatively steady last month, that leaves inflation as the hot topic.

Despite Fed Chair Kevin Warsh holding true to his signature tight-lipped style in the weeks leading up to the meeting — and despite September’s preliminary inflation numbers running high so far — futures traders were largely confident that the Fed would keep the federal funds rate as is this week after last month’s hike.

Not necessarily. Mortgage rates could be completely different tomorrow.

In fact, we’ll probably see rates shift in response to the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, or PCE, which is set to be released on Thursday, Oct. 29. This is the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. Central bankers didn’t have this data during voting, which may be one reason they decided against adjusting the federal funds rate again quite yet.

If this week’s PCE data shows inflation rising, mortgage rates will probably go up over the next few weeks as lenders look to protect their investment against a weakening dollar. Rising inflation also bolsters the case for a rate hike at the central bankers’ next meeting; according to the futures traders behind CME FedWatch, there’s a very good chance that the Fed will announce an increase on Dec. 9.

And there is reason to think that PCE will show growing inflation. September’s monthly Consumer Price Index (CPI), which measures changes in prices of everyday goods and services, was released on Oct. 14 and showed annual inflation rising to 3.7%.

Of course, mortgage rates respond to all sorts of things. Oil prices, the bond market, global and national events — any number of hard-to-predict happenings could swing rates in the coming days and weeks. But if market analysts dig their heels into the idea of a December rate hike from the Fed, you should probably prepare for higher mortgage rates in November.

So far, 30-year mortgage rates are averaging 7.3% for October, compared with September’s average of 6.98%. On this trajectory, it’s conceivable that we could see rates hit 7.5% this year — a monthly average we haven’t seen since October 2023.

If and when the Fed does raise the federal funds rate again, it will be meant as a temporary treatment for overheated inflation.

Think of it as bitter medicine: It might be tough to swallow, but getting inflation under control actually paves the way for lower rates down the line. Moderating inflation could also lead to lower prices on essential goods that have been eating away at the prospective home buyer’s wallet, freeing up more cash for your monthly mortgage payment.

#3110. Why Opendoor Stock Dropped 20% in October

Shares of digital real estate company Opendoor Technologies (OPEN +0.00%) fell 20% in October, according to data provided by S&P Global Market Intelligence. There was negative market sentiment as interest rates stayed steady and are expected to increase.

Opendoor operates a digital platform that hosts a real estate marketplace and buys homes to renovate and sell. Clearly, it's a capital-heavy business because homes cost a lot of money, which means it needs access to capital at cheap rates to keep going.

The model has been challenged by the poor housing market. High interest rates don't just mean it's harder for it to buy homes, but it also means that there are fewer homes for sale and fewer buyers looking.

The company brought in a new CEO last year to change things up and breathe life into the business, and there has been progress. In the second quarter, it bought 77% more homes than the first, and the percentage of homes on the market for over 120 Days declined from 10% to 9%, compared with 27% for the industry.

It's also becoming more cost-efficient. Operations expense per home closing declined from $8,400 last year and $5,000 in the first quarter to $3,000, and it made 6,908 on $5 million marketing spend, whereas the last time it topped 6,000 acquisitions, it spent $81 million.

However, the quarter-over-quarter metrics were still disappointing. Revenue dropped 44%, it sold 1,960 fewer homes, and net loss expanded from $29 million to $162 million.

New CEO Kaz Najatian claims that the company will have positive adjusted net income on a 12-month, go-forward basis by the end of the year, meaning the run rate for the forward period will be positive.

If interest rates do come down, or the housing market is somehow rejuvenated, Opendoor could have a shot at real growth. However, it looks like it could still be a long time until that happens. That's how the market is pricing the stock right now.

Not only did Opendoor stock lose 20% in October, but it's down 69% this year, and it's 95% off its high. It looks like the market was giving Nejatian a shot, but it doesn't see the light at the end of the tunnel.

However, Opendoor reports third-quarter results on Nov. 5, and if there's enough progress, the stock could jump higher.

#3109. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL). Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

In oil and gas, refiners and big energy stocks are generating cash for investors, and Morgan Stanley is optimistic more is coming.

The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF).

Two big calls to quickly highlight in power production.

First, Truist says you have to buy First Solar (FSLR). The analyst upgrades it to Buy with a $270 target. Tariffs should help the Phoenix-based company, giving it pricing power for at least four more years. The Section 232 tariffs—which are too complicated to detail here—should help First Solar raise solar module prices and boost earnings. We agree, having written about the company and stock back in July.

Another call on the Power Insider radar: TD Cowen is starting coverage of TeraWulf (WULF) with a Buy rating and a $21 target. That indicates about 50% upside for the stock, but it's actually one of the Street's lower price targets. TeraWulf and other AI power companies have seen their stocks hit hard following months of big gains, but Cowen analyst Michael Elias says the valuation is now attractive and a likely lease in the second half of 2027 at a Kentucky location could be a catalyst.

In the wake of the terror attacks on Saudi Arabia, we spoke with RBC Capital Markets' Helima Croft about the attacks, energy and more.

The entire energy world is watching Europe's natural gas storage levels. The question is whether the continent will have enough gas to make it safely through the winter. Power Insider wrote about the topic in the last issue.

The fact that JPMorgan highlights expected weather patterns should tell you how much temperature matters when it comes to gas storage. The early forecast calls for October and November to be average or slightly warmer than the 10-year average. The red line represents the 10-year average.

Europe has been largely "saved" by mild temperatures over the past few years. Natural gas storage levels are lower this year than in years past, so the thermometer will matter a lot when it comes to how well countries can, ahem, weather the winter. Random, but interesting.

#3108. Micron Said "Super Intelligence" Creates the Most Compelling Opportunity in Its History. Here's Why It Matters for Investors.

Micron is sitting on the biggest growth opportunity since its inception 48 years ago.

Micron Technology (MU -5.78%) has spent decades making memory chips. Now, the company believes artificial intelligence could create the greatest opportunity the company has ever seen.

"Super intelligence is creating the most compelling opportunity for Micron in its history," CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said during the company's fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call on Sept 30.

That is a bold statement from a company that has survived multiple memory-market booms and busts. But the interesting part isn't simply that AI needs more memory, but that memory could become a more important source of competitive advantage for AI companies, giving Micron greater opportunities to differentiate its products and capture value.

When investors think about AI infrastructure, they tend to focus on graphics processing units (GPUs) and other powerful processors. These chips perform the computationally intensive calculations that allow AI models to train and generate responses.

But those high-end processors need large quantities of data to work on, and they need to be able to access it rapidly. Think of a GPU as a chef working in a busy restaurant. The chef might be exceptionally skilled, but if the ingredients arrive too slowly, the chef stands around waiting, and the whole kitchen slows down. Similarly, a powerful AI processor can sit underutilized if it cannot reliably access the data it needs fast enough.

That's where memory comes in. High bandwidth memory (HBM) delivers data rapidly to AI processors. Conventional DRAM provides fast access to information while applications run. NAND-based storage holds the enormous data sets, models, and other information that AI systems use. These technologies perform different jobs, but they work together to determine how effectively an AI system operates.

As AI models become more capable and workloads grow, memory capacity, bandwidth, and power efficiency become increasingly important. That will continue to be a huge tailwind for companies like Micron.

On the fiscal Q4 earnings call, Micron management explained that AI applications run across competing platforms, whether they use open-source or proprietary models. Yet these platforms share a common characteristic: Their performance and value depend partly on the capabilities of their memory and storage.

Consider two AI platforms. One has relatively limited memory capacity and struggles to handle increasingly demanding workloads. The other can support larger workloads, retrieve information more efficiently, and deliver a better user experience. The second platform could attract more usage and create greater value for its customers.

That gives AI infrastructure providers a reason to care about more than the purchase prices of memory chips. Performance, power consumption, reliability, and availability can all be more important. For Micron, this creates an opportunity to compete on product quality and technological leadership rather than price alone.

The distinction is important because memory has historically been more of a commodity business, and the market has been highly cyclical as a result. When the supply of memory exceeded demand, prices would fall sharply, and because there was little to differentiate one maker's products from those of its peers, all of them were subject to that same dynamic.

If advanced memory becomes increasingly critical to AI performance, Micron could capture more value from its technology and product mix.

That doesn't mean the memory market will stop being cyclical. Competitors such as SK Hynix and Samsung will continue investing in their own R&D, and all the players in the space are building new chip foundries to increase production. At a certain point, that additional new capacity should shift the supply-and-demand dynamic back to a surplus. And along the way, customers will still negotiate aggressively. But the opportunity lies in making these chips more valuable to customers, rather than just competing for sales volume.

There are good reasons to be optimistic about Micron: its leading product and technology roadmap, its growing strategic customer agreements with major customers that lock in price floors and sales volumes for multiple years, and its investments in expanding production to meet anticipated demand.

Still, opportunities and shareholder returns are not the same things.

If Micron and its peers expand capacity aggressively, supply will eventually catch up with and surpass demand, which will create a glut that drives prices back down from their current lofty levels. If competitors develop better products or customers find ways to use memory more efficiently, Micron may capture less value than expected.

Investors should therefore watch whether Micron maintains its technological competitive edge, secures demand for its higher-value products, and generates attractive returns on its enormous manufacturing investments.

The opportunity may be unprecedented, but long-term appreciation in Micron's share price still depends on how well the company executes on these fronts.

#3107. The Guide to JetBlue Seat Selection

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

JetBlue's seat selection policy is based on the type of fare, so include the selection fee when comparing prices.

Airline miles, hotel points, travel insurance

JetBlue Airways charges more for seat selection than any other major U.S. airline, according to a NerdWallet analysis, so it pays to know when you can pick a seat for free.

The airline offers several seat options, including standard economy seats, extra-legroom seats and lie-flat Mint suites. But whether you can select a seat for free depends on the type of seat and fare you book, as well as whether you have Mosaic elite status.

Here’s what to know about JetBlue seat selection, including the different seat types, how much seat selection costs and when you can choose a seat for free.

JetBlue offers several onboard experiences, ranging from standard economy to lie-flat business-class seats.

JetBlue’s standard economy product is called Main, and there are three types of seats in this cabin.

Main: Economy seats throughout the Main cabin. These seats may be complimentary, depending on the fare type chosen.

Main Preferred: Economy seats located closer to the front of the cabin. They cost extra.

Extra Legroom: Seats with additional legroom that are located over the wing, in front of the Main Preferred seats. These seats also cost extra.

All Main cabin passengers receive complimentary snacks, drinks and Wi-Fi. Each seat also offers an entertainment screen with live television and movies.

EvenMore is JetBlue’s premium economy experience, and the seats are located in front of the Main cabin. These seats offer up to 38 inches of legroom and include priority boarding, priority security (at select airports) and dedicated overhead bin space.

Travelers receive three complimentary alcoholic drinks, unlimited nonalcoholic drinks and snacks, along with free Wi-Fi and a seatback entertainment screen with movies and live TV.

BlueFirst is JetBlue’s new domestic first class, which is expected to start flying on Dec. 8, 2026, on non-Mint aircraft and routes.

Adding a domestic first class product allows JetBlue to better compete for travelers who prefer to fly first class within the U.S., a market currently served by American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines.

JetBlue’s premium business class experience is called Mint, and it is available on select domestic and international routes.

The front row of the cabin also includes Mint Studios, which offer even more space than a standard Mint Suite. Mint Studios also have a large 22-inch television screen, a mirrored vanity, additional storage and a guest seat that can accommodate another Mint passenger during flight.

If a Mint Studio seat is available, it will be displayed on the airplane seat map.

The Mint travel experience also includes a dedicated check-in desk, lounge access (except with Mint Base fares), priority boarding, priority baggage and two checked bags (one with Mint Base fare).

» Learn more: JetBlue boarding groups explained

JetBlue offers three fare categories: Base, Standard and Flex. The table below shows how the categories compare in terms of flexibility.

Base fares are the most affordable but the least flexible.

Main Base fares do not include complimentary seat selection, but travelers can purchase a seat at any time. Those with an EvenMore Base fare can select a seat for free, but only at check-in. If a seat isn’t chosen, JetBlue will assign one automatically before departure. (BlueFirst Base fares include free seat selection only within 24 hours of departure.)

Comparatively, Standard and Flex fares include complimentary seat selection. This also applies to Mint, except for the new Mint Base fare, which charges for advance seat selection; complimentary seat selection is included only with Mint or Mint Flex tickets. Passengers who want to select a Mint Studio will need to pay extra, and the cost of the seat varies. In an October 2026 sample search for a flight from New York to Paris, a Mint Studio upgrade cost an additional $299 on top of the Mint fare.

Seat selection fees vary among airlines. To get an idea of what passengers can expect to pay, NerdWallet analyzed seat selection fees across major U.S. airlines and found that JetBlue had the highest average one-way seat selection fee at $73.

» Learn more: Airlines with the best (and worst) fees in 2026

JetBlue’s elite status is called Mosaic, and there are four tiers, ranging from Mosaic 1 to Mosaic 4. Mosaic members receive complimentary access to certain upgraded seats, with the benefits depending on their status level.

All Mosaic members, plus JetBlue Premier Card holders who book with their card, can get complimentary space-available upgrades to BlueFirst for themselves and one companion. Main Base and EvenMore Base fares aren't eligible.

Main Base fares are excluded from complimentary seat selection benefits, regardless of Mosaic status.

All Mosaic members receive complimentary access to Main Preferred seating, but EvenMore benefits vary by status level. Mosaic 1 members can select EvenMore seats for free starting 36 hours before departure for themselves and up to two companions, while Mosaic 2 and above can select them at booking. Mosaic 3 and 4 members can extend this benefit to up to four companions.

Mosaic 3 and 4 members receive Premium Upgrade Certificates, and starting Feb. 1, 2027, Mosaic 2 members can choose one through Perks You Pick. Mosaic 4 members earn 2 additional certificates for every 100 Tiles earned beyond the Mosaic 4 threshold. Certificates can be used to upgrade eligible Main or EvenMore fares to Mint or BlueFirst (once it starts flying).

» Learn more: JetBlue Mint: your guide to flying business class

You can select a seat during the booking process, or after, through JetBlue’s website or mobile app. During booking, you’ll first choose your fare type (Base, Standard or Flex), which determines whether complimentary seat selection is included.

After you’ve selected the flight, you’ll see a seat map displayed with the available seats and any applicable fees. For example, passengers who purchase a Main fare can choose eligible Main seats for free but will see prices for upgraded seats.

If you purchase a Main Base fare, all advance seat selections will include an additional fee. Mint passengers can select an available Mint Suite at no additional cost or pay extra for an available Mint Studio.

» Learn more: How to navigate costly airline seat selection fees

#3106. Can Reddit Shrink to Grow?

Shares of Reddit (RDDT -0.83%) were getting crushed in the pre-market Oct. 30, down over 21% as of this writing on Friday. That's an opportunity, Fools.

Before I get into why Reddit should interest you more, let's first discuss why institutions seem to want it less. It all comes down to growth.

Reddit is forecasting Q4 revenue will be up about 40% year-over-year, which is a marked slowdown from Q3's expectations-busting 53%. Adjusted EBITDA -- a key metric for the company -- is expected to be up about 51%, down from a 70% jump in the third quarter.

Forget for a moment that deceleration comes for every business. Algos still hate to see it. So do most investors.

Unfortunately, slowing growth is only part of what's causing Reddit's drawdown. Comments from co-founder and CEO Steve Huffman seem to have lit the match that's led to this morning's inferno.

"A key piece of work to retain new audiences is shifting Reddit to a logged-in-only experience. It's a big one for us, and it's a big one for me," Huffman wrote in the Q3 letter to shareholders.

Why the switch to logged-in only? Search traffic isn't helping Reddit as much as it used to. Pivoting to a more private experience forces Reddit to focus on the logged-in audience that drives 80% of the business. It's a risk, but there's logic to it.

Ask New York Times Co. (NYT -0.30%) whether it regrets going to a paywall-based business. Reddit demanding users log in is similar in that it may shrink the audience in the short term, but the long-term benefits of increased monetization could prove worth it.

Which brings us to why you may want to be interested. Even before Friday's action, Reddit was squarely on the way to generating $1 billion in annualized free cash flow. The shares trade for a 3.7% FCF yield, or about 27 times its real cash flow, as of this writing.

That might feel like a modest premium ... if Reddit hadn't spent the last three years more than doubling its cash from operations annually. There's a very real chance Reddit is going to keep growing cash flow at greater than 27% annually. Perhaps materially so. I sense a potential mispricing here.

Reddit's getting downvoted today. So be it. This stock story is far from over.

#3104. Lattice Semiconductor: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

AI tools and debt paydown signal the company is building durable competitive advantages beyond just riding the data center boom.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 2, 2026, Lattice Semiconductor (LSCC +2.66%) announced record quarterly revenue of $291 million, up 118% year over year. The chipmaker's rapid growth shows how artificial intelligence data center infrastructure and complex hardware architectures are driving expanding demand for small field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), which are semiconductor devices that customers can program after manufacturing. Three key takeaways from the call stand out for long-term investors.

Data center operators are adding more programmable chips per server to manage complex artificial intelligence workloads and security requirements. That surge expanded the company's fastest-growing business segment and drove total quarterly net income higher.

Management launched Lattice Prompt, an artificial intelligence development tool that lets software engineers build chip applications using natural language. By reducing technical friction, non-specialist developers can program chips more quickly. That opens up new customer markets the company couldn't easily reach before.

Following its acquisition of AMI, a firmware and management software provider, the business generated $77.6 million in quarterly free cash flow, which represents cash left over after operating expenses and capital investments. Management put that cash to work right away, paying down $50 million in debt during the quarter to avoid carrying excess interest expenses.

Data center expansion and industrial recovery are pushing order backlog into 2027, giving the company multiyear visibility across key end markets. The business relies on its small-chip focus, proprietary firmware integration, and customer supply commitments to hold gross margins. And management is watching channel inventory levels closely while targeting a 30% compound annual growth rate (CAGR), the consistent annual growth rate required to reach its long-term targets.

Operational execution and expanding chip attach rates give leadership confidence in long-term compounding. From here, management aims to turn top-line momentum into faster net income growth through strict operating discipline.

#3101. If I Only Had $500 to Invest Right Now, I'd Buy and Hold This ETF for the Next 25 Years

You don't need thousands of dollars to start building long-term wealth.

You don't need a lot of money to start investing. Even $500 can grow into a meaningful amount of wealth over time if you invest it wisely and give it enough time to compound. If I only had $500 to invest right now and couldn't touch the money for the next 25 years, I'd put it into the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD +0.34%).

Here's why I think it's an excellent long-term investment.

I think the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF is one of the best ETFs to buy for the long term. It passively tracks an index (Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index) that screens companies based on several dividend quality characteristics, including dividend history, five-year growth rate, yield, and financial strength.

That focus on dividend quality and growth is worth noting. According to data from Ned Davis Research and Hartford Funds, companies that grow their dividends have historically delivered a 10.2% annualized total return over the last 50 years, significantly outperforming companies with no dividend changes, dividend cutters, and those that don't pay dividends. SCHD's focus on the best dividend stocks has paid off. It has delivered a 13.1% annualized total return since its inception in 2011.

The fund currently holds 100 high-quality, higher-yielding dividend stocks. It has delivered a 3.2% dividend yield over the last 12 months, roughly triple the S&P 500's level (currently yielding 1.1%). SCHD provides access to these top dividend stocks for a very reasonable fee (0.06% expense ratio).

SCHD has been a wealth compounding machine over the years. Thanks to its robust returns, a $500 investment in SCHD at its inception 15 years ago would be worth about $3,456 today, assuming reinvestment of dividends. Here's a hypothetical look at what $500 could become over the next 25 years at different return scenarios:

SCHD has delivered an annualized total return of approximately 13.1% since its inception. If it maintained that pace over the next 25 years, a $500 investment would grow to nearly $10,900 with dividends reinvested.

However, expecting that performance to continue might be overly optimistic. Even at a more modest 10.2% annualized return, consistent with the historical performance of dividend-growth stocks over the past 50 years, that $500 would grow to nearly $5,700. At an even more conservative 6% annualized return, it would still grow to more than $2,100.

While the base case of $5,700 isn't necessarily life-changing money, it's a more than 10-fold return from a relatively lower-risk investment. You'd need to invest more than $500 over the next quarter century to comfortably retire. A good place to start is to invest $500 per month in SCHD, which would grow to over $640,000 in 25 years at a 10.2% annualized return.

SCHD won't outperform the market every year, and its stock holdings will experience volatility along the way. However, its focus on financially strong dividend-paying businesses, growing income potential, and minimal fees makes it an excellent candidate for a long-term portfolio. If I only had $500 to invest today, I'd be comfortable putting it into SCHD and letting the power of compounding work for the next 25 years.

TL;DR: Average mortgage interest rates jumped today.

If you're here looking for lower mortgage interest rates, today is definitely not your day.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage jumped to 7.32% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 22 basis points higher than yesterday and 24 basis points higher than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

This comes after the Federal Reserve announced central bankers’ decision to hold the federal funds rate steady yesterday. While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, the federal funds rate is one factor that moves them. Last month, when markets began pricing in a possible federal funds rate increase, mortgage rates spiked.

The next Fed meeting isn’t until December, so any rate movement in the next week will likely stem from other factors, like the upcoming jobs report. For more on that, read on.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Traders expected that the Fed would vote to hold the federal funds rate steady yesterday, so that wasn’t much of a factor for mortgage lenders as they set rates.

In his post-meeting press conference, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that September’s rate increase is “starting to work some” toward moving inflation down to the Fed's 2% goal, but that central bankers don't have any firm conclusions yet. He also acknowledged that the Fed’s monetary policy actions hadn’t achieved price stability yet, but that they’re “working on it.”

This hints that if inflation data continues to trend upward, central bankers might raise the federal funds rate again at their December 8-9 meeting.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, dropped this morning — a day too late for central bankers to consider it in their decision-making process.

The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on November 25.

Next week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out Friday, Nov.6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build an even stronger case for the Fed to raise the federal funds rate again in December, because it would suggest that the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3092. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3090. 3 Dividend Stocks to Buy in November That Keep Paying

These consumer dividend stocks raised their payouts for 50-plus years through rough stretches and good times.

Some companies treat their dividend like a bill they have to pay every month, not a bonus they hand out when times are good. That mindset is what separates a stock that merely offers a dividend from one that has actually built its business around protecting it, through recessions, inflation spikes, and years when growth simply wasn't there.

November arrives with the market still jumpy, after a month that saw AI and chip stocks swing wildly and the Nasdaq-100 flirt with correction territory, the kind of backdrop where a dependable check starts to matter more than a flashy return

These three consumer stocks fall firmly into the second category, and all three are worth a look heading into November.

Colgate-Palmolive (CL +2.25%), the maker of Colgate toothpaste and Palmolive soap, has raised its dividend every year for 63 consecutive years, a streak that puts it among a small handful of companies known as Dividend Kings. A Dividend King is a company that's grown its dividend payment for at least 50 consecutive years.

The current quarterly payout sits at $0.53 a share, up from $0.52, a modest increase but one made in a year when the stock has actually struggled enough to get bumped from the S&P 100 index in September. That's the kind of detail that would normally worry investors, but Colgate kept raising its dividend anyway, which says something about how the company prioritizes that payout even when the stock itself isn't cooperating.

Oral care and household products are about as recession-resistant as consumer spending gets, people don't stop buying toothpaste because the economy wobbles, and that steady demand is what's funded 63 straight years of increases.

McDonald's (MCD +2.91%) just crossed a threshold worth paying attention to. In September, the company announced its 50th consecutive year of dividend increases, officially joining the Dividend Kings club for the first time, with the quarterly payout rising 4% to $1.93 a share.

What makes this one interesting is the timing: McDonald's hit that milestone while its stock was trading near 52-week lows, with comparable sales growth slowing and competition across the restaurant industry intensifying. In other words, management didn't wait for a comfortable moment to lock in the milestone, it kept the streak alive through a genuinely tougher stretch for the business.

CEO Chris Kempczinski said, "We see an opportunity to raise the bar in the U.S. and accelerate performance in our largest market."

A company that treats a half-century dividend record as non-negotiable, even when same-store sales are under pressure, is sending a clear signal about where the payout ranks on its list of priorities.

Target (TGT +2.59%) is the one with the most dramatic backstory of the three.

The retailer went through three straight years of sales declines before new CEO Michael Fiddelke's turnaround plan began to show results this year, and the stock has swung wildly as a result. Through all of that, Target kept its dividend streak alive, raising its payout again this past summer to put 2026 on track to be its 55th consecutive year of increases, by the company's own count.

The quarterly dividend now sits at $1.16 a share, and the stock's recent struggles have actually pushed the yield up to around 3%, well above where it sat before the sales slump began.

Target is proof that a long dividend streak isn't just about steady growth, it's about a management team that keeps writing the check even while the rest of the business is getting fixed.

Here's the part that's easy to gloss over: none of these streaks, 63 years, 50 years, or 55 years, come with an actual guarantee. A dividend is a decision a board of directors makes one quarter at a time, not a contractual obligation like a bond's interest payment, and a long track record only tells you what a company has chosen to do in the past, not what it's legally required to do going forward.

Even Dividend Kings have been dethroned before when a business changed enough that the math no longer worked. That doesn't make these three bad picks. Their track records reflect real, repeated decisions to protect the dividend through hard years, but it's a risk worth sitting with before buying any stock for its yield. A long streak is a strong signal of intent, not a promise.

Micah Zimmerman has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Colgate-Palmolive and Target. TL;DR: Mortgage rates slid enough today to get home buyers' attention.

Mortgage rates have mostly recovered today after yesterday's jump scare.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.18% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and two basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

Mortgage rates were elevated this month. The average 30-year mortgage rate for all of October was 7.3%, compared to September's monthly average rate of 6.98%.

While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday. Happy Halloween!

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Traders expected that the Fed would vote to hold the federal funds rate steady on Wednesday, so that wasn’t much of a factor for mortgage lenders as they set rates.

In his post-meeting press conference, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that September’s rate increase is “starting to work some” toward moving inflation down to the Fed's 2% goal, but that central bankers don't have any firm conclusions yet. He also acknowledged that the Fed’s monetary policy actions hadn’t achieved price stability yet, but that they’re “working on it.”

This hints that if inflation data continues to trend upward, central bankers might raise the federal funds rate again at their December 8-9 meeting.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, dropped yesterday— a day too late for central bankers to consider it in their decision-making process.

The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on November 25.

Next week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build an even stronger case for the Fed to raise the federal funds rate again in December, because it would suggest that the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.68% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3086. Palo Alto Networks vs. Atlassian: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

One trades at a forward P/E of 87, while the other boasts a significantly cheaper valuation, but financial health and cash flow tell a starkly different story.

In an era defined by digital transformation, investors often choose between security and collaboration. Palo Alto Networks (PANW -3.87%) and Atlassian (TEAM -2.42%) represent two distinct paths within the software market.

Palo Alto Networks focuses on platformization, aiming to be a one-stop shop for cybersecurity needs. Atlassian provides the backbone for team productivity and software development through tools like Jira and Confluence. While both benefit from enterprise digitization, their financial profiles and market strategies offer very different propositions for retail investors.

Palo Alto Networks provides network security, cloud security, and AI-driven operations to over 70,000 customers globally. It focuses on large enterprise organizations and governments, serving nine of the Fortune 10 and eight of the largest U.S. banks. Two distributors accounted for nearly 30% of total revenue in fiscal 2026. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In fiscal 2026, revenue reached nearly $11.5 billion, representing approximately 24.5% growth over the previous year. The company reported net income of roughly $307.0 million, reflecting a net margin of about 2.7%. This represents a decrease from the net margin of approximately 12.3% seen in the prior fiscal year.

As of Palo Alto's July 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.1. This ratio measures total debt against shareholder equity, with lower numbers generally suggesting less financial risk. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to pay short-term obligations, was close to 0.9. Free cash flow for fiscal 2026 reached nearly $4.1 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 39% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Atlassian builds tools for collaboration and software development, serving more than 350,000 organizations worldwide. Its strategy relies on a product-led flywheel where users adopt software via self-service before moving to enterprisewide contracts. This approach has gained traction in the tech stock landscape, with over 85% of the Fortune 500 using its products, according to its latest annual report.

In fiscal 2026, revenue reached close to $6.6 billion, representing a year-over-year increase of approximately 26%. The company reported a net loss of nearly $53.8 million, resulting in a negative net margin of roughly 0.8%. Despite the loss, this was an improvement over the previous year, when the net loss was approximately $256.7 million.

Based on Atlassian's June 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 1.2. The current ratio was approximately 0.8, indicating the company has roughly $0.80 in current assets for every $1.00 of current liabilities. Free cash flow for fiscal 2026 was close to $1.3 billion. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 118.7% of operating cash flow, meaning reported cash generation is heavily inflated by this non-cash add-back.

Palo Alto Networks faces intense competition from established vendors such as Microsoft (MSFT -2.83%), Alphabet (GOOGL -0.30%)(GOOG -0.07%), and Cisco (CSCO -2.77%). The company also deals with integration risks from recent acquisitions and potential reputational damage from security incidents. Global economic and geopolitical environments, particularly in Israel, further complicate its risk profile.

Atlassian contends with competition from large technology vendors and AI-native start-ups. It faces challenges managing the transition to a cloud-focused model while sunsetting older products. Additionally, Atlassian's dual-class share structure concentrates control in the hands of its co-founders, and it remains dependent on third-party infrastructure like Amazon (AMZN +2.20%).

Atlassian appears more attractive on a price-to-sales basis, while Palo Alto Networks carries a significantly higher premium for its leadership in the cybersecurity market.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

The forward P/E compares a stock price to future earnings estimates, helping you gauge if a company is priced for growth. The P/S ratio measures market value relative to sales over the past 12 months.

Investing in these tech specialists doesn't necessarily have to be an either/or proposition. They serve different needs for large organizations, and allocating a modest amount to each stock may be attractive to some investors.

My initial thought is Palo Alto Networks looks like a better buy here. Network and cloud security for any organization isn't a "nice to have"; it's absolutely crucial. I am not as convinced Atlassian's software is equally vital, or that customers couldn't find decent substitutes for its offerings. Furthermore, while the companies posted similar revenue growth for the past year, Atlassian has reported a loss for two years running.

Now, it's obvious Palo Alto Networks is significantly more expensive than Atlassian, which may give some investors pause. But the stock's 10-year performance speaks for itself:

Palo Alto Networks' valuation makes me slightly nervous -- investors are pricing in continued outperformance, which isn't guaranteed -- but I think the stock is the better buy. As investor and economist Benjamin Graham said, "Price is what you pay. Value is what you get."
