#3085. Your AI Model Is A Program. Start Implementing It Like One

Kriti Faujdar, Lead Product Manager, Agentic Systems at Yelp, Speaks and writes about AI Safety and Security, Start up advisor.

​In early 2025, researchers at ReversingLabs found machine learning models on Hugging Face that carried malicious code. The malicious payload was a reverse shell to a hardcoded IP address when it loaded. The file was built to bypass the hub’s automated scanner. It used a compression trick the scanner couldn’t parse, so the scan ran and passed it.

Most business leaders still picture an AI model as a static data file, but loading one means executing code. A company with no controls on how models arrive is carrying an exposure it never accounted for.

Opening many common model files runs whatever code is packed inside them, just like installing a program. Loading a pickle-based model file runs the instructions stored inside it, so whoever built the file decides what code runs on your machine.

Python’s own documentation says the pickle module is insecure and warns against unpickling data you don’t trust.

PyTorch went further. In version 2.6, released January 29, 2025, the project switched torch.load to weights-only loading by default, accepting a change that broke backward compatibility to get there. An external model file is an untrusted input, and the maintainers have built that assumption into the defaults.

As of April 2025, Protect AI and Hugging Face had scanned 4.47 million model versions and reported roughly 352,000 unsafe or suspicious findings across about 51,700 models. Those flags are conservative by design and ignore intent, so they don’t mean 51,700 malicious models. JFrog’s 2024 analysis gives a better count of actual threats: after filtering out false positives, it found around 100 genuinely malicious instances, any one of which is enough if you load it.

Deciding which models a company can load is shifting from an engineering preference to a governance and vendor-management requirement.

The OpenSSF has published a model signing specification with a conformance suite, which gives you a way to verify who published a model. NVIDIA has signed the models in its own catalog against that spec since March 2025, and describes itself as the first major model hub to do so.

In March 2026, the NSA’s AI Security Center and seven allied agencies issued joint guidance defining AI supply chain risk across six components: training data, models, software, infrastructure, hardware and third-party services. Its recommendations are written to shape what you ask vendors before you buy, such as requiring an AI bill of materials and a software bill of materials or equivalent documentation, running threat modeling and vulnerability mapping, and keeping an incident response plan for AI dependencies.

The tools and guidance already exist, but most organizations lack processes at intake. Five controls should be in place before any external model touches a production system.

1. Keep an inventory. Every production model needs a recorded source, an exact version hash and a named owner who approved it.

2. Restrict formats. Don’t accept pickle-based checkpoints from outside your organization, and require weights-only loading and safer serialization formats such as safetensors.

3. Verify before execution. Run hash and signature checks in the pipeline, pin model versions and configure intake to fail closed when a check fails.

4. Sandbox the load. Run external models in an isolated environment with no outbound network access and no credentials attached. Blocking egress at the infrastructure level would have stopped the reverse shell above from reaching anything.

5. Assign ownership. A model is a dependency, and dependencies without owners don’t get audited, patched or retired.

File-level controls tell you about a model’s format and provenance but nothing about how it behaves. A backdoor can sit in the learned weights, where scanners and signatures can’t reach it.

Anthropic researchers showed this in 2024 with models they intentionally backdoored. The hidden behavior survived standard safety training, and adversarial training sometimes taught the model to conceal the backdoor rather than drop it. These were research artifacts built to test the question and not models found in the wild.

A 2025 study from Anthropic, the U.K. AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute approached the problem from the training data side. It found that roughly 250 poisoned documents were enough to implant a backdoor in models from 600 million to 13 billion parameters. The implanted behavior was narrow, though: the models produced gibberish after a trigger phrase. The authors say it’s unclear whether the result holds for more complex behaviors or larger models, and they consider this particular backdoor unlikely to pose significant risk in frontier models. The study shows how the attack works, not how dangerous it is in practice.

Since signatures can’t tell you how a model will behave, you have to handle that in the system around it. Until verification tools mature, treat model weights like unverified third-party code and bound the blast radius. Keep model execution decoupled from high-privilege actions, and route outputs through sanitization filters. Run a secondary monitor model that checks the primary model’s outputs as they’re produced, and keep an automated rollback path to a known-clean baseline for when something looks wrong.

Securing AI integration starts with operational discipline; tooling comes second. These three questions will show you where you stand:

1. Which external models are running in production right now?

2. Who approved each model version, and on what basis?

3. What happens tomorrow if one of them turns out to be compromised?

If your leadership team can’t answer those in a single briefing, fix the intake process first.

#3081. How to Make a $50 Holiday Gift Feel Like $100

Trade time and a little extra thought to enhance gifts this holiday season.

Each month, NerdWallet suggests one wallet win to help you feel more confident about your money. This month’s topic is making holiday gifts feel more valuable, and we’re going to show you ways to elevate a gift without overspending.

Making an inexpensive gift feel fancy is a winter challenge I relish.

As a relatively frugal person who often gets sticker shock when shopping for gifts, I’m always looking for creative ways to save money without diminishing the present. Over the years, I’ve developed a few strategies to make a $50 gift feel like it’s worth at least double that.

In the spirit of the season, I’m sharing these strategies with you. I hope you — and your recipients — find them as celebratory as I do.

What does your gift recipient love to do? It helps if they have a favorite hobby, sports team or other interest.

Let’s say your recipient likes to fish. Giving a gift card to a niche fishing store makes it feel far more valuable than the standard Amazon card because it shows that you considered who they are. And there are specialty stores for every hobby these days.

Maybe gift cards aren’t your go-to. You can easily enhance other gifts, too.

Paying $5 extra to engrave or embroider their name on the gift — whether it’s stationery, jewelry or a backpack — makes the item feel far more valuable than its price tag because it’s customized to the individual.

If you choose a gift that couldn’t have been given to anyone else, it increases its value.

Time required: A few extra minutes to think about your recipients’ preferences and apply them when shopping.

A vintage or thrifted scarf can be a wrapping paper alternative that also functions as a gift. Similarly, you could wrap a gift in tea towels, artwork or online prints that can be reused by the recipient.

Another idea: Wrap a gift in printed sheet music that contains a special meaning for the recipient.

Customizing the presentation of the gift elevates it without adding much to the expense.

Time required: Since you have to wrap the gift anyway, this method doesn’t need to take extra time. You’ll just need to find the cloth or paper you plan to use.

One of my favorite gifts in recent memory involved turning a family photograph into a Jane Austen-era image set on a bucolic English estate with the empire-waisted gowns to match. My mom is a big fan of Jane Austen, so I knew she would appreciate seeing the family in a Regency-style photo.

I hired an Etsy artist to transform my original image, but you may be able to do it yourself with a photo app. Similarly, you could create a custom song, illustration or other form of art made specifically for your recipient.

Adding your own creative spin on a gift shows you spent extra time thinking about the recipient to make something extra special for them.

Time required: Applying your own creativity can be time-intensive, but the process is enjoyable so it goes quickly.

I like to call this technique the hybrid gift approach: You buy something, then get crafty to transform the gift into something one-of-a-kind.

One of my favorite ways to do this is with a photo. I’ll buy a nice but inexpensive frame and then put a photo of the recipient, or the recipient alongside loved ones, inside it.

If the person you’re buying for posts on social media, you might not even have to ask them for a photo in advance. Instead, you can find a favorite one that they already shared and surprise them.

The options are endless, especially with online tutorials to help hone your crafting skills. Adding your own customization to a purchased gift makes it feel special, but doesn’t have to cost much.

Time required: Baking, crafting or creating can take several hours, but again, it’s an enjoyable process.

Experiential gifts tend to go over well, and you may even get to have some fun, too.

One year, I gave my mom a membership to a nearby art museum and tacked on an offer to attend an exhibit with her. We had something on the calendar to look forward to together, and she got the option to visit more times throughout the year.

My parents have given me memberships, too. More recently, they gave me one to a local nature center. It’s great because I can visit on my own or attend kid-friendly events at a discounted rate. It makes me feel part of the community, and I love supporting an organization that helps kids learn more about nature.

Another option is to donate to charity in a loved one’s name and then make plans to volunteer at the organization together.

Experiential gifts help create more family memories together, which is one of my favorite ways to celebrate the holidays.

Time required: Setting aside time to visit a museum or other destination can take an entire day, but it’s time well spent.

The bottom line is that giving a highly personalized gift adds value without eating too far into your own budget. Spend $50. Make someone feel like a hundred bucks.

If you’re following along with us on this monthly financial challenge, start by testing out the tips we shared today over the next few weeks. We’ll be back again next month to learn about setting money goals for the new year. And if you missed last month’s edition, take a look back at how to shop the holiday sales.

#3078. CME vs. Interactive Brokers Group: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

CME commands a 62% net margin but trades at a higher sales multiple, while Interactive Brokers posts stronger free cash flow despite lower profitability.

Market volatility often drives trading activity, creating a compelling environment for exchange and brokerage firms. Choosing between CME Group (CME +1.02%) and Interactive Brokers Group (IBKR -2.69%) requires analyzing their distinct roles in the global markets.

CME operates as a primary marketplace for derivatives, while Interactive Brokers serves as a high-tech gateway for traders. Both companies benefit from increased volume, yet they offer different risk and reward profiles for investors seeking exposure to the financial sector.

CME Group operates the world's leading derivatives marketplace, offering futures and options contracts for a global audience. The company provides clearing and trading services to a wide range of customers, including institutional investors, professional traders, and central banks. In late 2025, CME launched a joint venture with Flutter Entertainment (FLUT +6.14%) brand FanDuel to offer a prediction markets application to retail users. It maintains critical commercial relationships through licensing agreements with S&P Global (SPGI +1.85%) and Nasdaq (NDAQ +2.25%). Both CME and Interactive Brokers offer unique entry points into the financial stocks category for different types of investors.

In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $6.5 billion, reflecting growth of roughly 6.4% compared to the previous year. The company reported net income of close to $4 billion for the same period. This resulted in a net margin of approximately 62%, which measures the portion of revenue remaining after all expenses and taxes are paid. The steady growth in revenue and high profitability highlight CME's established position in the derivatives market.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.1. This ratio measures total debt relative to shareholder equity, indicating a low level of borrowing. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, was approximately 1.0. Free cash flow for the fiscal year was nearly $4.2 billion, calculated as cash from operations minus capital expenditures. These figures suggest CME has a solid financial foundation with significant cash generation.

Interactive Brokers Group serves a diverse global client base, including hedge funds, registered investment advisors, and individual investors. The company provides automated trade execution across more than 175 markets, allowing users to trade stocks, bonds, and options from a single platform. It also partners with third-party providers to facilitate the trading of Bitcoin (BTC -0.55%) for its customers. Interactive Brokers operates specialized services like white branding for introducing brokers. This global reach allows the company to capture trading activity across multiple asset classes and geographic regions.

In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $10.2 billion, representing growth of approximately 9.8% over the prior year. Net income for the period was close to $984 million. The resulting net margin was roughly 9.6%, indicating the percentage of sales converted into actual profit. While its net margin is lower than that of an exchange operator, Interactive Brokers has shown consistent growth in both revenue and profit as its account base expands.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the long-term debt-to-equity ratio was nearly 0, showing almost no debt relative to equity. The current ratio stands at approximately 1.1, suggesting the company has sufficient short-term assets to meet its immediate obligations. Free cash flow for fiscal 2025 was nearly $15.7 billion. This figure represents the cash generated from operations minus capital expenditures, providing a measure of cash available for expansion or shareholder returns.

CME Group faces intense competition from other global exchange operators such as Intercontinental Exchange (ICE +2.03%) and Cboe Global Markets (CBOE +4.08%). The business remains heavily regulated, and new oversight could lead to higher operating costs or capital requirements. Cybersecurity threats are a material concern, particularly because the company relies on third-party cloud services for its infrastructure. Revenue is also highly sensitive to market volatility and trading volumes, which can fluctuate based on macroeconomic shifts beyond the company's control.

Interactive Brokers Group deals with significant competition from online equity brokers and zero-commission platforms that could pressure its pricing. The company carries substantial credit risk through its margin lending and clearing activities, where a systemic market event might cause customer defaults. Its reliance on proprietary technology means any system failures or security breaches could cause major reputational damage. Additionally, Interactive Brokers' digital asset offerings depend on third-party providers, exposing the company to risks involving their security or regulatory standing.

Interactive Brokers Group appears more expensive based on future earnings estimates, while CME Group carries a higher premium relative to its sales over the past 12 months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

CME Group's eye-popping net margin would be the envy of most companies. However, revenue growth for fiscal 2025 was lackluster. Profitability is important, but investors typically want to see rising sales, too. Interactive Brokers' revenue growth wasn't especially impressive, either, and the company also reported a dramatically lower net margin.

As for their valuations, the two stocks are mixed depending on the metric used, so I think it's a wash.

There is one factor that does sway my opinion, however. Here's how CME Group and Interactive Brokers have performed over the past 10 years:

Past performance is no indication of future results, of course -- every investor has heard that before. There's no guarantee Interactive Brokers will continue to leave CME Group in the dust. Nevertheless, it's said that history doesn't repeat itself, but it often rhymes. I think Interactive Brokers looks like the better bet.

To save money on holiday gifts this year, Americans are using these 5 strategies that require coordination with friends and family.

Gift giving can bust a budget, so some Americans plan to have conversations with friends and family this year about setting limits around holiday gifting.

This isn’t as Scroogey as you might think: 55% of holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy that likely involves coordinating with loved ones, according to a new NerdWallet survey conducted online by The Harris Poll.

Money can be a taboo subject, especially among family and friends. But a focused discussion on gift boundaries could be the difference between staying within your budget and piling up debt this holiday season.

What other Americans are doing: 28% of holiday spenders plan to set a per-gift dollar limit with family or friends.

Why this works: It’s simple and easy to remember. Unlike some other ideas on this list, you can probably coordinate this one over text.

For best results: If you’re the one bringing up the topic, you should come with a dollar amount that would be reasonable for everyone in your gift exchange group, so no one feels excluded or overextended.

Your circle of friends and family has a lot of kids.

What other Americans are doing: 23% of holiday spenders plan to buy gifts for children in a family, but not the adults.

Why this works: Cutting out adult gifts altogether can rescue a gift budget that has undergone major “kidflation” as new children join the family.

For best results: If you still want to include adults, give a gift that’s fun for the whole family, like a board game or an experience. And make sure your kid-free loved ones are on board.

You traditionally exchange gifts one-on-one with a friend, but the last few gifts you’ve given — and received — were duds.

What other Americans are doing: 18% of holiday spenders plan to skip exchanging gifts with at least one friend or family member.

Why this works: If you’re feeling gift fatigue, there’s a chance they are, too.

For best results: Frame this as an improvement to the gift-giving tradition rather than a scaling back. Propose an alternative way to celebrate your friendship, like swapping out the $40 gift that’ll probably get shelved for a $7 coffee together.

What other Americans are doing: 16% of holiday spenders plan to do a secret Santa gift exchange, or another game that requires purchasing only one gift.

Why this works: 15% of holiday spenders list buying gifts for more people than they originally planned for as among the reasons they’re most likely to overspend this holiday season. This strategy keeps your list in check, even if the number of people playing grows.

For best results: There are bound to be people in your group for whom the rules to the game are important. If you’re the one organizing, be ready to answer questions — can you trade or steal gifts, for example, and, if so, how many times? Also, this works best for family or friend groups who aren’t likely to go rogue and buy extra gifts anyway.

You have no idea what your college friend’s kids (or spouse) are into.

What other Americans are doing: 12% of holiday spenders plan to give one shared gift per family instead of individual gifts.

Why this works: In addition to saving money, this avoids the awkwardness that comes with uninformed gift giving.

For best results: Presentation is key. Don’t sheepishly give an UNO game you clearly bought on the drive over. You may be cutting back, but enthusiasm is free.

Talking about the holidays and talking about money can be stressful conversation topics. About four in five Americans avoid discussing some money topics with family and friends, according to a 2026 survey by the CFP Board. So discussing both at once may seem daunting. But without a doubt, you’re not the only one thinking about them.

Nearly 9 in 10 (86%) holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy this holiday season. Start with an icebreaker: “Hey, have you noticed how expensive everything is lately? Would you be open to talking about how we can do gifts this year while keeping spending under control?” This conversation might be the thing that’s secretly on everyone’s wish list.

#3072. Digital Transformation Needs A New Talent Strategy

April Ho-Nishimura, VP Global Customer Experience, Infineon Technologies.

Over the past decade, organizations have invested billions in digital transformation. They’ve modernized technology stacks, adopted agile ways of working, migrated to the cloud and, most recently, accelerated investments in AI.

Technology matters, but technology has never been the competitive advantage. People are.

The organizations that consistently outperform their peers don’t simply purchase better platforms. They develop talent capable of turning technology investments into exceptional customer experiences. Digital product management is one profession emerging at the center of that opportunity.​

While many consumer-focused organizations have spent years maturing digital product practices, many B2B organizations are still defining what digital product management means for their business. Too often, digital product managers are viewed as project coordinators or feature owners at the mercy of business teams that are interpreting what should be built. In reality, they should orchestrate end-to-end customer experiences across discovery, evaluation, purchase, service and support.

That responsibility requires a unique blend of business strategy, technology, analytics, customer experience and design thinking. Orchestration is difficult without the authority, competencies and organizational support needed to bring those disciplines together. Establishing digital product management as a recognized profession helps create that foundation.

This presents a unique opportunity for HR leaders to intentionally design career pathways for this profession. Rather than fitting digital product management into existing career paths built for product marketing or technology delivery, organizations should establish dedicated competency models and progression frameworks. Career growth should reflect increasing expertise in customer journey management, experimentation, behavioral analytics, “voice of the customer,” accessibility, AI-enabled experiences and cross-functional leadership, not simply larger product portfolios.

Many organizations already have defined career ladders for engineering, marketing, sales and project management. Digital product management is often forced into marketing while borrowing elements from multiple disciplines without having a framework of its own. As a result, high-potential talent can struggle to understand advancement opportunities, while leaders struggle to identify and develop future capability. Recruiting becomes difficult as external hires often seek new employers specifically to grow their careers and experience. Establishing clear competencies, expectations and progression paths helps create consistency across the organization and elevates digital product management from another responsibility to a profession.​

As global head of customer experience in high tech and specialty chemicals industries, I’ve found that the best digital product management teams adopt a multidisciplinary approach. Organizations should recruit talent from multiple disciplines. Engineers, UX professionals, marketers, analysts, customer experience leaders and traditional product managers each bring valuable perspectives. The strongest digital product managers understand enough of every discipline to unite teams around customer outcomes validated by customer behavior.​

Today’s digital transformation is beyond just implementing technology. Instead, it’s about building organizational capability to read customer signals and innovate around experiences that involve both process and technology. Some may even compare digital experience design to an art.

Customer delight happens when you turn an unpleasant task into a simple, memorable experience. Designing those moments requires expertise in human behavior, interaction design, content strategy and visual communication. A creative director or art director may never have been considered part of a traditional product management organization, yet these disciplines are increasingly critical to modern digital product management.

HR leaders are uniquely positioned to develop the talent strategies needed to ensure people remain a competitive advantage. Investing now in the people, competencies and career frameworks behind digital product management will help you transform customer experiences long after the next wave of technology arrives.

#3070. The Latest Vishing Attacks Are A Warning For All Industries

Ryan Ikeler is the President of MOXFIVE, advancing business resilience and technical recovery for organizations navigating cyber incidents.

​Recently, a wave of attempted cyberattacks hit some of the largest investment firms on Wall Street. If you don’t work in finance, that might sound like someone else’s problem. It isn’t. ​

The attackers didn’t use a sophisticated exploit. They used a phone call that impersonated someone the target already trusted, a technique called vishing. Of several targeted firms, Bloomberg reported that Two Sigma Investments said it blocked the attempt, while Point72 Asset Management confirmed it had been targeted and was still reviewing the incident. ​

Stopping an attack is always one objective of cybersecurity, but was it luck, or was it a successful implementation of controls and pattern recognition? Knowing the true answer is what lets underprepared firms turn a lucky break into a repeatable defense.​

The tactics used against these firms are new spins on old tricks. Social engineering predates the existence of both the internet and Wall Street, and AI-powered voice and video cloning, also called deepfakes, makes these tactics much more dangerous. Similar vishing and voice-cloning activity has already been observed against law firms and professional services organizations, where attackers impersonate partners and IT staff to pressure employees into resetting credentials or approving urgent requests outside normal channels.​

Deloitte’s 2025 report identified the exploitation of human behavior as a growing threat. Put simply, the same call that might have sounded generic and suspicious in the past can now be tailored to a specific employee, referencing real names and real projects and using a voice that sounds like someone they know.

Vishing is particularly effective because a social engineering call can bypass almost all the efforts organizations put into their security stack. Vishing triggers no alerts, has no indicators of compromise and trips no firewalls. Rather than combating technical controls, it allows threat actors to simply ignore them. ​

Regulators are responding accordingly. FINRA launched its Financial Intelligence Fusion Center in March 2026 to help member firms share timely intelligence about cybersecurity and fraud threats. That response recognizes a fundamental reality of modern attacks. When the same tactics appear across organizations, the firms that learn from the earliest incidents have an opportunity to act before the threat reaches them.

​Very few industries have a resource like the Fusion Center, and most companies can’t build that kind of shared intelligence network on their own. That’s increasingly why organizations turn to outside partners who sit across many incidents at once and see the same tactics resurface across clients well before any single victim would notice the pattern on its own.​

A mature security program needs a mechanism for turning current incidents into changes in its own environment, whether that discipline lives in-house or comes from an outside partner who’s seen the pattern before. That does not mean chasing every new headline or adding a control every time another company is attacked. It means asking disciplined questions:

• If an attacker successfully used a trusted voice to bypass an organization’s normal processes, would ours work differently?

• If the same tactic appeared against our employees tomorrow, where would the attacker encounter resistance?

• Where would a legitimate request and a malicious one look identical?

• Which controls depend on an employee recognizing that something sounds wrong?​

These answers should lead to specific changes in procedures, technology or training. Looking at enough real incidents can reveal which controls hold up under pressure, which fail despite appearing effective on paper and which attacker behaviors repeatedly create openings—all valuable insights a theoretical risk assessment can’t offer. ​

In practice, security works best as a standing habit, not a one-time reaction. When a new incident trend surfaces publicly, a security team should dedicate a small window of time that same week, tracing it against existing defense procedures and flagging any gap to whoever owns that control. Small and frequent beats formal and rare.​

PwC found that nearly two-thirds of employed U.S. respondents said their company had already experienced at least one major digital harm, including attempted financial scams or suspected data breaches. Yet only 9% believed the groups responsible for managing digital threats were keeping pace. ​

For financial services specifically, PwC also found that 76% of financial institutions planned to increase cybersecurity budgets in 2026, but only 24% were spending significantly more on proactive than reactive security measures.​

The goal isn’t predicting the next attack perfectly; it’s reducing the number of surprises when it arrives. ​

Security teams have limited resources and cannot respond equally to every theoretical threat. That’s why leaders must determine which risks deserve attention now.​

The organizations best positioned for the next wave of attacks will not necessarily be those with the newest security technology. They will be those with the strongest mechanisms for learning and adapting to ongoing attack trends. Today’s threat landscape is more dangerous, and its threats are more varied, than ever in the history of cybersecurity, and that trend seems poised only to increase over time.

That means treating current incidents as intelligence, not just news. When another organization gets attacked, leaders shouldn’t ask, “Could this happen to us?” They should instead ask, “What does this incident tell us to change before it does?”​

The companies that adopt this habit can turn someone else’s breach into their own early-warning system. As attackers move successful playbooks from one industry to the next, the ability to learn from incidents before they become your own may be as important as the controls you deploy to stop them.​​

#3065. After Another Blowout Quarter, Is Palantir Technologies Stock a Buy?

The company's growth rate accelerated to 96% in the third quarter.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR -3.13%) continues to do the improbable: improve upon an already high growth rate. Every time I think the business is inevitably due to slow down, it proves me wrong.

The company did that yet again when it posted its third-quarter results on Monday. Its growth rate accelerated to 96% (it was 93% in the previous quarter), and it easily beat expectations. Yet the stock's been trading lower in recent days amid a great deal of softness in the tech sector.

Is Palantir's stock a no-brainer buy right now, and could this be the catalyst that sends it to a new all-time high?

The data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) company's latest results covered the three-month period ending Sept. 30. Revenue for the period totaled $2.31 billion (higher than analyst projections of $2.18 billion), marking the first time that the company generated more than $2 billion in revenue during a single quarter. It's a tremendous achievement for the business, as in 2022 its annual revenue was just below that level. Palantir has been on an incredible tear, with its growth accelerating as more customers seek AI-powered intelligence.

Another big milestone was the shift to a greater share of commercial revenue. For the first time, the company's U.S. commercial revenue exceeded its U.S. government revenue ($984 million versus $953 million). It's a great sign that the company is growing and expanding into other areas besides government agencies.

Palantir's adjusted earnings per share (EPS) came in at 44 cents, which was higher than the 41 cents analysts were looking for.

Overall, it was another tremendous quarter for the company, highlighting its impressive and incredible growth. But the stock has been trading lower in recent days, and in after-hours trading it was showing a big drop as well, as the market may be growing concerned about its high valuation at a time when tech stocks as a whole are under pressure.

Palantir's business is doing exceptionally well, but its profitability remains fairly low relative to earnings. At $0.44 EPS, that would extrapolate to an annual run rate of $1.76 if it maintained the same level of profitability for four quarters. The stock closed at just over $178 on Monday, meaning that it's trading at more than 100 times earnings. It's a steep multiple, which may be tough to justify, even given its high growth rate.

While Palantir's stock looks like an intriguing buy on weakness, and long-term investors may want to consider buying it in light of its consistently strong results, I wouldn't call it a no-brainer buy simply because its valuation is already fairly high; impressive levels of growth are already priced in, which is why the stock isn't a surefire bet to take off, even after posting such impressive numbers.

#3064. ​AI Is Growing Fast. The Chief AI Officer Role Is Not. Yet

Rob Sloan is VP of Cybersecurity Advocacy at Zscaler, where he helps organizations navigate cybersecurity risk and business resilience.

​AI now touches every part of the business. Far from simply being a technology initiative, AI is now a governance issue, an operating issue, a board-level priority and, increasingly, a security issue.

Given its importance, you would be forgiven for expecting most companies to have clearly assigned executive accountability for AI. Many probably do. But that accountability is not yet visible publicly in many cases.​

To find evidence that a company had publicly named a C-level executive with “AI” in the title, I reviewed press releases, SEC filings, company websites and public appointment announcements for every S&P 500 constituent. Only 75 organizations, or 15% of the index, publicly have one.​

That may be about to change. Regulation is taking shape, the threat landscape is shifting quickly, and boards and executive teams have a clearer view of both the opportunities and the risks AI creates across the business.

The White House has added to that momentum by requiring federal agencies to designate chief AI officers, signaling that AI governance is moving toward more visible executive accountability.​

Of the 75 companies in the dataset, 36 use the stand-alone chief AI officer title. Another 18 use chief AI and data officer.​

My findings contrast sharply with those reported in IBM’s 2026 CEO Study earlier this year. That research drew on an international sample of responses from 2,000 chief executives, 76% of whom said their organization had a chief AI officer. The reason for the gap is not obvious from the published findings alone. However, the IBM research starts with a different dataset than mine and may include companies that haven’t publicly announced the role.​

From my own research, the split between stand-alone chief AI officer roles and blended AI titles points to a deeper governance question: Where does AI actually belong inside the company?​

It makes sense that 18 companies blend chief AI and data officers into one role. AI depends on data pipelines, governance, access controls and quality, and many companies already have a C-suite leader with responsibility for those areas. Four companies created chief technology and AI officer positions, three fused AI and digital, and one company alone had a chief information and AI officer.​

There is also a practical reason companies might hesitate to create a new title: cost. Adding a C-level role is expensive once compensation, recruitment, onboarding and organizational change are counted, which helps explain why many organizations add AI to an existing remit.​

However, when AI sits inside a broader data, technology or operations brief, accountability can blur just as the stakes are rising.​

In my view, the S&P 500 companies without visible accountability in the C-suite fall into three broad categories:​

• First are companies where AI may already be embedded deeply enough in product, engineering or platform leadership that a separate chief AI officer does not yet seem necessary. This appears to be the case for technology companies in particular.​

• Second, and probably the largest group, are companies where AI responsibility exists but sits inside another executive’s remit—often under the CIO, CISO, CDO, CTO or chief digital officer—without a title change or a dedicated budget.​

• Third are companies that still do not appear to treat AI as a distinct C-suite issue, which includes utilities, real estate companies, commodity producers and materials companies.

AI ownership often exists in each of these categories but is either not clearly signaled or not present in the C-suite. That position gets harder to defend as AI use spreads through employee workflows, vendor products, customer interactions and internal decision-making.​

Security is one reason this will not stay optional. My company’s recent ThreatLabz study based on hundreds of enterprise AI security readiness assessments found that 91% of organizations had publicly reachable AI infrastructure, while none had identity-based access controls in place.

As AI systems become connected to enterprise data and workflows, the potential impact of misuse or external compromise grows. To reduce the likelihood of chaos spreading at machine speed, companies will need clearer ownership of guardrails, approvals and risk.​

Regulation is also a factor. The EU AI Act is moving from policy into enforcement, with penalties of up to 35 million euros or 7% of global revenue, turning AI governance into a practical compliance issue. Not every company will need a stand-alone chief AI officer, but more will need to show who is accountable for how AI is deployed, governed and secured.​

I expect the chief AI officer role, whether stand-alone or combined with another C-level function, to grow quickly. The closest precedent is the rise of the chief information security officer.​

For years, security sat within broader IT leadership, but over time that became less tenable. The CISO role emerged as companies recognized that cybersecurity required clear ownership: The risk was too material, the accountability too important and the board-level implications too obvious. AI now appears to be moving along a similar path, albeit at a much faster pace.​

Companies still have time to decide what AI leadership should look like on their own terms, but they may not have much time left to treat clear executive accountability as optional.​​

#3060. If I Had $1,000 to Invest Today, Here's the Trillion-Dollar Stock I'd Buy Instead of SpaceX

The recent correction in Alphabet stock creates a long-term buying opportunity for investors.

Elon Musk's Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.23%) went public in June. Its stock quickly soared to a peak of $225 as investors clamoured to buy a slice of the company, but that enthusiasm quickly faded, and it has since lost 40% of its value.

Its valuation might explain why. SpaceX still has a market capitalization of $1.83 trillion as I write this (Oct. 31), so based on the company's trailing 12-month revenue of $32 billion, its stock trades at a sky-high price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 57, making it eight times as expensive as the Nasdaq-100 index.

Therefore, although SpaceX is forecasting substantial revenue growth over the next few years, more downside might be on the horizon for its stock in the near term. I think investors can find better value elsewhere, so if I had $1,000 to deploy today, here's why I'd buy Alphabet (GOOG -0.07%)(GOOGL -0.30%) stock instead.

Alphabet is a technology conglomerate with a range of different businesses, but Google Search and Google Cloud are its most important. Search accounts for over half the company's total revenue, whereas Cloud consistently delivers the fastest growth. More importantly, these businesses are at the center of Alphabet's artificial intelligence (AI) strategy.

Google Search is evolving. Users no longer have to sift through web pages to find the information they need, because new features like AI Overviews and AI Mode provide them with comprehensive answers to their queries instantly. These features bridge the gap between the traditional search experience and the AI chatbot experience, and Alphabet says they are driving increased usage for Google Search overall.

In fact, search queries grew at the fastest year-over-year pace in five years during the third quarter of 2026 (ended Sept. 30), meaning users saw more ads, which allowed the platform to bring in more money. Google Search revenue actually set a quarterly record of $63.3 billion during Q3, up 12% compared to the year-ago period. However, that was slightly short of Wall Street's consensus forecast, which contributed to a sharp correction in Alphabet stock.

Google Cloud, on the other hand, topped Wall Street's expectations, with revenue exploding higher by 103% year over year to $30.7 billion. The platform benefited from the continued demand for data center computing capacity, ready-made foundation models, and development tools, which enterprises need to create and deploy AI software.

But Google Cloud 's growth story appears to be in the early innings, because the platform ended Q3 with an order backlog of $561 billion, which grew by a whopping 262% from the year-ago period. It was attributable to customers who were waiting for Alphabet to build more data centers so they can tap into the computing capacity, but part of it also came from customers who were awaiting delivery of the company's custom chips.

Broadcom has helped Alphabet design and fabricate several generations of its tensor processing unit (TPU) data center chips for AI workloads. The latest 8t TPU offers 2.7 times better performance in training workloads than the previous generation, while the 8i offers an 80% improvement in inference price performance. Direct TPU sales could become a significant financial opportunity for Google Cloud.

Alphabet stock is trading at a P/S ratio of 7.3, so it's only slightly more expensive than the Nasdaq-100 index which has a P/S ratio of 6.6. However, it's substantially cheaper than SpaceX by that valuation metric.

Plus, Alphabet is highly profitable, so we can value its stock using the more traditional price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio. Based on the company's trailing 12-month earnings of $19.15 per share, its stock has a P/E ratio of just 14.7 – half the P/E of the Nasdaq-100 which is 29.5. In other words, Alphabet looks heavily undervalued right now.

However, the company's second-quarter earnings received a massive one-off boost from its investment gains, primarily from its holding in SpaceX. Accounting rules required Alphabet to recognize the fair value of its SpaceX position after the company's recent IPO, resulting in a one-off earnings benefit of over $90 billion -- which had nothing to do with its operations.

Therefore, it's disingenuous to value Alphabet based on its trailing earnings. However, Wall Street's consensus estimate (provided by Yahoo! Finance) suggests the company could deliver earnings of $14.81 per share in 2027, placing its stock at a forward P/E of 19. Therefore, it's still cheaper than the Nasdaq-100 which has a forward P/E of 21.1.

As a result, I think Alphabet stock has a much greater chance of delivering upside from here than SpaceX stock.

Anthony Di Pizio has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet and Broadcom. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3057. Smart Drones In Agriculture: Revolutionizing Sustainability For Farmers

David Ly is the founder of Iveda, having served as CEO and Chairman of the Board of Directors since the company’s inception in 2003.

​Agriculture has always been a balancing act. Farmers are asked to produce more—more yield, more consistency, more efficiency—while simultaneously protecting the land, water and ecosystems that make farming possible in the first place. For most of history, those two demands have been in tension. Smart drones are changing that equation.

This isn’t about replacing the farmer’s intuition or experience. It’s about giving them a vantage point they’ve never had before: real-time, high-resolution visibility across every acre, without walking every row. The data that drones generate on crop health, soil conditions, livestock movement, resource usage and more is turning decisions that used to be based on instinct into decisions backed by precision.

I’ve spent years working at the intersection of AI and real-world deployment. Agriculture is one of the most compelling frontiers I’ve seen. The problems are concrete, the stakes are high and the technology is finally mature enough to meet the moment.

A farmer walking a field sees what’s in front of them. A drone sees everything simultaneously, consistently and with a level of detail no ground-level inspection can match.

Aerial imaging combined with multispectral sensors and AI-driven analysis allows farmers to monitor crop health across entire growing seasons. These include changes in plant color signaling early-stage disease, variations in canopy density indicating uneven growth and dry pockets invisible from the ground. By analyzing these alongside weather patterns, soil conditions and crop maturity, farmers can make smarter decisions on planting, irrigation and harvesting, ultimately reducing waste and improving yield quality.

Precision irrigation is one of the clearest examples. Traditional irrigation applies water broadly, which is typically efficient on average, but wasteful at the edges. Drone-generated soil moisture mapping allows farmers to irrigate exactly where water is needed, in the quantities the crop requires. Less water used, less runoff, healthier plants.

The problem is often simpler than people expect. I’ve spoken with cattle farmers who face a frustratingly basic challenge: When it’s time to bring the cows in for milking, they first have to find them. Across a large property, that search takes time and people, and it happens every single day. Livestock management across large or remote terrain has always been labor-intensive. Tracking movements, identifying injured animals and making sure the herd hasn’t strayed traditionally require significant manpower and still leave blind spots.

A view from above can change that. Drones change the coverage equation. In just a few minutes, a single drone can cover ground that would take hours on foot, sending back real-time location data so ranchers always know where their animals are at any moment. It helps a farmer know exactly where to go and spot the animal that’s separated from the herd before it becomes a bigger problem. That’s a practical application of technology I can get behind: Help people find their animals sooner so they can get on with caring for them.

Thermal imaging can detect signs of illness before they’re obvious to ground-level observers: elevated body temperature, unusual stillness, separation from the herd. AI-powered drones can also automate counting livestock, tracking weight gain and predicting breeding cycles, with that data feeding directly into farm management systems to inform decisions on herd movement, feed replenishment and grazing rotations.

Regulatory and consumer pressure around animal welfare is growing, and drone monitoring offers a way to demonstrate, with data, that animals are being managed responsibly.

The environmental cost of conventional farming is well-documented. Pesticide runoff contaminates waterways, excess fertilizer degrades soil and broad-spectrum chemical application harms non-target species including the pollinators agriculture depends on. These aren’t abstract concerns. They’re real operational and regulatory challenges farmers are dealing with more and more.

Drone-enabled precision application addresses this directly. By the time a pest infestation is visible at ground level, it has likely already spread. Drones equipped with thermal and multispectral imaging can detect anomalies before they become visible, flagging specific areas for targeted treatment rather than blanket application across the full field. According to UC Davis agricultural engineer Ken Giles, smart drone application has demonstrated 30% to 40% reductions in chemical application rates compared to conventional methods, with some cases reaching as high as 90%.

Water conservation follows the same logic. Agriculture accounts for roughly 70% of global freshwater withdrawals, according to the UN World Water Development Report, and inefficient irrigation is a major contributor. Drone-generated data, combined with soil sensors and weather modeling, allows irrigation systems to operate with a precision manual management can’t match. And because drones rely less on fuel-intensive heavy machinery, they can cut the carbon footprint of operations like targeted spraying, soil monitoring and land surveying. That matters more as farmers face growing pressure to report on sustainability and weigh new technology with that in mind.

The drone systems gaining real adoption in agriculture aren’t necessarily the most sophisticated. They’re the ones that are reliable, integrate into existing workflows without demanding an operational overhaul and produce insights farmers can act on without a data science team to interpret them.

Ease of use matters, durability matters and the hardware must be built for the environment, not the demo—industrial-grade, weather-resistant, with redundant fail-safe systems that keep operating when conditions aren’t cooperative. And trust, built through consistent performance over time rather than a single impressive demonstration, matters most of all.

Smart drones have the potential to meaningfully shift the sustainability calculus for farmers around the world. But that potential is only realized when the technology is designed around where farming actually happens, in variable weather, across imperfect terrain, by people who need it to work without a user manual.

That’s the standard worth building toward.​

#3056. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

TL;DR: Mortgage rates kicked off the week with a drop, but they’re still above 7%.

Mortgage rates are cooling off as we roll into November. However, they’re still above the 7% threshold.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.07% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 11 basis points lower than yesterday and 13 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

This week’s employment data could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other — more on that below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

Which were the primary driver of the shortfall. And also in the conversion across other channels for a period. #3051. Navigating The AI Platform Shift: How Leaders Actually Keep Up

Vivek Bhaskaran is founder & CEO of QuestionPro, a global leader in survey and research, data and insights services.

AI is not just another technology trend. It is a platform shift. In every true platform shift, the way value is created and delivered fundamentally changes, and the leaders who treat it like a routine upgrade usually experience the hardest surprise. In 2005, when I started my company, the shift was from shrink-wrapped software to cloud. Then came mobile. Today it is AI, and the speed and range of outcomes are unlike anything we have seen before.

What keeps many leaders up at night is not whether AI will change everything. It is whether they, their teams and their companies are keeping up. The good news is you do not need a 70-page AI readiness framework to respond. What you need are a few concrete behaviors you can put in place this quarter.​

Every platform shift introduces fog. You know something big is happening, but you cannot see exactly where it will land or how long the uncertainty will last. When the iPhone launched in 2007, BlackBerry’s revenue actually doubled over the next two years. If you were the CFO in 2009, the numbers would have told you everything was fine. We know how that story ended.

With AI, the fog is even thicker. The range of possible outcomes runs from “we all lose our jobs” to “we all sit on a beach drinking margaritas while agents do the work.” Smart people argue for both extremes. As a founder and CEO, worrying about outcomes I cannot personally influence does not help me run a better company. What matters is how my team and I navigate the next days, weeks and quarters.

One simple metaphor guides my thinking: do not sail into the wind, sail along with it. You do not need the wind perfectly behind you, but you cannot stubbornly fight it either.

There is a romantic narrative in tech that you must be an early adopter of everything or you are a laggard. I do not buy it. Blockchain and Bitcoin are a good example. Years ago, people told me we should put surveys on the blockchain. We could have. But there was no real movement, no real value creation at scale. Lots of froth, very little traction.

AI and mobile have been different. You can see real movement, real value, real users. This is where an “early majority” mindset pays off: wait just long enough to see real traction, then lean in hard.

I stopped asking “should we try this” and started asking three sharper questions before committing resources:

• Has this technology produced measurable value in use cases similar to ours?

• Are customers asking for it, not just vendors pitching it?

• Can we test it in a six-week project with limited downside?

When the answers start trending yes, that is your signal to move from watching to doing. Any leader can borrow this checklist tomorrow.

We never rolled out a formal AI readiness model. We run a company with a few hundred people, not a consulting case study. Instead we built around three behaviors any organization can adopt: awareness, selective adoption and adaptability.

We run a weekly all-hands town hall. One of our leaders suggested a 10-minute “AI hacks” segment. Every Thursday, teams demo how they are using AI in marketing, support, product or operations. Skeptics realize their peers are already using it. Informal champions emerge. Experimentation gets normalized.

We picked a bounded project: a chat-based interface for survey creation instead of the traditional point-and-click builder. Low stakes, fast to deploy. It taught us how AI actually behaves with our data and users, what skills our team had and lacked and where the experience needed to change to feel natural rather than gimmicky.

You cannot jump straight from confusion to moonshots. You earn that right by building awareness, practicing selective adoption and proving adaptability. Once that foundation is in place, you can ask bolder questions. For us, that is agentic workflows for customer experience: imagine every piece of customer feedback triggering an end-to-end, semi-autonomous workflow that diagnoses the issue, takes action in billing or support systems and closes the loop with the customer. With unlimited people, that is what you would build anyway. AI agents make a version of it feasible.

For your organization, a moonshot should feel slightly unreasonable but directionally aligned with where you already see value. Anchor it in real problems customers care about, constrain it enough that you can iterate and keep humans in the loop wherever trust and brand are on the line.

The lesson from this platform shift is simple. Accept that you are in the fog and decide to move anyway. Adopt an early-majority mindset. Institutionalize awareness, selective adoption and adaptability. Do that, and you give your teams permission to evolve with the technology instead of freezing in place.

The question is not “Is AI overrated or overhyped?” It is “What concrete behavior will you change inside your company in the next 90 days to sail with the wind instead of into it?” That answer will determine whether this platform shift becomes your opportunity or your post-mortem.​

#3049. A Disappointing IPO Didn't Stop Meta Platforms: Here's Why That Matters for the Anthropic IPO

Meta Platforms (then called Facebook) experienced a rocky first year on the market. Anthropic's stock could follow a similar post-IPO path.

As soon as the week of Nov. 16, artificial intelligence (AI) start-up Anthropic could go public. While details like the initial public offering (IPO) date and the initial pricing of the shares have still not been finalized, we do know three things: Anthropic will trade on the Nasdaq stock exchange, it will trade under the ticker ANT, and this is a highly anticipated IPO, as it will be one of the first major pure-play AI companies that retail investors can own a piece of.

There's no way to know what the early price action will look like. But even if Anthropic stock stumbles right out of the gate, that doesn't mean it won't eventually turn out to be a long-term winner. That's because exactly that happened with Meta Platforms (META -1.34%).

While Meta, formerly Facebook, isn't the same type of company as Anthropic, they share some key similarities. Before Meta went public, there really wasn't a way to invest in the rising trend of social media, just like there hasn't been a major pure-play AI company to invest in since privately held OpenAI launched ChatGPT in November 2022 and kicked off that trend.

The popular social media platform of the early 2000s, MySpace, never went public, and Twitter, now X, didn't IPO until 2013. So when Meta went public in May 2012, it generated a lot of fanfare, hype, and high expectations.

That said, the IPO did not go smoothly. Trading on IPO day was delayed due to technical difficulties; some investors didn't receive confirmation of their trading activity, and the stock closed its first day of trading to the public at $38.23, barely above its offering price of $38.

Following those first-day issues, things did not get much better. According to research from The Motley Fool, Meta was one of the top 10 IPOs of all time by capital raised, but it had the worst three-month stretch of any of those IPOs, with the stock price falling 47%. By early September, it was down even further. After that rough stretch, it was understandable that some shareholders were wondering whether investing in Meta early had been a mistake.

Those who held on or even added to their position, however, are likely glad they did. Not only was Meta's stock price up by 289% five years after its IPO, but by May 2026, 10 years afterward, shares were up 1,572%.

Anthropic may not follow a similar path when it debuts. But the overall lesson from Meta is that a company's first few months of trading don't necessarily make or break it as an investment. That's important to remember on an IPO day.

That said, it also means the early days around an IPO itself won't make retail investors rich. To capture the biggest gains that Anthropic may offer will require conviction to stand by the stock through difficult periods. Investors will need to give it enough time to deliver meaningful gains, which can take years. If you lack that sort of conviction about a given stock, or you don't have that type of long time horizon for the investment, that's not a bad thing for an investor to admit to themselves. Recognizing in advance where you stand can help you avoid a lot of headaches, not to mention spare you from potential losses if you'd be an emotional seller in the face of early stock price declines.

#3047. From Data Layer To Decision Layer: Why AI Agents Need More Than Information

Gary Kotovets, Chief Data, Analytics, and AI Officer at Dun & Bradstreet.

​As enterprises accelerate their transition from AI as a querying tool to AI as an autonomous executor, the fundamental role of data within organizational architecture must evolve in kind. The passive data layer, a reservoir sitting beneath the application stack and waiting to be queried, is no longer sufficient to meet the demands of agentic systems.​

Agents tasked with onboarding suppliers, approving customers, flagging risk exposures or recommending next-best actions require more than access to raw information. They need enriched, trusted business context delivered precisely at the moment a decision is being considered, with enough confidence and clarity to support action inside the workflow itself.​

Not all data is equal. What separates useful context from noise in an agentic workflow is provenance, meaning a clear understanding of where the data originated, how it was verified and whether it is authoritative enough to serve as ground truth for the decision at hand.​

This is where the concept of the data originator as truth becomes operationally significant. When an AI agent needs to evaluate a counterparty, assess a supplier’s risk profile or validate a business relationship, the only data worth trusting is data that has been verified at its source, structured around a persistent business identity and enriched with the commercial relationships that define how that entity actually operates in the world.​

In commercial contexts, that source of truth should begin with a persistent business identifier. Such an identifier is not simply a reference code; it is an anchor point that connects a verified legal identity to the broader web of attributes, relationships and signals that define a business.​

That connected view is what many organizations are beginning to understand as a commercial graph. At its best, a commercial graph links business identity, ownership structure, financial health signals, trade behavior, operational history and supply chain relationships into a structured view of how an entity participates in the global economy.​

In this model, a commercial graph can also provide deterministic answers to core identity and linkage questions. An agent should not have to infer probabilistically what trusted business context can establish in advance.​

For an AI agent, this distinction is critical. When an agent evaluates a business record anchored by a persistent, verified identifier, it is not acting on loosely matched names, scraped web data or self-reported attributes alone; it is acting on grounded business context that has been organized around a durable identity.​

This reframes data not as a static input, but as dynamic decision infrastructure. It becomes an operational substrate that must be woven into the execution layer itself rather than retrieved from the periphery only after a user or system knows which question to ask.​

The shift from retrieval to execution also changes the meaning of “next-best action.” In traditional analytics environments, next-best action is often treated as a recommendation surfaced to a human decision-maker. In agentic workflows, it becomes a governing framework for how autonomous systems evaluate options, apply policy and determine the appropriate next step.​

That next step may be simple, such as routing a supplier for additional review. It may also be consequential, such as recommending customer terms, flagging an ownership change, escalating a compliance risk or identifying a disruption in a critical supply chain relationship.​

These are not merely search problems; they are judgment problems. And judgment requires more than access to information; it requires context, confidence, thresholds and an understanding of relationships that may not be visible in any single data point.​

This is why accuracy, provenance and the identity of the data originator become non-negotiable as AI agents move from answering questions to executing high-stakes business decisions. Truth in an agentic workflow must be grounded and deterministic, not approximated, because the cost of approximation rises sharply when software is empowered to act.​

Enterprise leaders should therefore begin rethinking their data strategies not as a foundation beneath AI, but as an integrated component of the AI execution layer. Data should participate actively in every decision cycle, carrying with it verified identity, originator-backed intelligence, relationship context and risk signals that agents can apply in real time.​

That requires new scrutiny of the data environment. Leaders must ask not only whether information is available, but whether it is authoritative, current, connected and fit for autonomous decisioning.​

They must also ask whether their systems can distinguish between a company name and a verified business identity. Without that distinction, AI agents may confuse entities with similar names, miss relevant ownership relationships or act on incomplete risk signals hidden several layers away in a corporate family or supply chain.​

The organizations that solve this problem are the ones I believe will be better positioned to move AI beyond copilots and chat interfaces into true operational execution. Their agents will be more capable of distinguishing signals from noise, applying business context at the moment of decision and recommending next-best actions with a clearer understanding of the commercial reality surrounding each entity.​

As AI moves deeper into procurement, credit, compliance, sales and customer operations, autonomous systems will need more than access to information. They will need access to verified business truth, structured through persistent identity, enriched by a commercial graph and embedded directly into the workflows where decisions are made.​

This is the next frontier of enterprise AI. The new industry leaders will not be those with the largest reservoirs of data, but those with the most trusted decision infrastructure.​
