#3045. Sandisk Shares Sink Despite Surging Sales. Is It Time to Buy the Stock?

Sandisk has been a top-performing stock this year, despite being down more than 50% from its 2026 highs.

Sandisk (SNDK -6.59%) has been one of the market's best-performing stocks this year, but it slid 13.5% in the session following its fiscal Q1 earnings report on Oct. 29, despite the memory maker seeing its sales surge and profits soar. The stock is still up around 375% on the year, even after the pullback, though down more than 50% from its earlier highs. This could make this recent dip a buying opportunity.

Sandisk has been a big beneficiary of rising NAND (flash) memory prices, as supply shortages have caused prices to skyrocket as demand climbs. This is due to a combination of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers needing massive high-performance solid-state drives (SSDs) that use flash memory to hold training data and the big three memory makers shifting their focus toward high bandwidth memory (HBM), a special form of DRAM (dynamic random access memory) that gets packaged with graphics processing units (GPUs) and other AI chips to reduce latency.

As a pure-play NAND maker, Sandisk's revenue has been surging, as prices continue to rise rapidly. This continued in the company's fiscal Q1, with its revenue jumping 378% to $11 billion.

Data center revenue skyrocketed 1,682% year over year to $4.8 billion, driven by demand from its partnerships with three large U.S. hyperscalers. Its Edge segment, which includes smartphones and PCs, saw revenue jump 320% to $5.8 billion, while the consumer segment, which consists of things like flash drives, saw revenue decrease 39% to $397 million.

Sandisk said that 60% of its revenue growth came from volume increases and 40% from pricing. This is presumably based on its sequential growth. Pricing, meanwhile, has also boosted Sandisk's gross margins. For the quarter, gross margin climbed from 29.9% last year and 84.6% in fiscal Q4 to 85.1% in fiscal Q1. The company's adjusted earnings per share (EPS), meanwhile, rose from $1.22 to $49.51. That's well above the adjusted EPS of $44-$46 it previously forecast.

Looking ahead, Sandisk management guided for fiscal Q2 revenue to be between $12.2 billion and $12.6 billion, up from $3 billion a year ago. Gross margin is projected to be between 84.4% and 85.4%, up from 50.9% a year ago. Adjusted EPS, meanwhile, is expected to climb from $5.15 to between $55 and $57.

Sandisk said it has eight new business model (NBM) contracts, with an average weighted duration of more than four years. The minimum contract floor pricing on the deals is $93.9 billion, and it has $16.5 billion in financial guarantees. About half its bits are committed to NBMs this year and two-thirds in fiscal 2028.

Sandisk expects industry data center demand to grow by 40% in calendar year 2027. Meanwhile, it said that its NBM pipeline is greater than its supply through the end of this decade.

Memory stocks are cheap on a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio basis, and Sandisk is no exception, trading at just over 5 times fiscal 2027 analyst estimates. The cheap valuations in the space largely reflect the historically cyclical nature of the memory market, which tends to see large boom-and-bust cycles.

Arguably, this memory cycle will be much different than any seen in the past. Demand for both DRAM and NAND has been insatiable with AI, and companies have not been able to keep up. The big three memory makers of Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron are largely focused on HBM, which carries high prices and strong margins, and is seeing demand soar. While the NAND market has more players than the DRAM market, the priorities of the big three memory companies are generally to keep NAND supply growth in check, as their physical cleanroom space and fab capacity are shifting more toward HBM, which is a capacity hog.

Just like GPUs and CPUs, memory is often a short-term asset that needs to get replaced every several years. Combined with long-term contracts, continued rising demand, and clean room constraints, expect this NAND cycle to last much longer than past ones, making Sandisk a top AI stock to own on this dip.

The healthcare stock may finally have the catalyst that it needs to take off before the end of the year.

Pfizer's stock has been rallying this year, but it's still down more than 30% in five years, as investors remain cautious now that the business isn't generating huge amounts of revenue from its COVID vaccine and pill.

During the most recent quarter, the company reported $16.6 billion in revenue, which was far higher than analyst expectations of $15.9 billion. Its adjusted per-share profit of 87 cents was also comfortably higher than Wall Street estimates of 73 cents.

In addition, Pfizer raised its full-year guidance, projecting adjusted per-share profit in the range of $2.95 to $3.05, up from a prior forecast of $2.80 to $3.

While investors have been concerned about declining sales and patent cliffs, Pfizer has given the market reason to be more optimistic about its future, with revenue from launched and acquired products soaring 32% this past quarter. Meanwhile, it still has a promising pipeline with many drug candidates in development that could further bolster its sales in the future.

#3040. ​From Freight To Blueprints: How Generative AI Changed The Way Ideas Spread

Siri Swahari is VP of US Global Technology Operations at CGI, author of ThinkIn4D, and founder of WEC, Women Executives Circle.

For a century, ideas moved like freight. Organizations made finished products: ads, articles, videos. Distribution networks shipped those assets to millions. Competitive advantage came from owning the factories and the shipping lanes.

Most enterprise playbooks still assume this model. Marketing optimizes the asset. Security traces the shipment. Communications recalls the defective product.

Generative AI is adding a new distribution architecture. Ideas can now move like blueprints.

Instead of manufacturing once and distributing widely, we can distribute the instructions and let the audience manufacture locally. Millions of local factories. One blueprint. Infinite originals.

The same prompt reached me three times in one week: in my feed, in a team channel and in my family group chat. Three people, three different outputs, one set of instructions. That was the moment the pattern became impossible to ignore.

Millions of people were asking AI tools to roast them, describe them or warn others about them. The finished image or post didn’t have to be what spread. The instruction did.

It is a 3D-printer moment for culture and communication: a prompt, a style or a format travels, and everyone who runs it can produce an original.

Templates, memes and social challenges have long let audiences help create culture. Generative AI extends that behavior because the audience can now fabricate substantially different outputs from the same instructions. Prompt marketplaces suggest an economy forming around instructions themselves.

The barrier to producing a first version has fallen dramatically. The premium moves toward intent, judgment, taste, context and the ability to shape what others choose to create.

When instructions travel, and the audience becomes the production layer, marketing, security and trust deserve another look. Three executive functions may feel this shift first.

When every customer has a factory, the finished campaign is no longer the only source of leverage. Organizations can create attention by giving audiences something to make, personalize or reinterpret rather than simply watch. This adds new questions to the creative brief.

Increasingly: What will 10,000 people want to make for themselves?

Marketing leaders can apply a blueprint test to major campaigns. Is there a version of this idea that customers would generate, personalize and claim as their own?

The answer will not always be yes, and finished assets still matter. But organizations now have a second distribution mechanism: Create the artifact, or create the conditions for audiences to make their own.

A factory is only as safe as what gets fed into it. When employees use consumer AI tools, they may supply the raw material: their faces, voices, documents, data, code and ideas. That material leaves the enterprise perimeter voluntarily because the exchange feels useful, easy or entertaining.

The scale is no longer hypothetical. Cyberhaven’s “2026 AI Adoption & Risk Report” found that 39.7% of AI interactions involve sensitive data, much of it through personal accounts outside organizational visibility. Zscaler’s “ThreatLabz 2026 AI Security Report” found enterprise data transfers to AI applications surged 93% year over year, topping 18,000 terabytes.

Security programs were built around stopping hostile inbound traffic. The blueprint economy adds another front: friendly outbound traffic.

Leaders need input governance with the same clarity they apply to phishing. Define what may enter consumer AI systems. Make the policy understandable. Explain the rationale before the next viral AI moment arrives. Design ownership before rollout, not after the first bad output.

Blueprint cycles move faster than policy review cycles.

Product recalls work because a defective object can be identified, traced and pulled. Misinformation strategies often rely on the same logic: Find the false artifact, correct it at the source, watch the correction propagate.

Thousands of people can independently fabricate a misleading claim from a shared instruction set. There may be no single source to correct and no single object to pull.

When production is distributed, credibility has to be distributed, too.

The resilient response has to be built before the crisis. That means authenticated channels, content provenance standards such as C2PA Content Credentials and stakeholder relationships strong enough that people know where to verify before they trust the print.

The factories are becoming more autonomous. As AI moves from generation toward agency, organizations will increasingly work on systems objectives rather than individual prompts.

That raises a different class of leadership question: what systems are allowed to create, what inputs they may draw on, what decisions they can make and who remains accountable when the same instruction produces thousands of different outputs. The answers have to be part of the design, before anything deploys.

Two instincts dominate boardroom conversations about AI. Chase every new capability or prohibit the tools entirely. Both miss the structural change.

The durable move is an audit. Walk through your marketing, security and communications strategies and identify every place that assumes a finished object moving from one source through a traceable path. Those assumptions may now have an expiration date.

In a blueprint economy, governance cannot sit downstream at the point of output. It has to move upstream, into the instructions, the inputs and the permissions.

For executives, that means asking three questions. What are we still treating as a finished asset that could become a reusable blueprint? What are employees and customers now able to create without us? What inputs and permissions does that model require?

These are operating-model questions. The freight era rewarded whoever owned the factories and the shipping lanes. In the blueprint economy, customers, employees and communities have factories of their own. The leadership advantage will come from designing the blueprint, the boundaries and the trust around it.

The factory has moved closer to the audience.

#3039. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

iShares Select U.S. REIT ETF (ICF +0.69%) and Xtrackers International Real Estate ETF (HAUZ +0.93%) provide distinct approaches to real estate, with one focusing on domestic leaders and the other spanning hundreds of international properties.

Investors often look to real estate investment trusts for income and potential diversification. Choosing between these funds involves weighing the stability and recent performance of the U.S. market against the broader reach and lower costs associated with international exposure. This analysis compares their costs, risk profiles, and portfolios.

Beta measures price volatility relative to the S&P 500; beta is calculated from monthly returns over the available fund history (up to five years). The 1-yr return represents total return over the trailing 12 months. Dividend yield is the trailing-12-month distribution yield.

The Xtrackers fund is the more affordable option, costing less than one-third of the iShares fund. Beyond the lower expense ratio, it also offers a higher payout for income seekers, with a yield of 3.8% compared to 2.6% for its counterpart.

iShares Select U.S. REIT ETF focuses on a concentrated group of 30 holdings within the domestic market. Its largest positions include Welltower at 8.32%, Equinix at 7.8%, and American Tower at 7.6%. It was launched in 2001. iShares Select U.S. REIT ETF has paid $1.74 per share over the trailing 12 months, which on its recent ~$65.77 share price works out to a 2.6% yield.

Xtrackers International Real Estate ETF tracks hundreds of companies outside the United States, holding 410 securities in total. The portfolio consists primarily of real estate at 95%, with minor tilts toward communication services at 1.2% and consumer discretionary at 0.8%. Top holdings include Goodman Group at 4.2%, Mitsubishi Estate Co. Ltd. at 3.32%, and Mitsui Fudosan Co. Ltd. at 3%. It was launched in 2013. Xtrackers International Real Estate ETF has paid $0.82 per share over the trailing 12 months, which on its recent ~$21.44 share price works out to a 3.8% yield.

For more guidance on ETF investing, check out the full guide at this link.

Investing in real estate investment trusts (REITs) can be a good way to diversify your portfolio, take advantage of generous dividend yields, and capitalize on long-term trends. ICF and HAUZ both hold large industrial and infrastructure REITs, making them appealing ways to play high-growth themes like healthcare, logistics, and data centers without choosing a singular company or product. Which ETF is the better buy?

HAUZ offers a bigger dividend yield and a lower expense ratio, which will likely appeal to income-focused investors. But do those characteristics make up for the fact that the ETF has dropped more than 11% on a total return basis over the last five years? If you already have plenty of U.S. real estate exposure and are seeking broad diversification outside domestic real estate stocks, it might be worth taking a small position in HAUZ to capitalize on its low fees and large payments.

ICF is a much more concentrated play, with only 30 REITs in its portfolio, and a focus on U.S. companies. But remember that each of those companies owns thousands of properties, and while the companies are based in the U.S., many also operate internationally. Its concentrated focus on large caps has served it well as investor interest has returned to the REIT sector amid stabilizing interest rates, attractive valuations, and a desire for income.

Investors who believe in the long-term story of industrial and commercial property will likely be well served with a position in ICF. Those looking for broader diversification outside the U.S., and who can manage the additional fluctuations related to foreign exchange, interest rates, and tariffs that come with investing internationally, may be drawn to HAUZ's higher dividend payout and lower fees.

#3034. Your AI Budget Is Already A Headcount Decision

Prashant Jalan is the founder of Guickly and previously led applied AI teams in the mapping technology industry.

When I was a tech lead manager at Google, adding even one person to my team took almost a quarter. I had to write the justification, defend the scope in a planning meeting and then wait. Sometimes the answer came back as “yes”; at times, it didn’t. Every person on that team was a number somebody had signed their name to.

The same money moves very differently now. AI tools can be purchased through a corporate card or software subscription, often without the review or accountability that comes with adding a person to the team.​

​I hear a version of this from almost every company I talk to. A role opens up and never gets backfilled, because the team found a way to cover it. A manager who cannot get a requirement approved grows the AI tooling budget instead. Nobody questions it, because tooling is not headcount.

Those are labor decisions. They are just never called that.

It is also not little money anymore. Bain & Co. has modeled a scenario in which AI tokens eventually replace roughly a quarter of headcount operating expenses. Nothing reaches a quarter of operating expenses without displacing some other line item. In most companies, that line item is payroll.​​

The uncomfortable part is that nobody can actually compare the two options, because the two options do not live in the same place.​

The cost of an employee is relatively straightforward to calculate. Finance tracks a fully loaded cost tied to a specific person, with a manager, a start date and a place in the budget.​​

AI spend is the opposite. It arrives through annual contracts, corporate cards, employee expense reports and features quietly switched on inside software the company already bought. It changes every month. Most of it never gets attributed to a team, let alone a person. Plenty of companies cannot produce a full list of the AI tools their own employees use, which makes it difficult to determine how much they are spending on AI, what work that spending supports or how it compares with the cost of hiring.​

​The standard advice is to measure cost per unit of work and compare. Everyone tries this now, but it has limitations.

In sales, support and marketing, it is traceable. A resolved ticket. A processed claim. Those success metrics already exist and somebody already tracks them, so it is easier to map the cost against it and assess the impact.

Engineering, on the other hand, is harder to measure. It is also where much of the AI spend tends to go. Unlike a resolved support ticket or a processed claim, engineering output has no single, universally accepted unit of measurement. Lines of code, story points, commits and tickets closed can all offer some insight, but none captures the full value of the work. When these metrics become targets, they can also encourage activity that looks productive without necessarily improving the software.​

AI complicates this further by making it easier to generate code and complete discrete tasks without necessarily improving reliability, maintainability or business outcomes, leaving companies with a difficult measurement problem: engineering is a major area of AI investment, yet its impact is hard to isolate and quantify. Anyone claiming there is a simple, settled way to measure AI’s return in software development is either overlooking how much depends on the work being done, or they’re trying to sell you something.

When a team needs more capacity, it has two paths. One needs a headcount request, a finance review, a planning cycle and often a quarter of waiting. The other needs a card and 10 minutes.

Capacity flows toward the path of least resistance. That is not an anecdote about what AI can do, but more about how procurement works. A good share of the work shifting from people to AI is shifting because AI is easier to buy, not because anyone proved it was better at the job.

Sometimes it really is cheaper and better. When that holds, the shift is the right call. But a company substituting on friction rather than evidence has no way of knowing which case it is in. It finds out later, when quality slips or a bill arrives that nobody was able to accurately forecast.

I see this tension at my own company. When a team is small, even one hire represents a meaningful investment, and the choice between adding a person and expanding AI tooling becomes tangible. The challenge is that these options are evaluated differently, and only one of them comes with a number I trust.​

None of this gets better by arguing about whether AI replaces people. It gets better when the legitimate comparison becomes possible. ​

A useful starting point is an inventory of the AI tools running across the company, including those purchased outside formal procurement channels. Where possible, that inventory should connect usage to teams, users and business purposes, giving leaders a clearer picture of where the money goes and what work it supports. From there, they can begin evaluating what those tools actually deliver.​

Many organizations still lack that baseline, making it difficult to assess the value of their AI investments, let alone compare them with the cost of additional staff.​

Until AI spend becomes part of the same planning conversations as headcount, companies risk making labor decisions through procurement processes that were never designed to evaluate them. These decisions are already shaping how enterprise teams work and grow. The question is whether leaders have the visibility they need to understand the trade-offs.​​​

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

#3032. Why Sandisk Stock Dropped 24% in October

The market is worried about the end of the memory cycle.

Sandisk (SNDK -6.59%) stock lost 24% in October, according to data provided by S&P Global Market Intelligence. Although it reported another quarter of fantastic growth, the market is worried about a slowdown in the memory cycle.

Sandisk makes many of the products important for all kinds of technology, and it's one of the only makers of the NAND flash memory that's critical for artificial intelligence (AI) inference and reasoning. Product scarcity means that it can charge higher prices, and revenue growth has been through the roof.

In the fiscal 2027 first quarter (ended Oct. 2), revenue increased a whopping 378% year over year, and gross margin widened from 29.8% to 85.1%. Operating income increased from $176 million last year to $8.18 billion this year, and it generated $5.7 billion in adjusted free cash flow.

Sandisk makes many different products, but most of its growth is coming from its data center segment, where the AI is happening. Data center revenue increased 1,682% year over year, and the company is allocating more of its resources to meet demand.

Management is aiming to beat the memory cycle by locking in long-term revenue with its new business model (NBM) agreements. Historically, memory works in cycles, with clients procuring large amounts before technology changes and demand dries up. This is the height of the cycle, although management sees a large future market as data centers continue to require large amounts of memory to work.

Sandisk has already signed eight NBMs with partners it's choosing deliberately, and its agreements already stretch past 2030.

It also announced an eight-for-one stock split to occur on Nov. 19, to make the stock more accessible to investors and employees.

The market's reaction is pretty harsh for a company growing as fast as Sandisk. Either the fear is very real, or Sandisk is a great bargain. It's still up a stunning 352% year to date, and at the current price, it trades at less than nine times trailing 12-month earnings, which is incredibly cheap.

I think the market is overreacting here. Sandisk has a broad business that meets today's current AI needs, and so far, it's not slowing down. Beyond that, it also works with all kinds of tech partners and has a future beyond data centers. At the current price, Sandisk stock looks undervalued.

#3031. Upstart Beats Expectations in a Challenging Macro Environment. What It Means for Investors

Upstart stock fluctuated after results were released. Here's what the latest quarter means.

Shares of Upstart Holdings (UPST -7.43%)were fluctuating in premarket trading after the AI-based loan originator beat expectations on the top and bottom lines in its third-quarter earnings report.

Upstart reported revenue growth of 34% to $370.5 million, ahead of the consensus at $363.7 million. Loan originations were up 44% year-over-year to $4.1 billion, though they declined sequentially, hinting at the macroeconomic headwinds facing the company. For Q3, loans originated rose 34% to 574,089.

On the bottom line, contribution profit, the metric the company is most focused on, rose 48% to $218 million, reaching an all-time high. Contribution profit is essentially revenue from fees minus direct borrower acquisition and servicing costs, and gives a sense of the core profitability of the business before indirect expenses.

Generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) earnings per share was $0.33, up from $0.23 in the quarter a year ago and beating estimates at $0.23.

Upstart's guidance was mixed as it raised its full-year guidance for revenue from fees from $1.3 billion to $1.32 billion, though it cut adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) from around $294 million to $260 million, reflecting the weakening macro environment and lower profits on non-core parts of the business, such as loans it holds on the balance sheet.

Upstart has struggled over the years to clearly communicate to investors what the business does and what the risks are, but the underlying operations have improved significantly in the last few years, as demonstrated by the record contribution profit. The company can't control the aggregate demand for loans, nor can it control interest rates. However, it's executing in the areas it does control, continuing to gain share of overall loan originations, and driving contribution margin higher.

Importantly, the company also recorded its first quarter of positive contribution margin in its secured loan business, which includes auto and home loans. That represents a massive, fast-growing market for Upstart. Secured originations jumped 194% to $587 million, with 3x growth in the auto market and 2x growth in the home market.

Originations in the secured market were flat sequentially, reflecting some of the macro challenges, but reaching a positive contribution profit in the segment is a major milestone and occurred one quarter ahead of the company's goal.

Overall, Upstart is holding to its guidance to deliver compound annual revenue growth of 35% through 2028, and the improvement in profitability is a good sign for the long-term health of the business.

While the macro climate may put pressure on the business in the coming quarters, Upstart is demonstrating it can operate effectively in any environment. With the stock hovering at two-year lows, it offers a lot of upside potential from here if it can continue to grow contribution profit.

Jeremy Bowman has positions in Upstart. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Upstart. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3027. Here's My Top Stock to Buy for November

The company has disappointed with its execution in recent years, but it looks like management's updated guidance has reset expectations such that the stock has significant upside potential.

Enter Boeing (BA +2.24%) stock in a beauty contest, and it wouldn't get many votes. But long-term investing isn't a beauty pageant; it's about finding good value stocks with plenty of upside potential. Boeing is a winner in that regard, even though its recent update might have been disappointing for some. Here's why its worth a closer look.

The manufacturing giant operates out of three segments, and the takeaways from the recent third-quarter earnings are that its global services (BGS) business continues to generate solid earnings to support the other two larger businesses, namely Boeing Defense, Space & Security (BDS) and Boeing Commercial Airplanes (BCA).

BDS has returned to profitability as it continues to work through problematic fixed-price development programs that have caused significant charges and losses in recent years. The update from Boeing's most important business, BCA, was disappointing. Specifically, the pushback in expectations for a ramp-up in 737 MAX production. Still, I think management has reset expectations low enough now that there's plenty of opportunity for Boeing.

Investors have been able to point to the massive backlogs at the company (currently $745 billion) and at BCA ($612 billion, including more than 6,300 planes), and, to a lesser extent, at BDS, for years. Still, the reality is that the company has had issues executing on them. However, there are real signs of progress here.

Starting at BDS, management has previously maintained that its issues stem from a few problematic fixed-price development programs (including Air Force One and the KC-46 Tanker) that represent only 15% of its sales, with the rest of BDS generating profit. It's taken time, but Boeing is working through key milestones on these programs. In July, CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors the KC-46 program "feels very low risk" now that "we're getting to the end of the production, the fixed-price production that we have," with repricing to follow.

Moreover, Ortberg recently raised expectations for BDS growth from low-single-digit annual growth to "middle-single-digit or higher." Ortberg also believes BDS is booking better orders than the problematic ones noted above, as evidence of an improving environment between government and defense companies. I would strongly recommend reviewing the provisions in Lockheed Martin's (LMT +0.97%) recent agreements with the DOD.

The game plan here is simple: Ramp up production of the narrow-body 737 MAX, and, less importantly, the wide-body 787 Dreamliner. Meanwhile, BCA is aiming for the new wide-body 777X, with certification in 2027 and first delivery to follow.

All three are crucial for free-cash-flow generation, as more deliveries mean more revenue and usually margin expansion as more units are spread around Boeing's fixed costs. Meanwhile, any delay in the first delivery of the 777X simply increases cash burn on the program.

Unfortunately, management pushed back expectations for 737 MAX deliveries, telling investors that it would now take until 2027 to stabilize the production rate at 47 a month before targeting "52 in the back half of 2027."

As a reminder, BCA started 2026 with a stabilized rate of 42 a month on the 737 MAX, and expected to hit a rate of 47 a month by the summer. Naturally, this kind of pushout of expectations also led to a pushout of the market's penciled-in free cash flow (FCF) for Boeing. Here's management's FCF guidance on the recent call:

Data source: Boeing presentations, author's analysis. *Based on current market cap.

However, based on management's commentary, this guidance may prove conservative. For example, CFO Jesus Malave said the "building blocks of a $10 billion free cash flow on a normalized basis" are:

The 2029 conditions significantly exceed what's required for the "building blocks" of $10 billion in FCF, and note that management is guiding toward a production rate of 52 a month on the 737 MAX in the second half of 2027.

In other words, the main condition (737 MAX) for $10 billion in FCF will be satisfied in terms of production (deliveries will follow) by the end of 2027, and management has set a target of increasing production from 52 per month in 2027 to the "mid to high 50s" in 2029. This may prove conservative.

Putting it all together, BGS is solid, BDS has returned to profitability, and there's evidence that the Department of Defense is being more accommodating in its contracts with defense companies. Finally, BCA guidance may prove conservative, and if the building blocks for $10 billion in FCF are met in 2027, the market won't waste any time pricing it in. As such, the stock is attractive for value-oriented investors.

#3024. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#3023. Apple results put spotlight on ETFs with the biggest exposure to the stock

#3010. Knicks 103, Nets 90: Scenes from ShamWow, Clarkson, and Kolek sparking life into a dead game

The Brooklyn Nets came into Madison Square Garden looking up from the bottom of the conference with a 1–5 record. They're the league's youngest team, and it shows on the court. And they'd played yesterday in Indiana. Their game against the Knicks (3–4) was either going to be a gimme or a trap. For much of the night, it smelled like the latter.

The home team decided to hurl a ton of three-pointers (44 of their 75 shots came from deep), sleepwalk through three quarters, and let Landry Shamet carry them for much of the night. Meanwhile, Brooklyn got inspired play from rookie Mikel Brown Jr. and won the third quarter 35–24 to take a four-point lead into the fourth. In the final frame, the Knicks came alive (with a special appearances by Tyler Kolek and Jordan Clarkson), outscored the visitors 28–11, and pulled out a 103–90 win.

In the first quarter, the Nets took a four-point lead, which the Knicks deleted and flipped into a nine-point advantage. So far this season, OG Anunoby (18 PTS, 3-7 3PT, 2 STL, 38 MIN) has been up and down, and perhaps Mike Brown was hoping to inject some excitement into his wing by calling his number early. Anunoby attempted two three-pointers (making one) and converted a cutting layup (dimed by Karl-Anthony Towns) to get New York on the scoreboard.

The game featured a fair amount of jostling, but the refs let it go. Midway through the frame, Landry Shamet (22 PTS, 6-8 FG, 29 MIN), Andre Drummond (9 RBS, 4 PTS, 13 MIN), and Miles McBride (6 PTS, 16 MIN) subbed in. Jalen Brunson (19 PTS, 4-11 3PT, 6 AST, 33 MIN) made three of his first four attempts from the yard before Jose Alvarado (back from a sprained ankle) relieved him at the three-minute mark. Cap and Deuce combined for five treys in the first.

Brooklyn shot so poorly that the rims seemed magnetically opposed to their attempts. Twice or thrice, the ball rolled around the cylinder before flying off to become a defensive rebound. Julius Randle (21 PTS, 10 RBS) and Michael Porter, Jr. (18 PTS, 4-11 3PT) are Brooklyn's marquee players, but neither did much in the first frame. The former missed all three of his shot attempts, and the latter scored five points on five attempts. On the whole, the Nets missed 13 shots and turned the ball over four times. At the break, they trailed New York, 27–21.

Mercury is in retrograde, and the second quarter proved it with a few rarities. Mikal Bridges (6 PTS, 1-of-7 FG, 16 MIN) attempted his first free throws, six whole games into the campaign. Towns (11 PTS, 16 RBS) played 13 minutes before taking his second shot, but grabbed his tenth rebound of the night with six minutes left in the half. And Mohamed "Free Mo" Diawara (0 PTS, 6 MIN) appeared after playing just one minute so far this season. The sophomore grabbed a rebound.

While the Nets don't excel at any conventional basketball skills, they do have teeth. Brooklyn played yesterday (beating the Hoosiers of Indiana), but your lyin' eyes would convince you that New York had the more fatigued fellas. Even the Garden crowd seemed mid-yawn for most of the second period. This borough buddy has a rotten record, but they took Boston into overtime this season, and the Knicks watched them score nine unanswered points early in the frame. A late-quarter bomb from Brunson steadied the boat but failed to ignite the team. Only when the half had nearly closed did Josh Hart (8 PTS, 7 AST, 6 RBS, +22) and Shamet—14 flippin points and counting!—connect from deep to give New York an eight-point lead. Then, after Randle made two free throws, he fouled Brunson on a foot-on-the-line jumper with 0.5 seconds left. Oh, Julius, I remember ye well. Intermission score: 51–44.

Rookie Mikel Brown, Jr. was having quite a MSG debut:

The score was a lot closer than the game felt. Our heroes had been outshot 40% to 36% from the field. They'd survived on threes and free throws while barely making any hay inside the arc. Ten of their 13 buckets came from downtown (shooting 40% there), and they'd taken 16 freebies to Brooklyn's six. Rebounds and turnovers were even at 21 and seven, respectively. Shamet led all first-half scorers with 14 points, while Nolan Traore had 11 for the villains. No points for KAT yet, and don't look now, but Bridges was having another bad shooting night.

The third quarter brought more of the same. Bridges missed again (1-of-7 thus far), but he wasn't alone. Brunson missed a long shot, and Day'Ron Sharpe and Traore blocked Towns and Brunson, respectively. With the offense a pasty, anemic color, Mike Brown sent in Jordan Clarkson (7 PTS, 11 MIN, +17) at around the 8:45 mark. Clarkson guarded Porter tenaciously and made a contested shot despite being hacked (no whistle), but he got dinged for two quick personal fouls and picked up a tech for complaining about that absent whistle. It's a bummer, because the fouls got him a quick hook just when some of us were starting to wonder if he, Shamet, or Towns might resurrect this lifeless game.

Meanwhile, Towns was taking the ball straight down the painted boulevard on repeated drives. He collected his first nine points of the night, going 3-of-4 from the field and 2-of-3 at the line. After two driving layups, he buried a three off Brunson's dime at 5:58. During that stretch, Cap added five points on two buckets and a free throw, but missed a three and had a layup blocked.

(For those watching the third quarter at home, Clyde dropped a "Posting and Toasting" at the 7:42 mark AND at 6:30. We hear you, GOAT!)

Mikel Brown scored on consecutive drives down Broadway, and a flummoxed Mike Brown called an exasperated timeout around 4:30. Those hoops cut Brooklyn's deficit to five. Porter hit from deep after the timeout to make it two, and Mo Wagner swished a triple for a one-point lead. When Porter dropped another bomb, that made 13 straight points for the bad guys. Whatever Mike said in the timeout didn't motivate.

Diawara was back in the game, but Shamet was the one whose three-pointer gave us some hope for salvation (which the misses by Drummond and Brunson that bookended his shot did not). Another bomb by Shamet on an inbounds play gave him a season high and narrowed the gap with a minute left. But Randle made shots at the stripe, Anunoby and Brunson were both blocked on drives, and Brooklyn's 19–6 run gave them a 79–75 lead at the break.

Needing a spark, it was another bench player to the rescue. Tyler Kolek checked in to start the fourth quarter and hit the ground running. He dished to Hart for a triple, then Hart found a trailing Anunoby for another bomb, and the game took a more favorable turn. The crowd rejoiced when OG swished another three, and although Randle bucketed on a drive, Hart returned the favor to Kolek by finding him wide-open under the rim.

Brooklyn's coach Jordi Fernández needed a timeout to get his young troops back in line. Out of the break, Randle coughed up the ball twice and Hart made good on a fast-break layup. When Clarkson hit from the corner, he capped a 16-2 run and goosed the lead to 10. Randle blew a layup and Fernández yanked him with seven minutes left, and Mike Brown swapped Kolek for Brunson. The Nets had scored just five points by the five-minute mark, and New York had stretched their advantage to 12.

The Knicks' energized defense had forced six turnovers (and counting), while Bridges continued to sit after getting pulled with 8:44 left in the third quarter. With three minutes left, Mike Brown sent in all his starters—except Bridges, electing instead to ride with Shamet. Fernandez kept his starters in, too, but the outcome was decided. The home team had won the frame 28-11 and that was the ballgame.

Chicago will visit on Wednesday, hoping to avenge last week's loss to New York. Mo's got a recap in the chamber for you. Rest up, Knickerbockers.

#3005. Texas governor race tightens in prediction markets, but Abbott remains favored

Political observers are watching the Texas gubernatorial election for signs of an artificial intelligence data center backlash in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, and prediction market traders see growing odds of the Democratic candidate pulling off an upset.

Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican seeking a fourth term, has a 60% chance of beating Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa on Tuesday, according to speculators on platform Kalshi.

Hinojosa's odds to win have jumped from 8% in mid-July to 40% on Monday, with many of those gains coming in recent weeks as a series of polls have shown the race to be tightening. On Polymarket, Hinojosa has seen her odds jump from as low as 5% in late July to 39% on Monday.

Contracts are resolved using data from the Texas Secretary of State's office.

Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.

Hinojosa is seeking to be the first Democratic governor in Texas in more than 30 years. She has used Abbott's previous support for data center development in the state as an attack against the incumbent.

In November 2025, Abbott touted a $40 billion investment by Google — which included bringing three new data center campuses to the state — by saying that Texas will be the "epicenter of AI development." But Abbott has changed his tune as voters' opinion of data centers has soured over the past year.

Abbott in August ordered an audit of data centers that sought to connect to the state's grid, and then in September he halted the approval of all data center-related permits until an audit of the existing waitlist is conducted.

Hinojosa is running on an immediate data center moratorium until the legislature puts guardrails on the industry, according to her campaign website.

In-person early voting in Texas concluded on Friday, and more than 7.7 million Texans have already cast their ballots.

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

#3004. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander drops season-high 43 points including dagger 3 to lead hobbled Thunder past Cavs

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander had a poor shooting night and played without several of his top teammates Monday.

It did not matter. The two-time MVP scored a season-high 43 points including a late go-ahead 3 that iced a 117-112 win over the Cleveland Cavaliers. The win snapped a two-game losing streak as the Thunder continue to adjust to playing without several of their best players.

Starters Jalen Williams, Chet Holmgren and Cason Wallace are all sidelined with long-term injuries. The Thunder also played Monday without Alex Caruso, who's nursing a sprained right ankle.

OKC still had Gilgeous-Alexander, and that was a enough alongside a makeshift starting lineup for victory over the Eastern Conference hopeful Cavaliers. Gilgeous-Alexander shot just 40% from the field. But he hit the shots when they mattered most, most notably a late 3 that gave the Thunder the lead for good.

With the game tied at 112-112 in the final minute, Gilgeous-Alexander gained just enough separation from his defender, Sam Merrill, to pull up for a 3 from the left wing. The shot sank through the net for a 3-point Thunder lead with 32.6 seconds remaining.

The Cavaliers didn't score again, and the Thunder secured the win to improve to 5-2.

After the game, Gilgeous-Alexander spoke with NBC about the Thunder adjusting in the face of injury adversity after entering the season on the short list of favorites to compete for an NBA title.

"Just figuring it out," Gilgeous-Alexander said. "You never know what the future has in store for you. All you can do is play the cards you're dealt."

Gilgeous-Alexander tallied 43 points, 8 assists, 3 rebounds and 2 steals. He shot 14 of 35 from the field, 11 of 12 from the line and 4 of 8 from 3.

The 35 shots tied a career high and could be indicative of things to come with Williams and Holmgren sidelined. The All-Star tandem have been OKC's second- and third-leading scorers behind Gilgeous-Alexander for the past three seasons.

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander put up a career-high 35 field goal attempts in what could be a sign of things to come for Oklahoma City.

Instead, it was Ajay Mitchell, Jaylin Williams and Kenrich Williams who joined Gilgeous-Alexander and Isaiah Hartenstein in the starting lineup Monday night. Mitchell finished second on the Thunder in scoring with 20 points and five rebounds, while Kenrich Williams add 12 points on 5-of-7 shooting.

It's OKC's trademark smothering defense that could suffer the most through injuries. Williams, Wallace, Holmgren and Caruso have all earned All-Defensive team selections in their careers and can't be replaced. The result Monday night was just seven turnovers committed by the Cavaliers.

But none of Cleveland's offensive stars broke out. Donovan Mitchell tied for the team lead with 17 points alongside 11 assists and five rebounds. Instead, it was a balanced team effort with seven players in double figures that kept the game close. A 58% (14 of 24) effort from the free-throw line ultimately doomed the Cavaliers.

The two teams will play each other again Wednesday night as they complete their season series in Oklahoma City and the Thunder continue to learn to play with a new-look lineup.

#3001. Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.

The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.

Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.

In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.

For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.

John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.

"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.

Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.

Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.

Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.

Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.
